의사.nuance: 의사 is Sino-Korean 醫師 ('medicine' 醫 + 'master/teacher' 師), so the word literally frames a doctor as a master of medicine — which is why Koreans almost reflexively append 선생님 (의사 선생님) when addressing or referring to one, the way English keeps 'Doctor' as a title. Saying bare 의사 to or about a specific physician can sound flat or even slightly disrespectful, like calling them 'the doc'. Distinguish 의사 (the licensed physician) from 의자 'chair', which differs by a single vowel and trips up beginners constantly, and from 환자 'patient' and 간호사 'nurse', the other people in the room. The natural verb is 환자를 보다 ('see patients') or 진료를 보다/받다, never the English-style '의사를 하다'; a doctor 의사가 되다 ('becomes' a doctor), with the goal marked by 가, not 을.
의사.explanation: 의사 (uisa) means "doctor". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 의사 선생님 ("doctor (polite address)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 의사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.
의사.shortExplanation: 의사 means "doctor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 의사님 by analogy with other -님 titles; Koreans actually say 의사 선생님, treating 선생님 itself as the honorific.
Writing 의사를 되고 싶어요 with 를; the thing you become takes 가/이, so it must be 의사가 되고 싶어요.
Confusing 의사 'doctor' with the near-identical 의자 'chair' — one wrong vowel changes the whole sentence.

받다 'receive' is the verb that pairs with 진료, not 하다
goal/result takes 가/이, never 을/를

회사원.nuance: 회사원 is 會社員 ('company-member'), literally a member of a company, and it is the neutral catch-all a salaried employee of a private firm gives when asked 무슨 일 하세요? Contrast it with 직장인, which means 'a working person' in general (anyone with a paid job, including teachers or nurses): every 회사원 is a 직장인, but not every 직장인 is a 회사원. Also separate it from 사업가, the owner who runs the business — a 회사원 is employed by someone else. The pitfall for English speakers is twofold: 회사원 ends in a consonant so the copula is 회사원이에요, never 'office worker'-style 회사원예요; and don't translate 'I work at a company' as a job title — to name the job you simply say 회사원이에요 rather than literally rendering the English sentence.
회사원.explanation: "office worker" is 회사원 (hoesawon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 저는 회사원이에요. ("I am an office worker."). Watch the particle attached to 회사원 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.
회사원.shortExplanation: 회사원 means "office worker" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 회사원예요 — wrong, because 원 ends in a consonant you must use 이에요: 회사원이에요.
Using 회사원 for a self-employed shop owner — that person is 자영업자 or 사장님; 회사원 is specifically a salaried employee of someone else's company.
Calling any working adult 회사원 — a nurse or teacher is a 직장인 but not a 회사원; 회사원 implies a typical office/company job.

도서관.nuance: 도서관 is Sino-Korean 圖書館, literally 'pictures-books-building' (圖 picture + 書 writing/book + 館 hall), a public place to read, study, and borrow books where quiet is expected. The sharp contrast learners must hold is 도서관 vs 서점: a 도서관 is a LIBRARY where you borrow (빌리다) for free, while a 서점 is a BOOKSTORE where you buy (사다) — English 'library' and Spanish/French false friends like 'librería' push learners to mix these up. Note also 도서관 (the building) vs 도서 (books as items/collection). Register is neutral. Natural collocations: 도서관에서 공부하다, 책을 빌리다/반납하다, 도서관에 자리가 없다. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the library/bookstore mix-up, is the particle split: study or read AT a library is 에서 (도서관에서), but going TO it is 에 (도서관에 가다).
도서관.explanation: 도서관 (doseogwan) = "library". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 조용한 도서관 ("quiet library") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 도서관, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about getting around, reservations, directions, photos, and emergency help and swap just one element to make it yours.
도서관.shortExplanation: 도서관 means "library" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 도서관 when you mean a place that sells books. A bookstore is a 서점; 도서관 is strictly for borrowing, not buying.
Saying 도서관에서 가요 for 'I go to the library.' Motion verb 가다 needs 에 (도서관에 가요); use 에서 only for studying/reading done there.
Pairing 도서관 with 사다 (buy) for the books inside. At a 도서관 you 빌리다 (borrow) and 반납하다 (return), you do not 사다.

usagePhrases.note: 조용한 is the modifier form of 조용하다
에 marks the destination of 가다
에서 marks where the studying happens
빌리다 = borrow; the verb that pairs with 도서관

아침.nuance: 아침 is a native Korean word that does double duty: the early part of the day (roughly sunrise to mid-morning) and the breakfast meal — the same way English 'morning' differs from the meal but Korean merges the breakfast sense into the time word. The grammar disambiguates: with 에 (아침에) it's the time, with 을 (아침을 먹다) it's the food. Contrast 아침 vs 오전: 아침 is the felt, lived early morning, while 오전 午前 is the neutral clock-AM you put on timetables — so 아침에 일어나요 (waking life) but 오전 9시 회의 (a scheduled item). Habitual partners: 아침에 일어나다/운동하다, 아침을 먹다/거르다 ('skip breakfast'), 아침 일찍, 매일 아침. The big English-speaker pitfall is using 오전 for the breakfast meal — 오전 is only the clock period and can never name food, so 'eat breakfast' must be 아침을 먹다, never 오전을 먹다. Also don't force 에 onto the meal sense: you eat 아침을, you don't 'eat at morning'.
아침.explanation: 아침 (achim) = "morning; also breakfast". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아침에 ("in the morning") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아침, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
아침.shortExplanation: 아침 means "morning; also breakfast" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 오전을 먹어요 for 'eat breakfast' — 오전 is only the clock-AM span; the meal is 아침, so it must be 아침을 먹어요.
Marking the breakfast meal with 에 (아침에 먹어요 meaning the food) — as a meal-object it needs 을: 아침을 먹어요. 아침에 먹어요 only means 'eat (something) in the morning'.
Assuming 아침 always equals clock-morning like 오전 — on schedules and tickets Koreans switch to 오전 9시; 아침 is the lived, informal morning.

usagePhrases.note: time + 에 for the time-when reading
here 아침 is the meal, so it takes object 을
매일 + 아침 = habitual time phrase
아침 + adverb 일찍, a set collocation

병원.explanation: "hospital / clinic" is 병원 (byeongwon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 병원에 가요 ("I go to the hospital/clinic."). 할인.nuance: 할인(割引) is Sino-Korean — 割 'cut' + 引 'pull (down)' — literally 'cut and pull down', i.e. knock money off a price. The key contrast for learners is 할인 vs 세일: 할인 is the abstract act/amount of reducing a price on an item ('10% off', a discount), while 세일 (from English 'sale') names a store-wide selling event (백화점 세일 a department-store sale). So a 세일 contains many 할인s. Watch the voice carefully: from the price's point of view you say 할인이 되다/할인되다 ('it gets discounted'); from your point of view as buyer you say 할인을 받다 ('I receive a discount'); and to actively ask for one you say 할인해 주세요 ('please discount it for me'). The English-speaker pitfall is firing 할인해요 at a clerk hoping it means 'give me a discount' — bare 할인해요 just states 'someone discounts', so it lands as a flat description, not a request. Add 주세요/돼요 to make it work. Common partners: 할인되다, 할인받다, 할인 행사 (discount event), 할인 쿠폰.
할인.explanation: "discount" is 할인 (harin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 할인이 돼요 ("a discount applies"). Watch the particle attached to 할인 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.
할인.shortExplanation: 할인 means "discount" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 할인해요 to a clerk to mean 'please give me a discount'. Without 주세요 it is just a statement; the request form is 할인해 주세요 or the softer 좀 깎아 주세요.
Mixing up the receiver: customers say 할인을 받다 (receive a discount), shops say 할인을 해 주다 (give a discount). Saying 할인을 줘요 about yourself ('I give a discount') reverses the roles.
Using 세일 when you mean a discount on one item. 'This bag is 30% off' is 이 가방은 30퍼센트 할인이에요, not 세일이에요 — 세일 is the whole event, not the single markdown.

의견.nuance: 의견 is Sino-Korean (意見, 意 'mind/intention' + 見 'view/seeing'), literally 'how your mind sees something' — a considered position or judgment you can defend, usually about a topic, plan, or issue. The crucial contrast is with 생각: 생각 is the broad word for any 'thought' that crosses your mind, while 의견 is specifically a stance offered for discussion or evaluation, so a meeting asks for 의견 (positions), not just 생각 (musings). It is register-neutral and very common in school and workplace settings; the polite request 의견을 여쭤봐도 될까요? raises it a notch. Natural collocations: 의견을 말하다/내다/제시하다 (state/put forward), 의견이 다르다/같다 (disagree/agree), 의견을 모으다 (gather opinions), 반대 의견 (an opposing view). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 의견 every time you'd say 'I think' — 'I think it's good' is 좋은 것 같아요 or 좋다고 생각해요, NOT 좋은 의견이에요; 의견 is the opinion itself as a thing, not the act of thinking. Also don't say 의견하다 — there is no such verb; you 의견을 말하다.
의견.explanation: "opinion" is 의견 (uigyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 의견을 말하다 ("to state an opinion"). Watch the particle attached to 의견 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
의견.shortExplanation: 의견 means "opinion" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 의견하다 to mean 'to opine' — 의견 is a noun with no verb form; use 의견을 말하다 / 의견을 내다.
Using 의견 where English 'I think...' just hedges — 'I think it'll rain' is 비가 올 것 같아요, not an 의견; 의견 is a stance offered for discussion.
Confusing 의견 with 생각 — 생각 is any thought; 의견 is a position on a topic, so a survey or meeting collects 의견, while daydreaming is 생각.

usagePhrases.note: 의견 + 을 with 말하다, the default verb for voicing a view
의견 + 이 with 다르다, the set way to say 'we disagree'
의견 + 을 with 듣다, asking for input

작년.nuance: 작년 is Sino-Korean 昨年 ('past/previous' 昨, the same 昨 in 작일 'yesterday' + 'year' 年), so it literally means 'the previous year'. Crucially, unlike 올해, it normally DOES take 에 when used as a time point: 작년에 만났어요 (we met last year). It is the everyday word; the synonym 지난해 ('the year that passed') is a touch more formal and common in news writing, while 작년 dominates conversation. It completes the set 작년 – 올해 – 내년. Watch two English-speaker pitfalls. First, mirroring 올해's no-particle habit and dropping 에 — for past-time 작년, 에 is the natural marker. Second, the look-alike 작년/어제: both involve 'past', but 작년 is a whole year back and 어제 is just yesterday, so 'I arrived last year' is 작년에, never 어제.
작년.explanation: "last year" is 작년 (jangnyeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 작년 ("last year"). Watch the particle attached to 작년 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
작년.shortExplanation: 작년 means "last year" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Dropping 에 in time-point sentences — say 작년에 갔어요; bare 작년 갔어요 sounds incomplete here, unlike 올해.
Confusing 작년 (last year) with 어제 (yesterday) — both feel 'past', but one is a year and one is a day.
Using 작년 for 'the past few years' — that is 지난 몇 년; 작년 is strictly the one year before this.

examples.note: 작년 takes 에 — unlike 올해, which drops it

examples.note: 작년 + season = a specific past season

examples.en: I've been learning Korean since last year.
examples.note: 부터 marks the start of an ongoing action

ex.en: It is so cold today.

춥다.nuance: 춥다 is the ㅂ-irregular adjective for ambient air being unpleasantly cold — winter, a chilly room, a draft. The crucial contrast for English speakers is 춥다 vs 차갑다: 춥다 is how the WEATHER/AIR feels to your whole body, while 차갑다 is how a cold OBJECT feels to your hand (차가운 물 'cold water', 차가운 손 'cold hands'). Never say 추운 물 — water is 차갑다. As a ㅂ-irregular it conjugates 춥다 → 추워요 → 추운 → 추우니까 → 추워서, so writing 춥어요 or 춥은 (the regular pattern) is the classic beginner slip. It is register-neutral and universal. The matching noun is 추위, and 추위를 타다 means 'to be cold-sensitive,' the exact mirror of 더위를 타다.
춥다.explanation: "cold (weather)" is 춥다 (chupda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 날씨가 춥다 ("the weather is cold"). Watch the particle attached to 춥다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
춥다.shortExplanation: 춥다 means "cold (weather)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 춥어요 or 춥은 겨울 — because 춥다 is ㅂ-irregular the forms are 추워요 and 추운 겨울.
Saying 추운 물 or 추운 손 for cold water or cold hands. A cold thing you touch is 차갑다 → 차가운 물, 차가운 손.
Confusing 춥다 with 차갑다 in feelings: a cold-hearted person is 차갑다 (차가운 사람), never 추운 사람.

usagePhrases.note: the default collocation, exactly mirroring 날씨가 덥다 for heat
modifier form is 추운, never 춥은; the ㅂ becomes 우
the noun 추위 ('the cold') derives from 춥다, like 더위 from 덥다

usagePhrases.en: cold enough to sting your hands
usagePhrases.note: 시리다 ('to sting from cold') pairs with bitter winter weather

examples.en: It is cold today.
examples.note: bare polite form; 춥다 → 추워요, never 춥어요

examples.en: Cold winter has come.
examples.note: 추운 modifies 겨울 in the noun-modifier shape

examples.ko: 창문이 열려 있어서 방이 너무 추워요.
examples.romanization: changmuni yeollyeo isseoseo bangi neomu chuwoyo.
examples.en: The room is too cold because the window is open.
examples.note: real-situation -아서 reason clause

ex.en: Since it is the weekend, let's study even if just for one hour.
ex.note: Time noun that naturally supports 니까 and 라도 practice.

주말.nuance: 주말 is Sino-Korean, 週末 — 週 'week' + 末 'end', literally 'week-end', and its opposites are 평일 平日 'weekday' and 주중 週中 'midweek'. It refers to Saturday and Sunday as a block. The contrast worth noting is 주말 vs 휴일: 주말 is specifically the weekend, while 휴일 休日 is any day off including public holidays — so a Wednesday holiday is a 휴일 but not a 주말. Habitual partners: 주말에 쉬다/놀다, 이번/지난/다음 주말, 주말마다, 즐거운 주말, and the farewell 주말 잘 보내세요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: learners borrow 'at/on' loosely and write 주말에서, but 에서 marks a LOCATION or a source ('from'); the time-when always takes 에 → 주말에. A second subtlety: for 'this weekend' use 이번 주말 (이번 = the current instance), not 오늘 주말; and 다음 주말 'next weekend' vs 다음 주 주말 can differ, so keep 다음 주말 for the upcoming Sat–Sun.
주말.explanation: "weekend" is 주말 (jumal). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 주말에 ("on the weekend"). Watch the particle attached to 주말 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
주말.shortExplanation: 주말 means "weekend" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 주말에서 for 'on the weekend' — 에서 is for place/source; the time-when is 주말에.
Saying 오늘 주말 for 'this weekend' — use 이번 주말 (이번 marks the current weekend); 오늘 주말 mixes 'today' with 'weekend'.
Treating any day off as 주말 — a midweek public holiday is a 휴일, not a 주말 (which is strictly Sat–Sun).

usagePhrases.note: time + 에 (not 에서) for the time-when
이번 'this (current)' + 주말
주말 + 마다 'each weekend'
fixed Friday farewell

examples.en: I usually rest on the weekend.
examples.note: basic: 주말에 marks the time-when

examples.en: What are you doing this weekend?
examples.note: everyday: 이번 주말 + 에 + casual plan question

examples.en: Have a good weekend!
examples.note: real-situation: set parting phrase coworkers say on Friday

ex.en: Try asking at least one question.
ex.note: A small action that fits the minimum-option meaning of 라도.

질문.nuance: 질문 is Sino-Korean 質問 — 質 'substance/inquire into' + 問 'ask', literally 'to inquire and ask', i.e. a question put to someone. The set verb is 질문을 하다 (or the single verb 질문하다); the person you ask takes 에게/한테 (or honorific 께 for a teacher): 선생님께 질문을 하다. Its natural partner is 대답/답(答) — a 질문 is answered by a 대답. The big redundancy trap for English speakers is 질문을 물어보다 ✗: 물어보다 already means 'to ask', so this literally says 'ask a question-asking' — say either 질문을 하다 or just 물어보다, never both. Distinguish 질문 (a question seeking information/an answer) from 문제(問題, a 'problem' or exam item) — '3 questions on the test' are 문제 세 개, but 'I have a question for you' is 질문이 있어요. Note answering takes 에: 질문에 답하다, not 질문을 답하다.
질문.explanation: 질문 (jilmun) means "question". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 질문을 하다 ("ask a question"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 질문 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.
질문.shortExplanation: 질문 means "question" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 질문을 물어보다 ✗ — 물어보다 already means 'ask', so it doubles up. Use 질문을 하다 OR 물어보다, not both.
Using 를 to answer: 질문을 답하다 ✗. 답하다 takes 에: 질문에 답하다 / 질문에 대답하다.
Using 질문 for an exam item. A test question/problem is 문제; 질문 is a question you ask a person for an answer.

usagePhrases.note: Set verb is 하다; 질문하다 is one word too
Existence; the question is the subject, so 이
답하다 takes 에 for the question being answered
받다 = receive; what a speaker does at Q&A

examples.en: Any questions?
examples.note: Standard classroom check; 있어요 = exist/have

examples.en: I asked the teacher a question.
examples.note: 께 = honorific 'to' (for a teacher); 질문을 하다 = ask

examples.en: Good question. Let's think about it together.
examples.note: 좋은 질문 is a fixed compliment; -아 보다 = 'try ~ing'

ex.en: Where do I transfer if I want to get to Seoul Station?
ex.note: Official transit noun; 갈아타다 is the everyday action verb.

환승.nuance: 환승 means transferring between buses and subways. If you tap the same transit card, transfers within a time limit are usually discounted or free.
환승.explanation: 환승 (hwanseung) = "transfer (transit)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 어디서 환승해요? ("Where do I transfer?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 환승, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
환승.shortExplanation: 환승 means "transfer (transit)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Tap your card when getting off too, or you may lose the 환승 transfer discount.

usagePhrases.note: Question.
Obligation.
Cost.
Place.

examples.en: I transfer at City Hall Station.
examples.note: Place.

examples.en: I transferred from bus to subway.
examples.note: Route.

examples.en: It is cheaper if you transfer with one card.
examples.note: Condition.

ex.en: Transfer to Line 1 at City Hall Station.

갈아타다.nuance: 갈아타다 is a transparent compound of 갈다 'to change/replace' + 타다 'to ride', so it literally means 'change-ride' — you get off one vehicle and board a different one. The dividing line learners must feel is against plain 타다 (just 'to board/get on') and against 환승하다, the Sino-Korean twin (換乘, 換 'exchange' + 乘 'ride', literally 'change-ride') printed on every subway sign and announcement: 갈아타다 is the warm spoken word a friend uses ('여기서 갈아타'), while 환승하다 is the signage/official register ('환승 게이트'). The grammar trap is the particle: the vehicle you move TO takes 로/으로 (지하철로 갈아타다), the same directional 로 as 'change INTO', and the station where you do it takes 에서 — English 'transfer to the subway' tempts you to drop the particle or use 에. Because 타다 is regular, every form is regular too: the stem 타- already ends in ㅏ, so the 아 of 아요 merges in and disappears, giving 갈아타요 (not 갈아타아요), and the past is 갈아탔어요. Habitual collocations: 다른 노선으로 갈아타다, 같은 방향으로 갈아타다.
갈아타다.explanation: 갈아타다 (garata-da) = "to transfer". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 갈아타요 plus one useful sentence like 지하철로 갈아타다 ("to transfer to the subway"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 갈아타고 싶어요 for what you want, 갈아탈 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 갈아타요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off.
갈아타다.shortExplanation: 갈아타다 means "to transfer" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 갈아타다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 갈아타요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 지하철에 갈아타요 with 에. The destination vehicle is the thing you change INTO, so it needs directional 로/으로: 지하철로 갈아타요.
Using 타다 when you mean 'transfer': 버스를 타요 only means 'I board a bus', not 'I switch from another vehicle to the bus'. To express the switch you must use 갈아타다: 버스로 갈아타요.
Writing the polite form as 갈아타아요. 타다 already ends in ㅏ, so the 아 of 아요 merges and disappears — the correct form is 갈아타요.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 갈아타다 becomes 갈아탈 수 있어요 ("can") and 갈아탈 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
The new vehicle takes 로/으로, never 에서

examples.en: I transfer to the bus.
examples.note: Simplest frame: just the target vehicle + 로 + the verb

examples.en: Please transfer to line 2 at City Hall station.
examples.note: Everyday directions: 에서 marks where, 으로 marks which line

examples.ko: 환승하려면 다음 역에서 내려서 갈아타야 해요.
examples.romanization: hwanseungharyeomyeon daeum yeogeseo naeryeoseo garataya haeyo.
examples.en: To transfer you have to get off at the next station and change.
examples.note: Real situation: pairs 내리다 then 갈아타다, the natural commuting sequence

ex.ko: 알겠어요. 그런데 발표 전에 자료는 보내 줄 수 있어요?
ex.en: I understand. But can you send the materials before the presentation?
ex.note: Shifts from accepting the situation to asking for the next action.

그런데.nuance: 그런데 (spoken: 근데) is the soft, all-purpose 'but' that also works as 'by the way' to glide into a new topic — this double life surprises English speakers most. As contrast it is far gentler than 하지만 or 그렇지만; it doesn't slam two ideas together, it just notes that something slightly different follows. As a topic-changer it carries no contrast at all: 그런데, 우리 언제 만나요? simply means 'So/Anyway, when shall we meet?'. It is closely tied to the mid-sentence ending -는데, which sets background before a turn (비싼데 살까? = it's pricey, but shall I buy it?). The everyday pitfall is over-translating it as a strong 'however'; if you mean a firm, contrastive 'however', reach for 하지만. And don't write the long form in chat — Koreans type 근데.
그런데.explanation: "but; by the way" is 그런데 (geureonde). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그런데 ("but / by the way"). Watch the particle attached to 그런데 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
그런데.shortExplanation: 그런데 means "but; by the way" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 그런데 always means 'but'. Very often it just means 'by the way / so' and introduces zero contrast, as in 그런데 이거 얼마예요? (By the way, how much is this?).
Using 그런데 where you need a strong, clear 'however'. For a firm contrast 하지만/그렇지만 is stronger; 그런데 stays soft.
Saying 그런데 in fast casual speech. It's not wrong, but it sounds bookish — natural spoken Korean contracts it to 근데.

usagePhrases.note: Soft contrast OR a gentle pivot to a new topic.

usagePhrases.en: It's nice. But it's a bit pricey.
usagePhrases.note: Mild 'but' that softens the bad news.

usagePhrases.en: by the way, here's the thing…
usagePhrases.note: Set phrase that eases you into a new subject.
In speech almost everyone shortens it to 근데.

examples.ko: 이 식당 맛있어요. 그런데 사람이 너무 많아요.
examples.romanization: i sikdang masisseoyo. geureonde sarami neomu manayo.
examples.en: This place is tasty. But there are way too many people.
examples.note: Two facts, gently set against each other.

examples.ko: 잘 지냈어요? 그런데 그 얘기 들었어요?
examples.romanization: jal jinaesseoyo? geureonde geu yaegi deureosseoyo?
examples.en: Have you been well? By the way, did you hear that news?
examples.note: Here it isn't 'but' at all — it just changes the subject.

examples.en: I'd like to order — but is this spicy?
examples.note: Real ordering moment; softens straight into a question.

cluster.title: 그리고 vs 그래서 vs 그런데 vs 그러면
cluster.rule: Pick by the logical link back to the sentence you just said: 그리고 simply adds, 그래서 gives its result, 그런데 turns away from it, and 그러면 treats it as a premise ("if that's so, then…"). Note that in real speech 그런데/근데 is very often not contrast at all — it's just "by the way", a way to slide into a new topic.

example.en: I had dinner. And then I drank coffee.
It's raining. So I'm staying home.

members.when: soft contrast, or changing the topic

example.en: By the way, when are we meeting?

members.en: then, in that case, if so
members.when: reacting to what was just said

ex.en: The person in charge probably knows.

아마.nuance: 아마 means 'probably / perhaps,' expressing the speaker's reasonable guess, and its grammar is almost inseparable: it is normally completed by a conjecture ending — most often -ㄹ/을 거예요 ('will probably'), or -ㄹ 것 같다, -겠-, -ㄹ걸요. The bare statement 아마 비가 와요 sounds unfinished; you want 아마 비가 올 거예요. A near-synonym is 아마도, which is just a softer, slightly more deliberative version of 아마 (interchangeable; 아마도 can feel a touch more written or musing). Distinguish the certainty scale: 아마 is a fairly confident guess (~maybe 70-80%), 어쩌면/혹시 lean toward 'possibly, by any chance' (lower, more tentative), and 분명히/틀림없이 mean 'surely/definitely' (high certainty). The English-speaker pitfall is using 아마 with a flat present/past as if it were the English adverb that can float anywhere ('he's probably home'): in Korean the verb itself must carry the guessing form, so 'he's probably home' = 아마 집에 있을 거예요, not 아마 집에 있어요. Also avoid 아마 with established facts — 아마 물은 H2O일 거예요 sounds odd because you're hedging a certainty. Place 아마 near the front of the clause, and let the sentence-final ending do the conjecture work.
아마.explanation: "probably" is 아마 (ama). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 아마 올 거예요. ("They'll probably come."). Watch the particle attached to 아마 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
아마.shortExplanation: 아마 means "probably" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Pairing 아마 with a plain present/past tense; the predicate must take a guess ending — 아마 올 거예요, not 아마 와요, for 'will probably come.'
Using 아마 about a known fact or certainty; for 'definitely/surely' switch to 분명히/틀림없이, e.g. 분명히 맞아요, since 아마 hedges.
Confusing 아마 ('probably,' fairly confident) with 혹시/어쩌면 ('possibly, by any chance,' tentative); 혹시 시간 있어요? = 'do you by any chance have time?', a softer probe than a 아마 prediction.

usagePhrases.note: 아마 pairs with the -ㄹ 거예요 guess ending
아마도 is a slightly softer/heavier variant
아마 with the casual conjecture -ㄹ걸요
아마 over a negated guess

examples.en: That person is probably a student.
examples.note: Basic: 아마 + 일 거예요 (noun guess)

examples.ko: 내일은 아마 비가 올 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: naeireun ama biga ol geot gatayo.
examples.en: It'll probably rain tomorrow, I think.
examples.note: Everyday: 아마 reinforced by -ㄹ 것 같다

examples.en: Even if we leave now, we'll probably be late.
examples.note: Real situation: 아마 framing a resigned prediction

cluster.title: 아마 vs 혹시 vs 어쩌면
cluster.rule: 아마 and 어쩌면 are guesses that differ in confidence: 아마 leans yes ("probably"), 어쩌면 just opens a real possibility ("maybe, who knows"). 혹시 is not a guess at all — it fronts a question or request to soften it, like "by any chance".

members.hint: your best guess — pairs with -ㄹ 거예요

example.en: Do you have time, by any chance?

members.hint: less sure than 아마 — "maybe, who knows"

example.en: Maybe I won't be able to go.

ex.en: I think it will be cloudy tomorrow.

흐리다.nuance: 흐리다 is the all-purpose word for 'unclear,' covering CLOUDY weather (흐린 날 an overcast day), MURKY water (흐린 물), and BLURRY/out-of-focus images or hazy memories (사진이 흐리다, 기억이 흐리다). Its opposite is 맑다 (clear), and for weather these two are the everyday pair: 맑아요 (clear/sunny) ↔ 흐려요 (cloudy). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 흐리다 to mean DIRTY: murky water that's hard to see through is 흐리다, but water or a surface that is dirty/filthy is 더럽다 — 흐리다 is about lack of CLARITY, not presence of grime. Note also a near-synonym for blurriness: 뿌옇다/희미하다 also describe a hazy, faint look, but 흐리다 is the plain default learners should master first. The conjugation trap: like other ㅣ-stems, 흐리다 contracts in the 해요-form to 흐려요 (not 흐리어요), past 흐렸어요. As a descriptive adjective it does not take 있다: 하늘이 흐려요, not 흐려 있어요.
흐리다.explanation: 흐리다 (heurida) means "to be cloudy; to be blurry/murky". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 날씨가 흐리다 ("the weather is cloudy/overcast"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 흐리다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
흐리다.shortExplanation: 흐리다 means "to be cloudy; to be blurry/murky" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 흐리다 for dirty things — filthy water or a dirty floor is 더럽다 (물이 더러워요); 흐리다 means murky/unclear, not grimy.
Writing the 해요-form as 흐리어요 — the ㅣ-stem contracts, so it's 흐려요, and the past is 흐렸어요.
Mixing the weather opposites: 'it's clear/sunny' is 맑아요, not 안 흐려요 — use the positive adjective 맑다 rather than negating 흐리다.

usagePhrases.note: the most common everyday use
cloudy, not see-through water
out of focus / unclear image
흐리다 also fits a faint, fuzzy memory

examples.en: The weather is cloudy today.
examples.note: 흐리다 → 흐려요 (ㅣ + 어 contracts to 려); core weather word

examples.en: It rained, so the river water turned murky.
examples.note: 흐려지다 (-아지다) = became murky; shows the change of state

examples.ko: 사진이 흐려서 글씨가 잘 안 보여요.
examples.romanization: sajini heuryeoseo geulssiga jal an boyeoyo.
examples.en: The photo is blurry, so I can't read the text well.
examples.note: real-situation: 흐리다 = blurry/out of focus, with 흐려서 (-아서) giving the reason

ex.en: If it rains, take an umbrella.

우산.nuance: 우산 is Sino-Korean 雨傘, literally 雨 'rain' + 傘 'umbrella/parasol' — so the word transparently means 'rain-umbrella', which is your built-in reminder it's for rain. The verb is the deceptively busy 쓰다: to put up/use an umbrella is 우산을 쓰다, the same 쓰다 that covers wearing a hat (모자를 쓰다) and glasses (안경을 쓰다) — Korean groups 'things over your head/face' under 쓰다, distinct from 입다 (clothes on the torso/legs) and 신다 (footwear). The contrast to file away is 우산 vs 양산: both are 傘, but 우산 (雨傘) is the rain umbrella while 양산 (陽傘, 'sun-shade') is a parasol against sunlight — different words for different weather. Useful collocations: 우산을 쓰다/접다/펴다 (put up / fold / open an umbrella), 우산을 챙기다 (remember to grab an umbrella), 우산을 깜빡하다 (forget the umbrella). A folding umbrella is 접는 우산 or 3단 우산, a long one 장우산. Pitfall: English 'wear/carry an umbrella' must become 쓰다 (use over the head), never 입다, and don't reuse 우산 for a sun parasol — that's 양산.
우산.explanation: 우산 (usan) means "umbrella". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우산이 있어요 ("I have an umbrella"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 우산 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.
우산.shortExplanation: 우산 means "umbrella" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Putting up an umbrella with 입다 — 입다 is for clothing on the body; an umbrella (like a hat/glasses) goes with 쓰다: 우산을 쓰다.
Using 우산 for a sun parasol — sunshade is 양산 (陽傘); 우산 (雨傘) is specifically for rain.
Saying 우산을 열다 to open it — Koreans say 우산을 펴다/쓰다 (spread/put up) and 우산을 접다 (fold); 열다 (open like a door) is unidiomatic for an umbrella.

우산 + 을 + 쓰다

확실하다.nuance: 확실하다 (確實, 確 'firm/sure' + 實 'real/true') expresses certainty and confidence — you're sure something is true, settled, or reliable. The adverb 확실히 ('certainly, definitely, for sure') is very common when answering or confirming (확실히 그래요 'that's definitely so'). The sharp contrast is with 분명하다: 확실하다 centres on the speaker's subjective confidence ('I'm sure of it'), while 분명하다 centres on a thing being objectively obvious/unambiguous — so 나는 확실해 ('I'm certain') but 증거가 분명해 ('the evidence is clear-cut'). It also brushes against 틀림없다 ('there's no mistake / definitely'), which is even more emphatic. Crucially, 확실하다 is for certainty, not possibility: to say 'maybe' you need 아마 ('probably') or '-ㄹ지도 몰라요' ('might'), not 확실하다. The natural adverb is 확실히 in everyday speech (확실하게 is a touch stiffer).
확실하다.explanation: "to be certain / sure" is 확실하다 (hwaksilhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 확실한 N ("a sure / certain N"). Watch the particle attached to 확실하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
확실하다.shortExplanation: 확실하다 means "to be certain / sure" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 확실하다 when you actually mean 'maybe / probably' — for uncertainty use 아마 or '-ㄹ지도 몰라요'; 확실하다 asserts the opposite (full certainty).
Treating 확실하다 and 분명하다 as the same — 확실하다 = the speaker's confidence, 분명하다 = something objectively obvious.
Defaulting to 확실하게 in casual speech — the idiomatic adverb is 확실히 (확실히 알겠어요).

examples.note: 그건 = 'as for that'; speaker is sure

가능성.nuance: 가능성 is a noun, so it pairs with 있다, 없다, 높다, and 낮다. It is a little more formal than just saying -ㄹ지도 몰라요.
가능성.explanation: 가능성 (ganeungseong) means "possibility; chance". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 비 올 가능성이 있어요. ("There is a chance it will rain."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가능성 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
가능성.shortExplanation: 가능성 means "possibility; chance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 가능하다 when you mean 'chance' as a noun. Say 가능성이 있어요.
가능성이 높아요 means 'it is likely,' not 'the ability is high.'

usagePhrases.en: There is a chance it will rain.
usagePhrases.note: A more noun-based way to talk about probability.
Useful when you are not fully ruling something out.

examples.en: There is a chance they will be late, so let's order first.
examples.note: 가능성 gives the reason for a practical decision.

ex.en: When you are not sure, do not state it too firmly; guess carefully.

추측하다.nuance: 추측하다 is more explicit than -나 봐요. In conversation, the pattern often does the work, and 추측하다 names the thinking process.
추측하다.explanation: 추측하다 (chucheukada) = "to guess; to infer". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 단서로 추측해요. ("I infer from a clue.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 추측하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
추측하다.shortExplanation: 추측하다 means "to guess; to infer" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 추측하다 for facts you already know.
In casual speech, 너무 추측했어요 can sound odd; say 그냥 추측이에요.

usagePhrases.note: 로 marks the basis or means.
A useful hedge when you are not sure.

examples.romanization: usaneul bogo biga ona bwayorago chucheukaesseoyo.
examples.en: I saw the umbrella and guessed, 'It looks like it is raining.'
examples.note: The visible object supports the inference.

ex.en: It was quiet at first, and then there were quickly more people.

금방.nuance: 금방 is a two-faced time word: with a FUTURE verb it means 'in a moment / very soon' (금방 올게요 'I'll be right back'), and with a PAST verb it means 'just now / a moment ago' (금방 갔어요 'left just now'). The tense of the verb decides which reading you get, so the same word swings both ways around the present — that's the thing to internalize. The sharp contrast is 금방 vs 방금: 방금 'just now' is strictly PAST (방금 도착했어요 'I just arrived') and cannot mean 'soon', whereas 금방 covers both directions. Origin-wise 금방 is Sino-Korean 今方 'now-just', and it's thoroughly casual, everyday speech. The classic English-speaker error is forcing 방금 into a future sentence or assuming 금방 only means 'soon' and missing its 'a moment ago' use. It takes no particle, sits before the verb, and habitually pairs with 오다/가다, 되다 ('be ready'), and 끝나다.
금방.explanation: "in a moment; just now" is 금방 (geumbang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 금방 올게요 ("I'll be right back"). Watch the particle attached to 금방 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
금방.shortExplanation: 금방 means "in a moment; just now" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 방금 for the future, e.g. ✗ 방금 갈게요 for 'I'll go soon'. 방금 is past-only; the forward-looking 'soon' is 금방 갈게요.
Assuming 금방 only means 'soon' and missing its past sense. With a past verb, 금방 왔어요 = 'I just got here a moment ago', not 'I'll come soon'.
Adding 에: ✗ 금방에. No particle — 금방 attaches straight to the verb.

usagePhrases.note: Future use: promising a very quick return.

usagePhrases.en: it'll be done in no time
usagePhrases.note: Reassuring someone the wait is short.
Past use: it happened a moment ago.
On the phone, 'I'll be there in a sec'.

전화하다.nuance: 전화하다 is noun + 하다, so 전화 안 해요 is a natural short negative.
전화하다.explanation: 전화하다 (jeonhwahada) = "to call by phone". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 전화해요 plus one useful sentence like 전화해 주세요 ("Please call me."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 전화하고 싶어요 for what you want, 전화할 수 있어요 for what you can, 전화 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
전화하다.shortExplanation: 전화하다 means "to call by phone" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 전화하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 전화해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 전화하다 becomes 전화할 수 있어요 ("can") and 전화할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I have to call by phone.

Useful request.

examples.note: Promise.

examples.en: Please do not call at night.

아직.nuance: 아직 covers both 'still' and 'not yet', and which one surfaces depends on polarity: with a POSITIVE verb it means 'still' (아직 자요 'still sleeping'), and with a NEGATIVE verb it means 'not yet' (아직 안 잤어요 'haven't slept yet'). It is the natural counterpart to 벌써/이미 — 아직 안 끝났어요 ('not finished yet') is the mirror of 벌써 끝났어요 ('already finished'). It often rides with the ongoing form -고 있다 to stress an action in progress (아직 자고 있어요 'still sleeping right now') and shows up in fixed phrases like 아직 멀었어요 ('still a long way off'). Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is the 아직/벌써 confusion and the negation logic: because English 'yet' lives in questions/negatives, learners forget that Korean 아직 itself flips meaning with the verb's polarity — pair 아직 with 안/못 to say 'not yet', and use it with a plain positive verb to say 'still'.
아직.explanation: 아직 (ajik) = "still; yet". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아직 자요 ("they're still asleep") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 아직, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
아직.shortExplanation: 아직 means "still; yet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 아직 with 벌써. 아직 안 왔어요 = 'hasn't come yet'; 벌써 왔어요 = 'already came'. They point in opposite directions.
Trying to say 'not yet' with a positive verb. 아직 먹었어요 reads as 'still ate' and is odd; you need the negative: 아직 안 먹었어요.
Adding -았/었- when the state still holds. For 'I'm still hungry' say 아직 배고파요 (present), not 아직 배고팠어요; the past tense would mean the hunger is already over, which contradicts 아직.

usagePhrases.note: ongoing state, before verb
아직 + negative = 'not yet'

usagePhrases.en: there's still a long way to go
usagePhrases.note: set phrase, 'not nearly done'
ongoing not-knowing

examples.en: I'm still a student.
examples.note: Simple: with a positive noun-sentence, 아직 = 'still'.

examples.en: I haven't eaten yet.
examples.note: Everyday: 아직 + 안/못 + past = 'not yet'; the most common pattern.

examples.en: Almost done? — No, not yet.

cluster.title: 벌써 vs 이미 vs 아직
cluster.rule: 벌써 and 이미 differ in tone, not timing: 벌써 reacts with surprise ("already?!"), while 이미 just reports a settled fact. 아직 is the opposite pole — "not yet" with a negative verb, "still" with a positive one.

members.en: already (it's done and can't be changed)

ex.en: They may have already left work.

이미.nuance: 이미 means 'already,' emphasizing that an action or state is completed and now fixed — often colored by 'and there's no changing it now.' The sharp contrast every learner needs is 이미 vs 벌써. Both translate as 'already,' but 이미 is neutral and factual ('it is already done, that's just the situation'), while 벌써 adds emotional surprise that it happened so fast or so soon ('already?! that quick?'). 이미 끝났어요 = a calm statement of fact; 벌써 끝났어요?! = 'it's over already?!' with raised eyebrows. So choose 이미 when calmly noting that the moment/deadline has passed, and 벌써 when reacting to unexpected speed. 이미 is native Korean and is also future-blind: it only describes things already done, never things about to happen. It pairs naturally with completed clauses and with -더라고요, -았/었- past forms.
이미.explanation: "already (it's done and can't be changed)" is 이미 (imi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 이미 끝나다 ("to be already over"). Watch the particle attached to 이미 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
이미.shortExplanation: 이미 means "already (it's done and can't be changed)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Swapping it freely with 벌써: 이미 is neutral about timing, while 벌써 carries 'so soon?!' surprise. Use 이미 for a flat fact, 벌써 for astonishment.
Using it for the future: 이미 only describes things already done. 'It'll already be finished by then' needs a future-perfect feel like 그때면 끝나 있을 거예요, not 이미 + future.
Forcing English word order: in English 'already' floats around, but Korean 이미 sits before the verb/predicate it modifies — 이미 다 먹었어요, not 다 먹었어요 이미.

usagePhrases.note: States a finished, irreversible fact; 이미 끝난 일이에요 = it's a done deal
이미 늦었어요 = there's no point now, the moment has passed
이미 알고 있었어요 = I knew it beforehand, this is no news
이미 결정된 상태예요 = it's already (been) decided, fixed now

examples.en: I've already seen that movie.
examples.note: Simple: 이미 + completed action, a settled fact

cluster.title: 벌써 vs 이미 vs 아직
cluster.rule: 벌써 and 이미 differ in tone, not timing: 벌써 reacts with surprise ("already?!"), while 이미 just reports a settled fact. 아직 is the opposite pole — "not yet" with a negative verb, "still" with a positive one.

members.en: already (it's done and can't be changed)

ex.en: If the fine dust is bad, we cancel the plan.

취소하다.nuance: 취소하다 (取消하다, 取 'take' + 消 'extinguish/erase') means to cancel — to call off or undo something already arranged: a reservation, an order, an appointment, a plan. The neat way to remember it: it's the natural opposite of 예약하다/신청하다 (book/apply). Distinguish it from 그만두다, which is 'to quit/stop' an ongoing activity or job (회사를 그만두다, 'quit the company'; 운동을 그만두다, 'stop exercising'): you 취소해요 a future arrangement, but you 그만둬요 something already in progress. It also differs from 미루다 ('postpone', 약속을 미루다, push the appointment later rather than scrap it) — canceling removes it, postponing reschedules it. As a noun+하다 verb it's regular: 취소하 + 여요 → 취소해요, past 취소했어요, with 안/못 before 하다 (취소 안 해요, 취소 못 해요). English-speaker pitfall: 'cancel my subscription / unsubscribe' is more often 해지하다 (解止, end a contract) than 취소하다, and don't use 취소하다 for 'quit a job' — that's 그만두다.
취소하다.explanation: 취소하다 (chwisohada) = "to cancel". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 취소해요 plus one useful sentence like 예약을 취소하다 ("to cancel a reservation"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 취소하고 싶어요 for what you want, 취소할 수 있어요 for what you can, 취소 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
취소하다.shortExplanation: 취소하다 means "to cancel" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 취소하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 취소해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 취소하다 for 'quit a job/activity' — quitting something ongoing is 그만두다; 취소하다 calls off a future arrangement (booking, order, plan).
Confusing 취소하다 with 미루다 — canceling removes the plan, but 미루다 only postpones it: 약속을 미뤘어요 ('I pushed it back').
Saying 못 취소해요 — the noun+하다 negative is 취소 못 해요 / 취소 안 해요 (split goes before 하다).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 취소하다 becomes 취소할 수 있어요 ("can") and 취소할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
취소하다 undoes a booking/order; 예약을 취소해요

examples.en: I cancel the reservation.
examples.note: Noun+하다 compound, regular: stem 취소하 + 여요 → 취소해요

examples.en: Something came up, so I canceled the appointment.
examples.note: 일이 생기다 = 'something comes up'; -아서 gives the reason; past 취소했어요

examples.ko: 이미 결제해서 지금은 취소 못 해요.

examples.en: I already paid, so I can't cancel now.
examples.note: 이미 ('already') + past reason; 못 splits as 취소 못 해요

ex.en: These days, the waiting time has decreased, I noticed.
ex.note: Opposite of 늘다 for observed change.

줄다.nuance: 줄다 is the exact opposite of 늘다 — it means an amount, number, or size gets smaller — and the two are learned as a pair (늘다/줄다). Like 늘다 it is a ㄹ-irregular verb, so the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, giving the formal 줍니다 (not *줄습니다). The crucial synonym contrast is 줄다 vs 줄이다: 줄다 is intransitive — the thing shrinks by itself (소리가 줄었어요 = the sound got quieter on its own), while 줄이다 is the causative — you deliberately reduce something (소리를 줄였어요 = I turned the sound down). Its formal report-style synonym is 감소하다 (Sino-Korean 減少, 'reduce-decrease'), used for statistics; 줄다 is the natural conversational word. The English-speaker pitfall mirrors 늘다: don't say *줄습니다 (the ㄹ drops to make 줍니다), and don't put an object with 줄다. 'I reduced my spending' needs the transitive 줄이다 (지출을 줄였어요); 'my spending decreased' uses 줄다 with the subject particle (지출이 줄었어요).
줄다.explanation: 줄다 (julda) = "to decrease". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 줄어요 plus one useful sentence like 살이 줄었어요 ("I lost weight"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 줄고 싶어요 for what you want, 줄 수 있어요 for what you can, 줄 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
줄다.shortExplanation: 줄다 means "to decrease" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 줄다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 줄어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Writing the formal form as 줄습니다 — the ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다, so it is 줍니다.
Confusing 줄다 with 줄이다. 'The cost decreased' is 비용이 줄었어요 (by itself); 'I cut the cost' is 비용을 줄였어요 (you did it). 이/가 goes with 줄다, 을/를 with 줄이다.
Saying 살을 줄었어요 to mean 'I lost weight' — 줄다 takes no object, so it's 살이 줄었어요 (with 이). If you mean you deliberately slimmed, Koreans more often say 살을 뺐어요 (from 빼다).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 줄다 becomes 줄 수 있어요 ("can") and 줄 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 줄다 has an irregular stem (ㄹ). Memorize its polite form 줄어요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

examples.en: The shop's customers decreased a lot
examples.note: Simple drop in numbers, past tense

examples.en: Work has decreased lately so I'm a bit free
examples.note: -어서 ties the decrease to having free time

examples.en: My allowance is gradually shrinking
examples.note: -고 있어요 plus 점점 stresses a slow ongoing fall

ex.en: For an interview, a neat shirt is good.

면접.nuance: 면접 (面接, 'face-contact/meet') literally means meeting face-to-face, and refers to the job interview where you sit before evaluators. The most important thing to lock in is the FIXED verb: 면접을 보다, literally 'to see an interview,' which uses the same 보다 as 시험을 보다 (take a test) — Korean treats undergoing an evaluation as 'seeing' it. The synonym contrast: 면접 is the oral, face-to-face interview, while 시험 (試驗) is a written test/exam, and 면담 (面談) is a softer counseling-style talk (e.g., with a professor), not a hiring screen. After a 면접 you hope to 합격하다 (pass) rather than 떨어지다 (fall/fail) or 불합격하다. Register: neutral, used in any job-search context. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 하다: 면접을 하다 sounds off from the candidate's side — you 면접을 보다 (take it); the company that conducts it may 면접을 진행하다. Also note you pass 면접에 (with 에), patterning like 시험에 합격하다.
면접.explanation: 면접 (myeonjeop) = "job interview". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 면접을 보다 ("to have a job interview") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 면접, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.
면접.shortExplanation: 면접 means "job interview" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 면접을 하다 as the candidate. The fixed verb is 면접을 보다 (just like 시험을 보다).
Confusing 면접 (oral, face-to-face interview) with 시험 (a written exam). Different formats, different prep.
Using 를 with 합격: 면접을 합격하다 is wrong. You pass INTO it with 에 → 면접에 합격하다.

usagePhrases.note: 보다 'to see' is the FIXED verb here, exactly like 시험을 보다 (take an exam).
합격하다 (合格, pass) + 에 marking the interview you pass; opposite is 떨어지다 (fail).
면접 + 준비 (準備, preparation) — getting ready for the interview.
1차 (1次, first round); Korean hiring often has 1차, 2차 면접 stages.

examples.en: I have a job interview tomorrow.
examples.note: 면접을 보다 → present 봐요; literally 'see an interview' = have one.

examples.en: I prepared hard for the interview.
examples.note: 면접 준비 + 하다, past 했어요; 열심히 = diligently.

examples.en: I'm so happy I passed the interview.
examples.note: 면접에 합격하다 + ~아서 (reason) + 기쁘다 (glad).

ex.ko: 상황을 먼저 설명하면 상대방이 이해하기 쉬워요.
ex.en: If you explain the situation first, it is easier for the other person to understand.
ex.note: The larger situation tells you which marker fits.

상황.nuance: 상황 (狀況, '狀 condition/form + 況 circumstances' — the configuration of circumstances) describes the overall set of conditions surrounding a moment or event, broader than a single 경우 (a specific case or instance — 이런 경우 = 'in this one case', vs 이런 상황 = 'in this whole situation'). The reflexive phrase 상황에 따라(서) 다르다 ('it depends on the situation') is one of the most useful hedges in Korean, and 이런/그런 상황에서 sets up advice or reactions. Register is neutral. Two pitfalls: keep 상황 (the circumstances around an event) distinct from 상태 (狀態, the state/condition of a single thing or body — 건강 상태 'health condition', 배터리 상태 'battery state'); you describe a person's mood with a 상태, but the events around them with a 상황. And use 에 따라 (not 으로) for 'depending on': 상황에 따라, never 상황으로.
상황.explanation: "situation, circumstances" is 상황 (sanghwang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 현재 상황 ("the current situation"). Watch the particle attached to 상황 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
상황.shortExplanation: 상황 means "situation, circumstances" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't confuse 상황 (the situation/circumstances around an event) with 상태 (the state or condition of a thing or body): 건강 상태, not 건강 상황.
Use 에 따라 for 'depending on the situation', not 으로: 상황에 따라(서), never 상황으로.
For one specific instance, 경우 is sharper than 상황: '이런 경우' = 'in this particular case' vs '이런 상황' = 'in this whole situation'.

usagePhrases.note: 상황 follows a noun/modifier naming the state of affairs
상황이 좋다/나쁘다/심각하다 describe how things stand; subject takes 이/가
frames advice or a reaction to a set of conditions
상황에 따라(서) 다르다 = it depends on the situation

examples.en: How's the situation right now?
examples.note: Simple: 상황 with 이/가 asking after the state of things

examples.ko: 이런 상황에서는 어떻게 해야 할지 모르겠어요.
examples.romanization: ireon sanghwangeseoneun eotteoke haeya halji moreugesseoyo.
examples.en: In a situation like this, I don't know what I should do.
examples.note: Everyday: 이런 상황에서(는) framing a reaction to circumstances

examples.ko: 회사 사정이 어려워서, 상황에 따라 채용 일정이 바뀔 수도 있어요.
examples.romanization: hoesa sajeongi eoryeowoseo, sanghwange ttara chaeyong iljeongi bakkwil sudo isseoyo.
examples.en: Since the company is in a tough spot, the hiring schedule may change depending on the situation.
examples.note: Real situation: the hedging phrase 상황에 따라 in a workplace context

ex.en: My parents are coming to the wedding too.

부모님.nuance: 부모님 is Sino-Korean 父母 ('father' 父 + 'mother' 母) plus the honorific suffix 님, so the respect is baked into the word itself and it is the everyday polite default — there is no need to add anything to make it courteous. The bare root 부모 exists but is abstract and institutional ('부모의 역할' the role of parents, '부모 교육' parenting education); aimed at a real person it sounds cold, so for your own or anyone's parents you say 부모님. Because 님 marks the referent as worthy of respect, every verb around it must climb to its honorific tier: 있다→계시다, 주다→드리다, 집→댁, 에게→께, and the topic/subject can even take 께서. The classic English-speaker pitfall is pairing 부모님 with plain verbs ('부모님이 있어요', '부모님한테 줬어요'); grammatically the words exist, but to a Korean ear it clashes like saying 'Her Majesty ate fast' — you must use 계세요 and 드렸어요/께.
부모님.explanation: "parents" is 부모님 (bumonim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우리 부모님 ("my parents"). Watch the particle attached to 부모님 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
부모님.shortExplanation: 부모님 means "parents" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 부모 instead of 부모님 for an actual person ('제 부모는…') — without 님 it sounds blunt and textbook-like; always use 부모님 for real parents.
Using plain 있어요/없어요 with 부모님 ('부모님이 있어요') — the honorific subject demands 계세요/안 계세요.
Writing 부모님한테 or 부모님에게 — with the honorific 님 the dative must rise to 부모님께.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 + the built-in honorific 님 = the polite default
use 계시다, the honorific of 있다, to match 님
께 is the honorific of 에게/한테, required by 님
댁 is the honorific of 집 (house)

examples.en: I live with my parents.
examples.note: 살다 (to live/reside) drops its ㄹ before some endings but keeps it in 살아요

examples.en: I call my parents every day.
examples.note: 드리다 is the humble form of 주다/하다 — you 'give' the call up to elders

examples.en: My parents are in Busan right now.
examples.note: 계세요 (honorific 있어요) is obligatory because the subject is 부모님
