ex.en: Actually, today's materials are not finished yet.

사실은.nuance: 사실은 does not mean every sentence is a dramatic confession. It often simply prepares the listener for background or a correction.
사실은.explanation: 사실은 (sasireun) = "actually; to be honest". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사실은 아직 다 못 했어요. ("Actually, I have not finished it yet.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 사실은, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
사실은.shortExplanation: 사실은 means "actually; to be honest" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 사실은 and then giving information the listener already knows very well. 잖아요 may fit better for shared information.
Translating 'actually' into 사실은 in every English sentence; sometimes 그런데 or 아니면 no marker is more natural.

usagePhrases.en: Actually, I have not finished it yet.
usagePhrases.note: Softly reveals the real situation.

usagePhrases.ko: 사실은 제가 먼저 말을 꺼내고 싶었어요.
usagePhrases.romanization: sasireun jega meonjeo mareul kkeonaego sipeosseoyo.
usagePhrases.en: Actually, I wanted to bring it up first.
usagePhrases.note: Useful before a sensitive topic.

examples.ko: 사실은 오늘 자료가 아직 안 끝났는데요.
examples.romanization: sasireun oneul jaryoga ajik an kkeunnanneundeyo.
examples.en: Actually, today's materials are not finished yet.
examples.note: Opens bad news with a softer frame.

ex.en: But that is a little difficult, though.
ex.note: Casual version of 그런데 for spoken conversation.

근데.nuance: 근데 is common in speech, but it can sound too casual in a presentation, email, or formal announcement.
근데.explanation: "but; by the way (casual shortened 그런데)" is 근데 (geunde). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 근데 오늘 시간 돼? ("But / by the way, are you free today?"). Watch the particle attached to 근데 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
근데.shortExplanation: 근데 means "but; by the way (casual shortened 그런데)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 근데 in formal writing where 그런데 is safer.
Using 근데 every sentence; it becomes filler if there is no real contrast or topic shift.

usagePhrases.en: But / by the way, are you free today?
usagePhrases.note: Casual topic opener.

usagePhrases.en: But that is a little difficult, though.
usagePhrases.note: Soft pushback with -는데요.

examples.ko: 근데 자료는 언제 보낼 수 있어요?
examples.romanization: geunde jaryoneun eonje bonael su isseoyo?
examples.en: But when can you send the materials?
examples.note: Spoken contrast in a team conversation.

ex.ko: 그러니까 먼저 회의를 시작해도 된다는 말이죠?
ex.en: So you mean we can start the meeting first, right?
ex.note: Checks the implied meaning before moving on.

그러니까.nuance: 그러니까 means 'so / that's why' and presents what follows as the reason-driven result of what came before. It comes from 그렇다 + -(으)니까 ('because it is so'), and that -니까 root is the key to its flavor: -니까 is the 'because' that naturally leads into commands, requests, and urging, which is exactly why 그러니까 pairs so well with advice (일찍 자요) and 'I-told-you-so' lines. This is the sharp dividing line from near-synonym 그래서: 그래서 (from 그렇다 + -아서) merely REPORTS a result neutrally ('so, as a result'), and crucially 그래서 cannot head a command, while 그러니까 actively REASONS and PERSUADES and happily does. Beyond logic, 그러니까 is a heavy conversational filler — 그러니까 내 말이 means 'exactly, that's my point!' (strong agreement), and a trailing 그러니까... works like English 'I mean...' when you restate yourself. English speakers who treat it as a plain synonym of 그래서 miss both the urging nuance and these idiomatic uses.
그러니까.explanation: "so, that's why, what I mean is" is 그러니까 (geureonikka). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 그러니까 내 말이 ("Exactly, that's what I'm saying"). Watch the particle attached to 그러니까 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
그러니까.shortExplanation: 그러니까 means "so, that's why, what I mean is" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating it as identical to 그래서; 그러니까 reasons/urges and can introduce a command (그러니까 일찍 자요), while 그래서 only reports a result and cannot head an order
Missing the agreement idiom 그러니까 내 말이, which means 'exactly!' not a literal 'so my words'
Overusing it to start every sentence; as a filler it's fine in speech but looks sloppy if it opens written sentences repeatedly

usagePhrases.note: 그러니까 내 말이 is a strong 'I totally agree' phrase

usagePhrases.en: That's why I told you to be careful
usagePhrases.note: Drawing an 'I-told-you-so' conclusion
Stating the logical takeaway as advice

usagePhrases.en: So, what do you mean by that?
usagePhrases.note: Filler-like use to reorganize or push a thought

examples.en: They say it'll rain. So bring an umbrella.
examples.note: Simple: derives a piece of advice from a fact

examples.ko: 주말엔 사람이 많아요. 그러니까 평일에 가는 게 나아요.
examples.romanization: jumaren sarami manayo. geureonikka pyeongire ganeun ge naayo.
examples.en: Weekends are crowded. That's why going on a weekday is better.
examples.note: Gives the reasoning behind a recommendation

examples.ko: 그러니까 제 말은, 지금 결정하지 말자는 거예요.
examples.romanization: geureonikka je mareun, jigeum gyeoljeonghaji maljaneun geoyeyo.
examples.en: What I mean is, let's not decide right now.
examples.note: 그러니까 제 말은 restates and clarifies your own point

ex.en: The meeting time is short, you know.
ex.note: Use when the listener already knows the reason.

잖아요.nuance: 잖아요 is for shared information. For new background, use -거든요 instead.
잖아요.explanation: 잖아요 (janayo) means "you know; as you know". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회의 시간이 짧잖아요. ("The meeting time is short, you know."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 잖아요 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
잖아요.shortExplanation: 잖아요 means "you know; as you know" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 잖아요 to announce new information. That can sound like 'You should have known this.'
Using it in formal public speech. It is conversational.

usagePhrases.en: The meeting time is short, you know.
usagePhrases.note: Shared constraint.
Can sound pointed depending on tone.

examples.en: The team lead is busy now too, you know.
examples.note: Uses shared context to justify a suggestion.

ex.en: Something suddenly came up yesterday, you see.
ex.note: Use when the listener does not know the background yet.

거든요.nuance: 거든요 gives new background. It is softer than just dropping a reason, but it can sound defensive if the tone is too clipped.
거든요.explanation: "you see; the thing is" is 거든요 (geodeunyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어제 갑자기 일이 생겼거든요. ("Something suddenly came up yesterday, you see."). Watch the particle attached to 거든요 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
거든요.shortExplanation: 거든요 means "you see; the thing is" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 거든요 for something everyone already knows. 잖아요 is usually better for shared information.
Treating it as a full replacement for because. It carries conversational background, not just logic.

usagePhrases.en: Something suddenly came up yesterday, you see.
usagePhrases.note: New background.

usagePhrases.en: That cafe has a nice atmosphere, you see.
usagePhrases.note: Reason for liking or choosing the cafe.

examples.ko: 오늘은 먼저 시작해 주세요. 제가 조금 늦거든요.
examples.romanization: oneureun meonjeo sijakae juseyo. jega jogeum neutgeodeunyo.
examples.en: Please start first today. I am running a little late, you see.
examples.note: Explains a request with new background.

ex.en: The materials are not finished yet, though.
ex.note: Leaves space for the listener to respond.

는데요.nuance: 는데요 is not only 'but'. It often sets up background and hands the next move to the listener.
는데요.explanation: 는데요 (neundeyo) = "though; you see; soft trailing ending". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 지금 좀 바쁜데요. ("I am a little busy right now, though.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 는데요, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
는데요.shortExplanation: 는데요 means "though; you see; soft trailing ending" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 는데요 as a random polite ending in every sentence.
Forgetting the adjective form: 바쁜데요, not 바쁘는데요.

usagePhrases.en: I am a little busy right now, though.
usagePhrases.note: Soft refusal or hesitation.

usagePhrases.en: The materials are not finished yet, though.
usagePhrases.note: Bad news without sounding too blunt.

examples.ko: 그 의견도 좋은데요, 시간이 조금 부족해요.
examples.romanization: geu uigyeondo joeundeyo, sigani jogeum bujokaeyo.
examples.en: That opinion is good too, but we are a little short on time.
examples.note: Soft contrast before disagreement.

ex.en: I will explain the background first.
ex.note: Context that helps the listener understand the situation.

배경.nuance: 배경 is broader than 이유. 이유 is the reason; 배경 is the surrounding context that makes the reason understandable.
배경.explanation: "background; context" is 배경 (baegyeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 배경을 설명하다 ("to explain the background"). Watch the particle attached to 배경 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
배경.shortExplanation: 배경 means "background; context" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 이유 when the listener needs a fuller context. 배경 may sound more natural.
Overusing 배경 in very casual chat where 그냥 왜냐하면 is enough.

usagePhrases.note: Useful before a proposal or disagreement.
A soft way to introduce context.

examples.en: I will explain the background first.
examples.note: Keeps the conversation organized.

ex.ko: 상대방이 모르는 내용이면 거든요가 더 자연스러워요.
ex.en: If the other person does not know it, 거든요 is more natural.
ex.note: The listener's knowledge decides the marker.

상대방.nuance: 상대방 is neutral. It is not necessarily an opponent; it can simply mean the other person in the interaction.
상대방.explanation: 상대방 (sangdaebang) = "the other person; conversation partner". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 상대방이 모를 때 ("when the other person does not know") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 상대방, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
상대방.shortExplanation: 상대방 means "the other person; conversation partner" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 상대방 always means an enemy or opponent. In conversation study, it usually means the listener.
Ignoring what the 상대방 already knows when choosing 잖아요 or 거든요.

usagePhrases.en: when the other person does not know
usagePhrases.note: Important for choosing 거든요 instead of 잖아요.

usagePhrases.en: to consider the other person's feelings
usagePhrases.note: Conversation strategy.

examples.ko: 상대방이 처음 듣는 내용이면 거든요가 더 자연스러워요.
examples.romanization: sangdaebangi cheoeum deunneun naeyongimyeon geodeunyoga deo jayeonseureowoyo.
examples.en: If the other person is hearing it for the first time, 거든요 is more natural.
examples.note: Explains the usage boundary.

ex.ko: 그 의견에는 부드럽게 반대하는 게 좋아요.
ex.en: It is better to disagree with that opinion gently.
ex.note: Names the tone this chapter is practicing.

부드럽게.nuance: 부드럽게 is about manner or tone. It does not automatically make the content polite if the sentence itself is too direct.
부드럽게.explanation: 부드럽게 (budeureopge) means "softly; gently; smoothly". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 부드럽게 말하다 ("to speak gently"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 부드럽게 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
부드럽게.shortExplanation: 부드럽게 means "softly; gently; smoothly" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling every polite sentence 부드럽게. The sentence must actually soften the delivery.
Forgetting that tone and grammar work together in Korean.

usagePhrases.note: Tone of delivery.
Useful for polite disagreement.

examples.ko: 그 의견에는 부드럽게 반대하는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: geu uigyeoneneun budeureopge bandaehaneun ge joayo.
examples.en: It is better to disagree with that opinion gently.
examples.note: Connects tone with disagreement.

ex.ko: 자료가 늦어진 이야기는 제가 먼저 말을 꺼낼게요.
ex.en: I will bring up the delayed materials first.
ex.note: 말 means words or speech here.

말을 꺼내다.nuance: 말을 꺼내다 is about starting a topic, not physically taking words out. It often implies a little hesitation or tact.
말을 꺼내다.explanation: "to bring up a topic" is 말을 꺼내다 (mareul kkeonaeda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 먼저 말을 꺼내다 ("to bring it up first"). Watch the particle attached to 말을 꺼내다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
말을 꺼내다.shortExplanation: 말을 꺼내다 means "to bring up a topic" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 말 as an unrelated animal noun. In this phrase, 말 means words or speech.
Using 말하다 when the point is initiating a difficult topic. 말을 꺼내다 is more precise.

usagePhrases.note: Starting a topic before someone else does.
Used for sensitive topics.

examples.ko: 자료가 늦어진 이야기는 제가 먼저 말을 꺼낼게요.
examples.romanization: jaryoga neujeojin iyagineun jega meonjeo mareul kkeonaelgeyo.
examples.en: I will bring up the delayed materials first.
examples.note: A real meeting or team-project sentence.

ex.en: I agree with that opinion too.
ex.note: Pairs with 의견 and polite discussion.

동의하다.nuance: 동의하다 is 同意(동의, 'same-meaning/intent') + 하다 — literally to be of the same mind, i.e. to agree with an opinion or consent to terms. Its key grammar point is the particle 에: you agree 'to/with' something, so 의견에 동의하다, 약관에 동의하다 — never 을/를. Contrast it with 찬성하다 (贊成, 'approve/support'), which is voting in favor of a proposal or course of action ('그 계획에 찬성해요'), a public stance, whereas 동의하다 is sharing a viewpoint or giving consent; you can 동의하다 that a problem exists yet not 찬성하다 the proposed solution. Also contrast 인정하다 (concede a truth) — agreeing is positive alignment, acknowledging is conceding. As a 하다 verb: 동의해요 / 동의했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: the particle (don't say 의견을 동의해요 — use 에), and the structure 'I agree that...', which in Korean is ~다는 것에 동의하다 or simply ~다고 생각해요; a bare 'I agree' in casual reply is more often 맞아요 ('that's right') or 그러게요, with 동의하다 sounding a touch formal.
동의하다.explanation: "to agree" in Korean is 동의하다 (donguihada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 동의해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 동의하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 의견에 동의하다 ("to agree with an opinion") — then reshape the same stem into 동의하고 싶어요 (desire), 동의할 수 있어요 (ability), and 동의할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
동의하다.shortExplanation: 동의하다 means "to agree" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 동의하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 동의해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Marking the opinion with 을/를 (그 의견을 동의해요). 동의하다 governs 에: 그 의견에 동의해요.
Confusing 동의하다 with 찬성하다. Consenting to a view (동의) ≠ supporting a proposal (찬성). 'I'm in favor of the plan' is 계획에 찬성해요.
Using formal 동의해요 for every casual 'yeah, I agree'. In chat Koreans more often say 맞아요 / 그러게요; 동의하다 fits opinions, debates, and official consent.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 동의하다 becomes 동의할 수 있어요 ("can") and 동의할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
What you agree with takes 에: 그 말에 동의해요, 생각에 동의해요.

examples.en: I agree with that too
examples.note: 도 ('also') + 말에 동의하다 — backing someone up in conversation.

examples.en: Do you agree to the terms of service?
examples.note: 약관에 동의하다 in its native habitat, the consent checkbox.

examples.en: I agree on that point, but I'm against the method
examples.note: 동의하지만 ('agree but') sets up a polite disagreement on the how.

ex.en: I disagree with that opinion a little, though.
ex.note: Use -는데요 to make disagreement less abrupt.

반대하다.nuance: 반대하다 means to oppose, object to, or be against something (反 'reverse/anti' + 對 'face/oppose', literally 'to face in the opposite direction'). The single most important thing for intermediate learners is the PARTICLE: the thing you oppose takes 에, never 을/를 — 의견에 반대하다, 계획에 반대하다. English 'oppose X' treats X as a direct object, so learners overwhelmingly write 의견을 반대해요, which is wrong. As a 하다 verb it contracts to 반대해요. Its clean antonym is 찬성하다 (to be in favor), which shares the same 에 frame. Keep it apart from 거부하다 (to refuse): 반대하다 is taking a stance against an idea in discussion, while 거부하다 is actively turning down a concrete request or offer.
반대하다.explanation: "to oppose" in Korean is 반대하다 (bandaehada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 반대해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 반대하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 의견에 반대하다 ("to oppose an opinion") — then reshape the same stem into 반대하고 싶어요 (desire), 반대할 수 있어요 (ability), and 반대할 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
반대하다.shortExplanation: 반대하다 means "to oppose" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 반대하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 반대해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 을/를 — the verb is intransitive here, so it must be 의견에 반대해요, not 의견을 반대해요.
Writing 반대하요 instead of the contracted 반대해요.
Mixing it with 거부하다 (refuse a request); 반대하다 is opposing a view, 거부하다 is rejecting a concrete offer.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 반대하다 becomes 반대할 수 있어요 ("can") and 반대할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Critical particle: the thing opposed takes 에, NOT 을/를.

examples.en: I don't oppose that opinion
examples.note: 에 반대하다 in the negative; 그 의견에 marks what you're against.

examples.en: My parents opposed the marriage
examples.note: 결혼에 반대하셨어요 with honorific -시-; the classic family-drama line.

examples.en: Why do you oppose the plan?
examples.note: Asking someone's reason; 계획에 반대하세요 keeps the 에 particle.

ex.en: If you say it like that, the mood becomes a little stiff.
ex.note: Discourse markers affect the mood of a conversation.

분위기.nuance: 분위기 (雰圍氣, 雰 'mist/vapor' + 圍 'surround' + 氣 'air/energy') is literally 'the air that surrounds you' — the collective mood of a place, gathering, or moment. The sharp contrast is 분위기 vs 기분: 분위기 is the SHARED vibe in the room (회식 분위기가 좋다), while 기분 is one person's INNER feeling (제 기분이 좋다 'I'm in a good mood'). Mixing them is the classic error: 'I'm in a good mood' is 기분이 좋아요, not 분위기가 좋아요 (which describes the room, not you). Habitual partners: 분위기가 좋다/편안하다/어색하다, 분위기를 띄우다/바꾸다, 분위기가 가라앉다, 분위기를 깨다 ('kill the mood'). 분위기 있다 colloquially means 'has a classy/romantic ambiance.' The English-speaker pitfall, beyond 기분 confusion, is the particle: 분위기를 좋다 ✗ → 분위기가 좋다 ✓.
분위기.explanation: 분위기 (bunwigi) means "atmosphere; mood". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 분위기가 좋아요 ("the atmosphere is nice"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 분위기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
분위기.shortExplanation: 분위기 means "atmosphere; mood" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 분위기 (shared room vibe) with 기분 (your own mood) — 'I feel good' is 기분이 좋아요, not 분위기가 좋아요
Saying 분위기를 좋다 ✗ — 좋다 is descriptive, so use 가: 분위기가 좋다 ✓
Forgetting 분위기를 깨다 ('to kill the mood') when describing someone spoiling the vibe

usagePhrases.note: descriptive 좋다 takes 가
띄우다 (lift) takes object 를
바꾸다 = change the vibe
어색하다 describes a tense vibe

examples.en: The atmosphere is nice.
examples.note: simplest vibe sentence with 가

examples.ko: 이 카페는 분위기가 정말 편안해서 자주 와요.
examples.romanization: i kapeneun bunwigiga jeongmal pyeonanhaeseo jaju wayo.
examples.en: This cafe has a really relaxing atmosphere, so I come often.
examples.note: 분위기가 편안하다 — describing a place's vibe

examples.ko: 회식 분위기가 가라앉아서 제가 농담으로 분위기를 띄웠어요.
examples.romanization: hoesik bunwigiga garaanjaseo jega nongdameuro bunwigireul ttuiwosseoyo.
examples.en: The company-dinner mood sank, so I lifted it with a joke.
examples.note: real-situation: 분위기가 가라앉다 vs 분위기를 띄우다 (passive sink / active lift)

ex.en: When I tried going, it was better than I expected.
ex.note: Experience leads into a firsthand observation.

보니까.nuance: 보니까 is evidence-based. It sounds odd if you did not actually see, try, or check the thing.
보니까.explanation: 보니까 (bonikka) = "when I saw/tried/checked". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 가 보니까 ("when I went and saw / tried going") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 보니까, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
보니까.shortExplanation: 보니까 means "when I saw/tried/checked" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 보니까 for pure hearsay. If someone only told you, use a reported-speech form instead.
Forgetting the try/check meaning in 가 보다 or 확인해 보다.

usagePhrases.en: when I went and saw / tried going
usagePhrases.note: Useful after visiting a place.
Useful for information you verified.

examples.ko: 그 식당에 가 보니까 생각보다 조용하더라고요.
examples.romanization: geu sikdange ga bonikka saenggakboda joyonghadeoragoyo.
examples.en: When I tried going to that restaurant, it was quieter than I expected.
examples.note: Experience leads to a firsthand observation.

ex.en: There were more people than I expected, I noticed.
ex.note: Reports what the speaker personally saw.

더라고요.nuance: 더라고요 is not just past tense. It carries the speaker's evidence and realization.
더라고요.explanation: 더라고요 (deoragoyo) means "I noticed; it turned out". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 생각보다 괜찮더라고요. ("It was better than I expected."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 더라고요 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
더라고요.shortExplanation: 더라고요 means "I noticed; it turned out" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 더라고요 for something you only heard from someone else.
Using it for your own planned action as if you observed yourself from outside.

usagePhrases.en: It was better than I expected.
usagePhrases.note: Common review-style observation.

usagePhrases.en: There were a lot of people, I noticed.
usagePhrases.note: Firsthand scene report.

examples.en: These days, the atmosphere has changed a lot, I noticed.
examples.note: Reports a noticed change.

더니.en: I observed X, and then Y happened

ex.en: It was quiet at first, and then it quickly got crowded, I noticed.

더니.nuance: Plain -더니 has an eyewitness feel. For your own action causing a result, -았/었더니 is usually the safer form.
더니.explanation: "I observed X, and then Y happened" is 더니 (deoni). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 처음에는 조용하더니 ("it was quiet at first, and then..."). Watch the particle attached to 더니 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
더니.shortExplanation: 더니 means "I observed X, and then Y happened" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 내가 가더니 for your own neutral action. Use 갔더니 when your own action led to a result.
Using -더니 when there is no change or result after the first observation.

usagePhrases.en: it was quiet at first, and then...
usagePhrases.note: Observed state followed by change.
Observed repeated action followed by result.

examples.en: It was quiet at first, and then there were quickly more people.
examples.note: A direct observed change.

ex.en: It was quiet at first, and then there were quickly more people.
ex.note: Sets the first stage before a change.

처음에는.nuance: 처음에는 points to the first stage. It needs a later stage to feel complete.
처음에는.explanation: 처음에는 (cheoeumeneun) means "at first". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 처음에는 조용하다 ("to be quiet at first"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 처음에는 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
처음에는.shortExplanation: 처음에는 means "at first" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 처음에는 without showing what changed afterward.
Confusing 처음에는 with 처음으로, which means 'for the first time.'

usagePhrases.note: Early state before a change.
Before later realization.

examples.en: It was quiet at first, and then it quickly got crowded.
examples.note: Natural setup for an observed change.

ex.en: I heard there used to be fewer people.

예전에는.nuance: 예전에는 is broader than 어제 or 지난주. It points to an earlier period, not one exact moment.
예전에는.explanation: "in the past; before" is 예전에는 (yejeoneneun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 예전에는 조용했어요. ("It used to be quiet."). Watch the particle attached to 예전에는 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
예전에는.shortExplanation: 예전에는 means "in the past; before" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 예전에는 for a single recent event when 어제 or 지난번 is clearer.
Forgetting the contrast when using 예전에는 in a change sentence.

usagePhrases.note: Past state.

usagePhrases.en: There used to be few people.
usagePhrases.note: Past comparison.

examples.en: It used to be quiet, but these days there are many people, I noticed.
examples.note: Before-now contrast.

ex.en: These days, the atmosphere has changed a lot, I noticed.

요즘은.nuance: 요즘은 is not just today. It means the recent/current period.
요즘은.explanation: 요즘은 (yojeumeun) = "these days; nowadays". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 요즘은 사람이 많아요. ("These days there are many people.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 요즘은, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
요즘은.shortExplanation: 요즘은 means "these days; nowadays" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 요즘은 for one event that happened only today.
Forgetting that 요즘은 often invites a contrast with before.

usagePhrases.en: These days there are many people.
usagePhrases.note: Current state.

usagePhrases.en: The atmosphere has changed these days.
usagePhrases.note: Current change.

examples.en: These days, the number of customers has increased a lot, I noticed.
examples.note: Current observation after change.

ex.en: At first, the restaurant was quiet, I noticed.

조용하다.nuance: 조용하다 is the opposite of 시끄럽다 and covers both a quiet PLACE/sound and a calm, reserved PERSONALITY (성격이 조용하다 = soft-spoken, low-key). As a 하다-adjective it conjugates regularly: 조용하다 → 조용해요 → 조용한 → 조용히(adverb, note the special 히 form) → 조용해서. The most useful distinction for English speakers is the adverb: 'be quiet!' is 조용히 해! (using 조용히), not 조용하게 — Koreans overwhelmingly use 조용히 here, so memorize it as a set phrase. The near-synonym 고요하다 is more literary/poetic and means a deep, serene stillness (고요한 밤 'a serene night'), whereas 조용하다 is the everyday neutral word you'd actually speak. Pitfall: writing 조용하요 instead of the contracted 조용해요, and reaching for 조용하게 when 조용히 is the natural adverb. Register is neutral and extremely common.
조용하다.explanation: "quiet" is 조용하다 (joyonghada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 조용한 곳 ("a quiet place"). Watch the particle attached to 조용하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
조용하다.shortExplanation: 조용하다 means "quiet" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 조용하요 — the 하다 contraction yields 조용해요.
Saying 조용하게 해 for 'be quiet.' The idiomatic adverb is 조용히, so it should be 조용히 해 주세요.
Using 조용하다 of a person to imply they are boring; it neutrally means calm/reserved, and adding nuance like 'boring' needs a different word such as 재미없다.

usagePhrases.note: modifier 조용한 (하 + ㄴ); the go-to phrase for a peaceful spot
adverb 조용히 + 하다; 조용히 해! is the everyday 'be quiet!'

관찰하다.nuance: 관찰하다 is useful for deliberate observation. For a casual visit, 가 보니까 or 보니까 often sounds more natural.
관찰하다.explanation: "to observe" is 관찰하다 (gwanchalhada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 변화를 관찰하다 ("to observe a change"). Watch the particle attached to 관찰하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
관찰하다.shortExplanation: 관찰하다 means "to observe" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 관찰하다 for every casual noticing. It can sound too deliberate or academic.
Forgetting that 더라고요 still needs firsthand evidence, even if the verb 관찰하다 is not used.

usagePhrases.note: Careful observation over time.
Watching how someone responds.

다고 했어요.nuance: 다고 했어요 reports a statement, not a question or command. Match the inner ending to the sentence type.
다고 했어요.explanation: 다고 했어요 (dago haesseoyo) means "said that...". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 금요일에 본다고 했어요. ("They said we will take it on Friday."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 다고 했어요 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
다고 했어요.shortExplanation: 다고 했어요 means "said that..." and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using -다고 for questions. A reported question needs -냐고.
Forgetting present action-verb forms like 간다고 and 먹는다고.

usagePhrases.en: They said we will take it on Friday.

usagePhrases.en: They said they are busy today.

ex.en: My friend asked what time we are meeting.

냐고 물어봤어요.nuance: 냐고 is for reported questions. Do not switch to -다고 just because the whole sentence now ends like a statement.
냐고 물어봤어요.explanation: "asked whether/if..." is 냐고 물어봤어요 (nyago mureobwasseoyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 몇 시에 만나냐고 물어봤어요. ("They asked what time we are meeting."). Watch the particle attached to 냐고 물어봤어요 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
냐고 물어봤어요.shortExplanation: 냐고 물어봤어요 means "asked whether/if..." and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 언제 온다고 물어봤어요 when you mean 'asked when they are coming'. Use 언제 오냐고 물어봤어요.
Overusing the formal textbook -느냐고 in everyday conversation when -냐고 is natural.

usagePhrases.en: They asked what time we are meeting.

usagePhrases.en: They asked whether I submitted the homework.

examples.en: My friend asked when the exam is.

ex.en: Do you know when the exam is?

는지.nuance: 는지 is not reported speech by itself. It embeds a question so verbs like 알다, 모르다, 확인하다, and 궁금하다 can use it.
는지.explanation: 는지 (neunji) = "whether; what/when/where... inside a sentence". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 시험이 언제인지 알아요? ("Do you know when the exam is?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 는지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
는지.shortExplanation: 는지 means "whether; what/when/where... inside a sentence" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using -냐고 when no one asked a question. If you just do not know the answer, use -는지.
Using -는지 for a direct quote instead of an embedded question.

usagePhrases.en: Do you know when the exam is?
usagePhrases.note: Embedded question with 이다.

라고 하다.nuance: 라고 하다 for instructions is separate from noun +(이)라고 하다, as in 학생이라고 했어요.
라고 하다.explanation: 라고 하다 (rago hada) means "to tell someone to...". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 숙제를 제출하라고 하셨어요. ("They told us to submit the homework."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 라고 하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
라고 하다.shortExplanation: 라고 하다 means "to tell someone to..." and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using -다고 하다 for commands: 제출한다고 하셨어요 means 'said they will submit', not 'told us to submit'.
Confusing reported command -(으)라고 with noun quote -(이)라고.

usagePhrases.en: They told us to submit the homework.

대요.nuance: 대요 is common, but first learn what it expands from so you do not mix statements with questions.
대요.explanation: "they say; I heard that" is 대요 (daeyo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 내일 온대요. ("They say they are coming tomorrow."). Watch the particle attached to 대요 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
대요.shortExplanation: 대요 means "they say; I heard that" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 대요 for reported questions. Questions contract to 냬요 in casual speech.
Forgetting the source of the information when using 대요.

usagePhrases.en: They say they are coming tomorrow.

다시 말하다.nuance: 다시 말하다 is not just the adverb 다시. It is a practical repair phrase when reported information is unclear.
다시 말하다.explanation: 다시 말하다 (dasi malhada) means "to say again; to repeat". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 다시 말해 주세요. ("Please say it again."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 다시 말하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
다시 말하다.shortExplanation: 다시 말하다 means "to say again; to repeat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 다시 말하다 as only the word 다시. The useful chunk is the whole phrase.
Using it when you need 확인하다 instead: 다시 말하다 repeats; 확인하다 checks.

usagePhrases.note: Polite repeat request.
Restating the point.

cluster.title: 말하다 vs 이야기하다
cluster.rule: Use 말하다 for producing words — saying one thing, or speaking a language. Use 이야기하다 when there's a back-and-forth or a story being told: chatting with someone, usually marked with 와/과 or 하고.

members.hint: the two-way chat verb, with 하고/와

ex.en: They asked whether I submitted the homework.
ex.note: A practical school/work verb for reported questions.

제출하다.nuance: 제출하다 is Sino-Korean 提出 — 提 'lift/raise up' + 出 'out' — so 'put forward, hand out', i.e. formally submit a document, application, or assignment to an authority. Its register is the key point: 제출하다 is the formal, official word, while everyday speech often just uses 내다 'to put out/hand in' — students say 숙제를 냈어요 casually but write 과제를 제출했습니다 formally. The opposite side of the transaction is 받다 'to receive'/접수하다 'to accept (a submission)'. The English-speaker pitfall: 'submit TO the office' tempts an English-style structure, but the destination simply takes 에 (사무실에 제출하다) and the document is a direct object (서류를 제출하다). As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (제출해요, 제출했어요, formal 제출합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (제출 안 해요, 제출 못 해요). Note pronunciation [제출하다] is straightforward, but watch the polite request form 제출해 주세요.
제출하다.explanation: 제출하다 (jechulhada) means "to submit". Start from the polite form 제출해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 제출하다. A strong first sentence is 서류를 제출하다 ("to submit documents"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 제출하다 also becomes 제출하고 싶어요 (want), 제출할 수 있어요 (can), and 제출 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.
제출하다.shortExplanation: 제출하다 means "to submit" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 제출하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 제출해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 제출하다 in casual chat where it sounds stiff — among friends, handing in homework is naturally 숙제 냈어? 제출하다 is the formal/written register.
Confusing it with 받다 (receive) — you 제출하다 (submit) papers TO an office, which then 받다/접수하다 (receives) them; they are opposite ends.
Writing the negative as 안 제출해요 — split it: 제출 안 해요 (impossible = 제출 못 해요).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 제출하다 becomes 제출할 수 있어요 ("can") and 제출할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
서류 = documents/papers; the thing handed in takes 을/를

examples.en: I have to hand in the homework by today.
examples.note: 오늘까지 = by today (deadline with 까지); obligation 제출해야 해요

examples.en: Please submit this application here.
examples.note: 여기에 = to here; ~아 주세요 = please do (for me)

examples.ko: 서류가 부족해서 지금 제출 못 해요.

examples.note: 부족하다 = be lacking; impossible split: 제출 못 해요

ex.en: I checked the message content.

내용.nuance: 내용 (內容, 內 'inside' + 容 'contain') is the substance or gist inside something — a book, message, lecture, contract — as opposed to its outer form. The sharp contrast is 내용 (what it says) vs 형식 (the form/format): a report can have weak 내용 but proper 형식. Don't confuse it with a physical container either; the box itself is 상자/봉투, while 내용물 specifically means the physical 'contents' (items) inside a package. Typical partners: 내용을 이해하다/정리하다/확인하다, 내용이 어렵다/풍부하다, 회의 내용, 문자 내용. The English-speaker pitfall is particle choice driven by the adjective: 'the content is hard' becomes 내용이 어렵다 ✓, not 내용을 어렵다 ✗ — 를/을 attaches only to action verbs like 이해하다, never to descriptive 어렵다.
내용.explanation: "content; contents" is 내용 (naeyong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 내용이 어려워요 ("the content is hard"). Watch the particle attached to 내용 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
내용.shortExplanation: 내용 means "content; contents" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 내용을 어렵다 ✗ — 어렵다 is descriptive, so use 이: 내용이 어렵다 ✓
Using 내용 for the physical box/wrapper — that is 상자/봉투; physical contents inside are 내용물
Confusing 내용 (substance) with 형식 (form/format) when contrasting what a text says vs how it looks

usagePhrases.note: descriptive adjective takes 이, not 을
이해하다 (understand) takes object 을
정리하다 = organize/sum up neatly
확인하다 = verify; common in work email

examples.en: The content is hard.
examples.note: simplest state sentence with 이

examples.en: I summarized the meeting content briefly and sent it.

올라온 공지.nuance: 올라온 is not a separate full sentence here. It sits before 공지 and tells you which notice.
올라온 공지.explanation: "a notice that was posted" is 올라온 공지 (ollaon gongji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어제 올라온 공지 ("the notice posted yesterday"). Watch the particle attached to 올라온 공지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. 올라온 공지.shortExplanation: 올라온 공지 means "a notice that was posted" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 올라온 as a separate sentence and losing the final noun 공지.
Confusing 올라온 공지 with 올라갈 공지. 올라온 is already posted; 올라갈 is going to be posted.

변경된 일정.nuance: 변경된 focuses on the resulting state. It sounds natural in notices, emails, and announcements.
변경된 일정.explanation: 변경된 일정 (byeongyeongdoen iljeong) means "changed schedule". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 변경된 일정 ("changed schedule"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 변경된 일정 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. 변경된 일정.shortExplanation: 변경된 일정 means "changed schedule" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

제출할 보고서.explanation: 제출할 보고서 (jechulhal bogoseo) = "a report to submit". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 내일 제출할 보고서 ("the report to submit tomorrow") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 제출할 보고서, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
제출할 보고서.shortExplanation: 제출할 보고서 means "a report to submit" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading 제출할 as a standalone future sentence instead of a modifier for 보고서.
Confusing 제출할 보고서 with 제출한 보고서.

먹이다.nuance: The subject is the causer, not the person eating.
먹이다.explanation: 먹이다 (meogida) = "to feed / to make someone take". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 아이에게 약을 먹이다 ("to give a child medicine") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 먹이다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. 먹이다.shortExplanation: 먹이다 means "to feed / to make someone take" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

앉히다.nuance: 앉다 is what the person does; 앉히다 is what someone else does to seat them.
앉히다.explanation: 앉히다 (anjhida) means "to seat someone". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 앞자리에 앉히다 ("to seat someone in the front row"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 앉히다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
앉히다.shortExplanation: 앉히다 means "to seat someone" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Do not say 손님을 앉았어요; use 손님을 앉혔어요.

ex.ko: 안내 문자가 변경 사항을 알려 줬어요.
ex.en: The 안내 text message informed me of the changes.
ex.note: Causative-like lexical verb: make information known.

알리다.nuance: 알리다 is the causative of 알다 ('to know'), so literally 'to make (someone) know' — you give a piece of information to a person, who takes 에게/한테, while the fact taught takes 을/를. The form you will reach for ten times a day is 알려 주세요 ('please let me know'), used to ask for an address, a time, a price, or any update. The near-synonym 가르치다 also means 'let know', but 가르치다 leans toward teaching a skill or directions ('역으로 가는 길 좀 가르쳐 주세요'), while 알리다 is just transmitting a fact ('결과를 알려 주세요'). The classic learner error is using plain 알다: 알아요 means 'I know' (a state), and you cannot make a request with it — you must use the causative 알려 주세요 to mean 'inform me'. Beyond person-to-person, 알리다 also covers public announcing — '진실을 세상에 알리다' (reveal the truth to the world).
알리다.explanation: 알리다 (alli-da) = "to inform / let know". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 알려요 plus one useful sentence like 주소 좀 알려 주세요. ("Please let me know the address."). After that the endings carry the meaning — 알리고 싶어요 for what you want, 알릴 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 알려요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
알리다.shortExplanation: 알리다 means "to inform / let know" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 알리다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 알려요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Use 알려 주세요 to ask someone to tell you; plain 알아요 only means 'I know' (a state) and cannot make a request.
Do not say 알려 주세요 when you mean teaching a route or skill — that is closer to 가르쳐 주세요; 알려 주세요 is for transmitting a fact.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 알리다 becomes 알릴 수 있어요 ("can") and 알릴 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not inform / let know.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to inform / let know.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to inform / let know.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.

usagePhrases.en: Please let me know the address.
usagePhrases.note: Everyday request for a piece of information

examples.en: Please let me know as soon as you arrive.
examples.note: Note 알려 주세요, the form you will use constantly

examples.en: If the schedule changes I will let you know in advance.
examples.note: 알려 줄게요 = a promise to inform you

examples.en: Do not tell anyone about this yet.
examples.note: 알리지 마세요 = please keep it quiet

ex.ko: 긴 문장은 먼저 명사구를 찾아서 읽어요.
ex.en: For long sentences, first find the noun phrases.
ex.note: This chapter is about unpacking compressed sentence structure.

문장.nuance: 문장(文章)은 '글월 문 + 글 장'으로, 주어와 서술어를 갖춰 생각을 완결되게 표현하는 한 덩어리의 말이에요. 비슷해 보이는 '글'은 문장이 여러 개 모인 더 큰 글덩이(에세이·기사 전체)를 뜻하고, '문구'는 짧은 어구나 문장 한 토막을 가리켜서 범위가 달라요. 또 '단어/낱말'은 더 작은 단위라, 낱말 하나만으로는 '문장'이 되지 않아요. 영어 화자는 sentence를 무조건 '문장'으로 옮기지만, 표지판의 'No smoking' 같은 짧은 문구는 한국어로 '문구'가 더 자연스러울 때가 있어요. 또 sentence에 '형(刑)을 선고하다'라는 뜻도 있는데 그건 한국어 '문장'과 전혀 무관하니 직역하면 안 돼요. '문장을 만들다/짓다/외우다/읽다'와 잘 어울립니다.
문장.explanation: 문장 (munjang) means "sentence". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 문장을 만들다 ("make a sentence"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 문장 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.
문장.shortExplanation: 문장 means "sentence" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
낱말 하나는 '문장'이 아니에요. 주어와 서술어가 갖춰져 뜻이 끝나야 문장이라고 해요.
'문장을 외우다'(이미 있는 문장을 암기)와 '문장을 만들다'(새로 짓기)는 뜻이 달라요. 새로 작문하는 것은 '만들다/짓다'입니다.
영어 sentence의 '형벌 선고' 뜻을 '문장'으로 옮기면 안 돼요. 그 뜻은 한국어로 '선고/형'이고 '문장'과는 관계가 없습니다.

usagePhrases.note: 새로 짓는다는 뜻이라 '만들다'를 써요
형용사 '짧다'가 관형형 '짧은'으로 꾸며요
소리 내어 읽을 때 '읽다'를 써요
보기 예(例) + 글월 문(文), 즉 보기로 드는 문장

examples.en: Try making a sentence with this word.
examples.note: '-아/어 보세요'는 가볍게 시도해 보라는 권유예요.

examples.en: I practice starting from short sentences.
examples.note: '부터'는 시작점을 찍어 '~에서부터'의 출발을 나타내요.

examples.en: The teacher read the sentences slowly for us.
examples.note: '읽어 주다'는 남을 위해 읽어 줌, '-셨-'은 선생님 높임이에요.

ex.ko: 기사에는 변경된 일정과 새 규칙이 함께 나왔어요.
ex.en: The article included the changed schedule and the new rule together.
ex.note: News prose often uses noun modification and passive/result forms.

기사.nuance: 기사 (記事, 記 'record/write down' + 事 'matter, event') means a news article or report — a single written piece of journalism in a newspaper, magazine, or online; the hanja literally means 'a written record of an event'. Distinguish it carefully from neighbors: 언론 is the press as an institution, 보도 (報道) is the ACT of reporting, and 기사 is the concrete written unit of content that results. A crucial English-speaker pitfall is the homonym trap: 기사 is also a completely separate word meaning 'driver' (司機/운전기사) — and historically 'knight' (騎士) — so 택시 기사 is 'taxi driver', not 'taxi article'; only context tells which 기사 is meant. Natural collocations: 기사를 쓰다, 기사가 나다, 신문 기사, 기사를 검색하다. Don't reach for 기사 when you mean the abstract media institution — that is 언론.
기사.explanation: "(news) article; report" is 기사 (gisa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 기사를 쓰다 ("to write an article"). Watch the particle attached to 기사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
기사.shortExplanation: 기사 means "(news) article; report" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing the two senses of 기사 — 'news article' (記事) versus 'driver' (운전기사); 택시 기사 is a taxi driver, so rely on context to disambiguate.
Using 기사 for the abstract media institution — that is 언론, while 기사 is one specific written article.
Saying 기사를 만들다 ('make an article') by translating loosely — a reporter 기사를 쓰다 (writes it); 만들다 doesn't collocate with a news article.

usagePhrases.note: 쓰다 is the standard verb from the journalist's side; 기자가 기사를 쓰다 ('a reporter writes an article').

usagePhrases.en: an article comes out / is published
usagePhrases.note: 나다 ('come out') is idiomatic for an article appearing in print or online.
신문 ('newspaper', 新聞) + 기사; the most common compound for a print article.
검색하다 ('search', 檢索) for finding articles online, e.g. by keyword or date.

examples.en: I read one article in today's newspaper.
examples.note: Graded-simple: 신문에서 = 'in the newspaper'; 하나 counts the article casually.

examples.ko: 그 사건에 대한 기사가 모든 신문에 났어요.
examples.romanization: geu sageone daehan gisaga modeun sinmune nasseoyo.
examples.en: An article about that incident came out in every newspaper.
examples.note: Everyday: ~에 대한 기사 = 'an article about ~'; 기사가 나다 = 'an article comes out', the set verb.

examples.ko: 요즘은 종이 신문보다 온라인 기사를 더 많이 봐요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun jongi sinmunboda ollain gisareul deo mani bwayo.
examples.en: These days I read online articles more than paper newspapers.
examples.note: Real-situation: 온라인 기사 = 'online article'; ~보다 더 많이 = 'more than ~', a comparison frame.

수밖에 없다.en: to have no choice but to

ex.en: The deadline is today, so we have no choice but to work late.
ex.note: No-choice situation caused by a real constraint.

수밖에 없다.nuance: 수밖에 없다 is resignation to the only remaining option, not inability.
수밖에 없다.explanation: "to have no choice but to" is 수밖에 없다 (subakke eopsda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 야근할 수밖에 없어요. ("I have no choice but to work late."). Watch the particle attached to 수밖에 없다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
수밖에 없다.shortExplanation: 수밖에 없다 means "to have no choice but to" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 할 수 없어요 when you mean 'I have no choice but to do it.' 할 수 없어요 means you cannot do it.
Writing 수 밖에 with a space in this fixed expression. Use 수밖에.

usagePhrases.en: I have no choice but to work late.
usagePhrases.note: Deadline pressure.

usagePhrases.en: I have no choice but to check again.
usagePhrases.note: Only realistic next step.

examples.ko: 마감이 오늘이라서 이 방법을 선택할 수밖에 없어요.
examples.romanization: magami oneuriraseo i bangbeobeul seontaekal subakke eopseoyo.
examples.en: The deadline is today, so we have no choice but to choose this method.
examples.note: No-choice situation plus reason.

ex.en: There is no way we would give up now.
ex.note: Strong disbelief, not a soft guess.

리가 없다.nuance: 리가 없다 carries confidence or emotional conviction. It is not a neutral maybe-not.
리가 없다.explanation: 리가 없다 (riga eopsda) = "there is no way that". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 지금 포기할 리가 없어요. ("There is no way we would give up now.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 리가 없다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
리가 없다.shortExplanation: 리가 없다 means "there is no way that" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 방법이 없다 for 'there is no way that.' 방법이 없다 means there is no method.
Using 리가 없다 when you only mean a soft guess. For uncertainty, use -(으)ㄹ지도 몰라요 or 아마 아닐 거예요.

usagePhrases.en: There is no way we would give up now.
usagePhrases.note: Strong disbelief about giving up.

usagePhrases.en: There is no way the data is wrong.
usagePhrases.note: Past possibility is strongly rejected.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 마감을 잊었을 리가 없어요.
examples.romanization: geu sarami magameul ijeosseul liga eopseoyo.
examples.en: There is no way that person forgot the deadline.
examples.note: Strong logical disbelief.

ex.en: The only thing left is this method.
ex.note: Limits the situation to one option.

뿐이다.nuance: 뿐이다 closes the scope. It differs from 뿐만 아니라, which opens the sentence to an additional point.
뿐이다.explanation: 뿐이다 (ppunida) means "to be only; to be nothing but". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 기다릴 뿐이에요. ("I am only waiting."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 뿐이다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
뿐이다.shortExplanation: 뿐이다 means "to be only; to be nothing but" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 뿐이다 with 뿐만 아니라. 뿐이다 means only; 뿐만 아니라 means not only but also.
Using 만 when the whole action, not just a noun, needs limiting.

usagePhrases.note: Only this action, nothing more.

usagePhrases.en: The only thing left is this method.
usagePhrases.note: Only remaining option.

examples.ko: 결국 우리가 할 수 있는 건 수정뿐이에요.
examples.romanization: gyeolguk uriga hal su inneun geon sujeongppunieyo.
examples.en: In the end, all we can do is revise it.
examples.note: Limits the choice to one remaining action.

ex.en: If the deadline is today, it cannot be helped.

어쩔 수 없죠.nuance: Casual-polite phrase for gracefully accepting something outside your control — a verbal shrug built from 어찌하다 ('to do how/what') contracted to 어쩌다 → 어쩔 수 없다 ('there's no way to do anything about it'). The -죠 softens the inevitability with 'right? / don't you agree?' — making the resignation feel communal rather than bitter. The closest near-synonym is 할 수 없죠, nearly interchangeable in most situations. The sharper contrast is with 포기하다 ('to give up'): 어쩔 수 없죠 is passive ACCEPTANCE of a situation that was never in your hands, while 포기하다 is an ACTIVE choice to stop something you could have continued. Tone is everything: said calmly it reads as mature and easygoing; said with a sharp sigh or flat affect, it tips into passive-aggressive 'fine, whatever.' The adverb variant 어쩔 수 없이 is a separate form that modifies verbs ('I unavoidably went') and cannot substitute for the standalone phrase.
어쩔 수 없죠.explanation: "It can't be helped / Nothing we can do / Oh well (accepting an unavoidable situation)" — that is 어쩔 수 없죠 (eojjeol su eopjyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 비가 오니까 어쩔 수 없죠. ("Well, it's raining, so it can't be helped."). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
어쩔 수 없죠.shortExplanation: 어쩔 수 없죠 is a practical expression meaning "It can't be helped / Nothing we can do / Oh well (accepting an unavoidable situation)".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Don't use it about things within your control. Saying 어쩔 수 없죠 about a choice you could make sounds like a dodge — it claims the situation is genuinely out of your hands.
Don't confuse the two forms: 어쩔 수 없죠 (a standalone 'it can't be helped') vs 어쩔 수 없이 (the adverb 'unavoidably' before a verb, e.g. 어쩔 수 없이 갔어요).
Watch the spelling/sound: it's 어쩔 (double ㅉ), not 어절. And 없죠 is pronounced 'eopjyo', a contraction of 없지요.

usagePhrases.en: Well, it's raining, so it can't be helped.
usagePhrases.note: -(으)니까 gives the reason the situation is fixed

usagePhrases.en: Can't be helped — let's go next time.
usagePhrases.note: 어쩔 수 없지 = casual

usagePhrases.en: If it's sold out, oh well, nothing to do.
usagePhrases.note: Trailing 뭐 adds a resigned shrug

usagePhrases.en: I had no choice but to take a taxi.
usagePhrases.note: 어쩔 수 없이 = the adverb 'unavoidably'

examples.ko: A: 오늘 문 닫았네요. / B: 어쩔 수 없죠.
examples.romanization: A: oneul mun dadanneyo. / B: eojjeol su eopsjyo.
examples.en: A: They're closed today. B: Oh well, can't be helped.
examples.note: Quick, calm resignation — no blame, no distress, just acceptance

examples.ko: A: 기차표가 다 매진이에요. / B: 그래요? 어쩔 수 없죠, 버스 타죠 뭐.
examples.romanization: A: gichapyoga da maejinieyo. / B: geuraeyo? eojjeol su eopsjyo, beoseu tajyo mwo.
examples.en: A: The train tickets are all sold out. B: Oh well — let's just take the bus then.
examples.note: Graceful acceptance followed immediately by a practical fallback — the -죠 on 버스 타죠 recruits agreement

examples.ko: 몸이 안 좋으면 쉬어야죠, 어쩔 수 없어요.
examples.romanization: momi an joeumyeon swieoyajyo, eojjeol su eopseoyo.
examples.en: If you're not well you have to rest — there's no other way.
examples.note: 어쩔 수 없어요 = flatter, plainer final statement; used when the concession has already been discussed

ex.en: Today I have no choice but to work late.

야근하다.nuance: 야근하다 is the verb every Korean office worker knows: to stay and work into the evening, past regular hours. The hanja 夜勤 is 夜 'night' + 勤 'work/service' (the same 勤 as in 근무), literally 'night-work'. Its form is neutral, but in real use it almost always carries a tired, faintly complaining tone, because overtime is a charged feature of Korean work culture; the noun 야근 anchors a whole vocabulary of grievance — 야근 수당 (OT pay), 야근 잦아요 (lots of overtime), 칼퇴 (leaving right on time, the dream). The sharp boundary is against 야간근무: 야근 is staying late on an otherwise daytime job, whereas 야간근무 is a scheduled night shift (nurses, security, factory lines). Don't equate it with English 'overtime' as a contractual category either — that abstract concept is 초과근무 / 시간 외 근무. And for an all-nighter it escalates to 밤샘. Habitual collocations: 야근하다, 야근 수당, 야근이 잦다, 야근 안 하다.
야근하다.explanation: 야근하다 (yageunhada) means "to work overtime (work late)". Start from the polite form 야근해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 야근하다. A strong first sentence is 야근 수당 ("overtime pay"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 야근하다 also becomes 야근하고 싶어요 (want), 야근할 수 있어요 (can), and 야근할 수 없어요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.
야근하다.shortExplanation: 야근하다 means "to work overtime (work late)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 야근하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 야근해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
야근하다 is not the contract concept 'overtime' — that's 초과근무 / 시간 외 근무. 야근 specifically = staying and working into the evening on a day job.
Don't use 야근하다 for a planned night shift; that's 야간근무. A nurse on rotation works 야간근무, not 야근.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 야근하다 becomes 야근할 수 있어요 ("can") and 야근할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not work overtime (work late).
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to work overtime (work late).
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to work overtime (work late).
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
야근 + 수당 'allowance'; the money you get for staying late — a frequent gripe topic.

examples.en: I'm working late again today.
examples.note: 오늘도 'again today' nails the weary office mood; present tense for a recurring reality.

examples.ko: 마감 때문에 이번 주 내내 야근했어요.
examples.romanization: magam ttaemune ibeon ju naenae yageunhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I worked late all week because of the deadline.
examples.note: 때문에 = 'because of'; 내내 = 'the whole time/all through'. 마감 = deadline.

examples.en: Don't work late, head home soon.
examples.note: -지 말고 = 'don't ~ but rather'; 들어가다 here = 'go home'. A caring thing to say to a coworker.

ex.en: With the current method, it is almost impossible.

불가능하다.nuance: 불가능하다 (不可能, the prefix 不 'not/un-' on 가능 'possible') is the direct antonym of 가능하다: 불 flips it to 'cannot be done, impossible'. The 不-prefix pattern recurs across Sino-Korean adjectives (불편하다 'uncomfortable', 불확실하다 'uncertain'), so recognising 불- as a negator unlocks many words. In service settings 불가능하다 is a firm but polite way to refuse, and Koreans habitually cushion it with 좀 ('a bit') or pair it with a 'but...' offer (환불은 불가능하지만 교환은 가능해요) to soften the blow. For an everyday personal 'I can't', the '-ㄹ 수 없다' pattern (갈 수 없어요 'I can't go') is more natural than forcing 불가능하다, which leans toward declaring something infeasible in principle. As a 하다-adjective the pre-noun is 불가능한, never 불가능하는.
불가능하다.explanation: 불가능하다 (bulganeunghada) means "to be impossible". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is N 불가능하다 ("N is impossible / not available"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 불가능하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
불가능하다.shortExplanation: 불가능하다 means "to be impossible" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 불가능하다 (impossible) with 가능하다 (possible) — the 불- prefix flips the meaning, so listen for that first syllable.

글쎄요.nuance: 글쎄요 is the classic Korean verbal hedge — a non-committal 'hmm, well, I'm not sure' that lets you avoid both 'yes' and 'no.' It buys time, signals reluctance or uncertainty, and very often functions as a soft pre-refusal or a polite way to withhold agreement without contradicting the other person. The 요 makes it polite; 글쎄 alone is 반말 and can also mean 'we'll see' or even an insistent 'I told you…' depending on tone. Register: 글쎄요 polite, 글쎄 casual. The dividing line from 모르겠어요 ('I don't know') is intent: 모르겠어요 states genuine lack of knowledge, while 글쎄요 is a strategic hedge — you may well have an opinion but are choosing not to commit, so it's softer and more diplomatic for declining or dodging. The English-speaker trap is hearing 글쎄요 as a real 'I don't know' and re-explaining or pressing for an answer; in many cases it politely means 'eh, probably not' or 'I'd rather not say', and pushing is impolite. Another error is overusing it as a filler the way English uses 'well' — too many 글쎄요s can read as evasive or wishy-washy. Pair it with 잘 모르겠는데요 ('I'm not really sure') or 생각해 봐야겠어요 ('I'd have to think') to extend the hedge gracefully. Crucially, recognize it from the other side: when a Korean answers your request with 글쎄요, treat it as a likely soft 'no', not an invitation to argue your case.
글쎄요.explanation: 글쎄요 (geulsseyo) means "Hmm, I'm not sure…". Say it as one set phrase — for example 글쎄요 ("Well… I'm not sure"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
글쎄요.shortExplanation: 글쎄요 is a practical expression meaning "Hmm, I'm not sure…".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Taking 글쎄요 as a literal 'I don't know' and pressing harder.
It's often a strategic hedge meaning 'eh, probably not' or 'I'd rather not commit'. Re-explaining or pushing for a yes ignores the soft refusal and feels pushy.
Confusing 글쎄요 with 모르겠어요.
모르겠어요 = genuine 'I don't know (the fact)'. 글쎄요 = a diplomatic 'well, I'm not sure / we'll see' used to dodge or soft-decline. They aren't interchangeable.
Overusing 글쎄요 as an English-style filler 'well'.
Sprinkling it on every sentence reads as evasive or noncommittal. Use it deliberately when you actually want to hedge, then follow with a reason or a defer.

제 생각에는.nuance: 제 생각에는 is the standard polite opener that signals 'this is just my view, not a command or fact'. 제 is the humble form of 나 ('my'), and 에는 sets up a frame — literally 'as for within my thinking'. It works with anyone: strangers, seniors, classmates, colleagues, customers. To go casual with a close friend, swap to 내 생각에는; for a more considered, slightly formal feel use 제 생각으로는 (the -으로는 particle stresses the viewpoint angle). The nearest alternative is 제가 보기에는 — the dividing line is thinking vs observing: 제 생각에는 comes from your internal reasoning, while 제가 보기에는 is based on what you see or sense from evidence. The classic English-speaker mistake is calquing 'in my opinion' literally as 제 의견에는, which is bookish and rare in spoken Korean. A second trap: dropping the particle entirely (제 생각 좋아요) — without 에는 or 엔 the opener is ungrammatical.
제 생각에는.explanation: "In my opinion / I think..." — that is 제 생각에는 (je saenggageneun). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 제 생각에는 ("in my opinion"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
제 생각에는.shortExplanation: 제 생각에는 is a practical expression meaning "In my opinion / I think...".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 제 의견에는 as a literal translation of 'in my opinion' — it sounds bookish; natural speech uses 제 생각에는.
Using 제 생각에는 with a friend — it's polite register; with friends drop to 반말: 내 생각에는.
Omitting the particle (제 생각 좋아요) — you need 제 생각에는 / 제 생각엔; the bare noun can't open the clause this way.

ex.en: If we say it this way, I think it feels a bit pressuring.

부담.nuance: 부담 is essential for navigating Korean social give-and-take, where accepting too much puts you in someone's debt. It is Sino-Korean 負擔 (負 'to carry on the back' + 擔 'to shoulder'), literally 'a load you shoulder', and it covers both a *financial* weight (rent, a pricey gift) and an *emotional* one (expectations, obligation). When a host says 부담 갖지 마세요, they are pre-emptively lifting that load off you; when you call a gesture 부담스러워요, you are politely signaling 'this is too generous, I'd feel indebted.' The contrast to learn is 부담 (mental/social pressure or weight) vs 짐 (a literal piece of luggage, or a metaphorical 'I'm a burden to you' = 짐이 되다). The English-speaker trap is translating it only as 'burden' and missing the warm 'please don't trouble yourself' social move, and confusing the formal verb 부담하다 (to bear a *cost*, as in 비용을 부담하다) with feeling pressure, for which you want 부담스럽다 or 부담이 되다.
부담.explanation: 부담 (budam) means "burden; pressure". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 부담이 되다 ("to become a burden"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 부담 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
부담.shortExplanation: 부담 means "burden; pressure" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating it only as 'burden' and missing the social layer. 부담스러워요 is often a courteous 'this is too much for me,' and 부담 갖지 마세요 means 'relax, no strings attached' — pure Korean social grease.
Using 부담하다 when you mean 'to feel pressured.' 부담하다 = to bear a cost formally (비용을 부담하다). For feelings, use 부담스럽다 or 부담이 되다.
Saying 부담이 많다 for heavy pressure. The natural verb is 부담이 되다 or 부담이 크다, not 많다.

혹시.nuance: 혹시 is the Sino-Korean 或是 (或 'perhaps' + 是 'be so') and lives at the FRONT of a question to soften it, exactly like English 'by any chance' or 'do you happen to': it signals you are unsure and refuse to assume, so requests and guesses land politely rather than pushily. Do not confuse it with 만약 (萬若, 'if / supposing'): 만약 sets up a conditional clause and pairs with -면 (만약 비가 오면 = if it rains), whereas 혹시 colors a whole question with tentativeness and does NOT need -면. The big English-speaker trap is dropping 혹시 into a flat statement; it belongs with a question or with the set phrase 혹시 몰라서 / 혹시 모르니까 ('just in case'). It also collocates with 혹시나 (an even softer, more anxious variant) and with 혹시 ~ 거 아니에요? for a worried hunch.
혹시.explanation: 혹시 (hoksi) means "by any chance". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 혹시 시간 있어요? ("Do you have time, by any chance?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 혹시 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
혹시.shortExplanation: 혹시 means "by any chance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 혹시 (by any chance, in a question) with 만약 (if/supposing) — 만약 needs a -면 conditional (만약 늦으면), while 혹시 just softens a question and takes no -면.
Putting 혹시 in a plain statement like 혹시 비가 와요 to mean 'maybe it's raining' — for a guessing statement use 아마 or -ㄹ지도 몰라요; 혹시 fronts a QUESTION (혹시 비 와요?).
Forgetting the set phrase form: 'just in case' is 혹시 몰라서 / 혹시 모르니까, not a bare 혹시 tacked onto the end.

cluster.title: 아마 vs 혹시 vs 어쩌면
cluster.rule: 아마 and 어쩌면 are guesses that differ in confidence: 아마 leans yes ("probably"), 어쩌면 just opens a real possibility ("maybe, who knows"). 혹시 is not a guess at all — it fronts a question or request to soften it, like "by any chance".
