퇴근하다.nuance: 퇴근하다 is Sino-Korean 退勤 — 退 'withdraw/retreat' + 勤 'duty' — literally 'withdraw from your duty', i.e. finish the workday and head home. It is the precise mirror of 출근하다 (出勤). Don't confuse it with 끝나다 'to end' or 쉬다 'to rest': 퇴근하다 specifically means YOU leave the workplace, whereas 일이 끝나다 means the work is finished and 쉬다 means to take a break. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates entirely on 하다: 퇴근해요, 퇴근했어요, formal 퇴근합니다. The English-speaker pitfall is the same family of splits — the negative is 퇴근 안 해요 and the impossible form 퇴근 못 해요, never 안 퇴근해요. A second trap: English 'get off work' tempts learners to invent a particle, but 퇴근하다 takes no object at all; the time is enough — 여섯 시에 퇴근해요. Beware the very common slang 칼퇴근(하다), 'knife clock-out', meaning you leave at the exact end time without a second of overtime.
퇴근하다.explanation: "to leave work" in Korean is 퇴근하다 (toegeunhada). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 퇴근해요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 퇴근하다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 제시간에 퇴근하다 ("to leave work on time / clock out on time") — then reshape the same stem into 퇴근하고 싶어요 (desire), 퇴근할 수 있어요 (ability), and 퇴근 못 해요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
퇴근하다.shortExplanation: 퇴근하다 means "to leave work" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 퇴근하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 퇴근해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Translating 'I'm done with work' as 퇴근했어요 when the work itself ended but you're still there — that's 일이 끝났어요. 퇴근하다 means you physically left the workplace.
Adding an object like 회사를 퇴근해요 — 퇴근하다 is intransitive; just say 퇴근해요 with only a time word if needed.
Forming the negative as 안 퇴근해요 — split the noun: 퇴근 안 해요 (and impossible = 퇴근 못 해요).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 퇴근하다 becomes 퇴근할 수 있어요 ("can") and 퇴근할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

ex.en: Yesterday was really hot.

덥다.nuance: 덥다 is the ㅂ-irregular adjective for FELT air temperature being unpleasantly high — hot weather, a stuffy room, a sweaty body. The key English-speaker trap is that English 'hot' covers four different Korean words: use 덥다 ONLY for ambient air/weather. A hot object you touch is 뜨겁다 (뜨거운 커피, never 더운 커피), spicy food is 맵다, and pleasant warmth is 따뜻하다. Because it is ㅂ-irregular, the ㅂ becomes 우 before a vowel: 덥다 → 더워요(polite) → 더운(modifier) → 더우니까(reason) → 더워서. Beginners constantly write 덥어요 or 덥은 by treating it as regular — that is the number-one error. It is neutral in register and used by everyone; the related noun is 더위 ('the heat'), and people say 더위를 먹다 to mean 'suffer heatstroke.'
덥다.explanation: 덥다 (deopda) means "hot (weather)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 날씨가 덥다 ("the weather is hot"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 덥다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
덥다.shortExplanation: 덥다 means "hot (weather)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 덥은 날 or 덥어요 — 덥다 is ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ changes to 우: the correct forms are 더운 날 and 더워요.
Calling hot coffee or hot soup 덥다 (더운 커피). Objects that are hot to the touch take 뜨겁다 → 뜨거운 커피.
Using 덥다 for spicy food. 'This is too hot!' about chili means 매워요 (from 맵다), not 더워요.

the modifier form is 더운 (the final ㅂ drops and 우 appears), not 덥은
the mimetic 푹푹 찌다 ('to steam') intensifies it for a humid Korean summer
the noun 더위 ('the heat') comes from 덥다; 더위를 타다 means heat affects you badly

ex.en: If you do not know, ask the teacher.

묻다.nuance: 묻다 means 'to ask (a question / inquire)' and takes the object marker 을/를 for the thing asked about: 길을 물어요. It is a ㄷ-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the stem ㄷ changes to ㄹ, giving 물어요 and 물었어요 and 물을 거예요, but before consonant endings the ㄷ stays — 묻습니다, 묻고, 묻지 마세요. The person you ask takes 에게/한테, or honorific 께 for someone of higher status: 선생님께 물어요. In real speech Koreans far more often say 물어보다 ('ask and see', literally 묻다 + 보다), which sounds softer and more tentative than the bare, slightly abrupt 묻다 — so 물어보세요 ('please ask') is the natural request, not 물으세요. Two contrasts: do not confuse this 묻다 with the homograph 묻다 meaning 'to bury' (regular: 땅에 묻다), and distinguish 묻다 ('ask a question') from 부탁하다 ('to request a favor'). The English-speaker pitfall is keeping the ㄷ before a vowel to say 묻어요 (which actually reads as the 'bury' verb) instead of the irregular 물어요.
묻다.explanation: "to ask" in Korean is 묻다 (mutda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 물어요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 묻다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 길을 물어요 ("I ask for directions") — then reshape the same stem into 묻고 싶어요 (desire), 물을 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 물어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
묻다.shortExplanation: 묻다 means "to ask" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 묻다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 물어요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Keeping the ㄷ before a vowel ending and saying 묻어요 — as a ㄷ-irregular the ㄷ becomes ㄹ, so 'I ask' is 물어요 (past 물었어요). (묻어요 is the unrelated verb 'to bury'.)
Using bare 묻다 where it sounds blunt — everyday Korean prefers 물어보다: 좀 물어볼게요 / 물어봐도 돼요? rather than a flat 묻겠어요.
Marking the person asked with the object 를 (선생님을 물어요) — the recipient takes 에게/한테/께: 선생님께 물어요, and the question content takes 를.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 묻다 becomes 물을 수 있어요 ("can") and 물을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem: ㄷ → ㄹ
conjugationTips.body: 묻다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb. The final ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel ending, so it conjugates to 물어요, never the literal ㄷ + 어요. The ㄷ stays ㄷ before a consonant ending (듣고, 듣습니다).

cluster.title: 묻다 vs 물어보다 vs 질문하다
cluster.rule: 물어보다 is what people actually say out loud; 묻다 is the same act but terser and more written (and ㄷ-irregular, so it becomes 물어요). 질문하다 is "ask a question" where questions are a formal event — a class, a meeting, a Q&A.

ex.en: My cold got completely better.

낫다.nuance: 낫다 means an illness or wound heals, and it is a ㅅ-irregular verb: the ㅅ disappears before a vowel (나아요, 나았어요, 나을, 나으세요) but stays before a consonant (낫습니다, 낫고, 낫지). It is intransitive — the cold or the cut is the subject (감기가 나았어요, 상처가 나았어요) — so you never 'heal something' with it; for that you'd use 치료하다 (to treat) or 고치다 (to cure/fix). The big trap for everyone, native and learner alike, is the homophone cluster: 낫다 'heal', 낳다 'give birth', and 났다 (from 나다, 'broke out/occurred') all sound like [낟따] but mean totally different things, so 나았어요 (got better) must never be spelled 낳았어요 (gave birth). Note 낫다 also has a second meaning, 'to be better/preferable' (이게 더 나아요 = this one's better), which shares the exact same conjugation. It collocates with 빨리/금방/곧 낫다 (heal fast/soon) and 다 낫다 (fully heal).
낫다.explanation: "to heal / to get better" in Korean is 낫다 (natda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 나아요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 낫다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 빨리 나으세요 ("Get well soon") — then reshape the same stem into 낫고 싶어요 (desire), 나을 수 있어요 (ability), and 나을 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
낫다.shortExplanation: 낫다 means "to heal / to get better" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 낫다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 나아요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Spelling the past as 낳았어요 (that means 'gave birth') instead of 나았어요 for 'got better'. The dictionary form is 낫다, not 낳다 — listen for the meaning, not just the sound.
Keeping the ㅅ before a vowel — it's 나아요/나았어요/나을, NOT 낫아요/낫았어요. The ㅅ only survives before consonants (낫습니다, 낫고).
Making it transitive like English 'heal it' — 감기를 나았어요 is wrong; the illness is the subject, so it's 감기가 나았어요. To 'cure' something actively, use 치료하다 or 고치다.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 낫다 becomes 나을 수 있어요 ("can") and 나을 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 낫다 has an irregular stem (ㅅ). Memorize its polite form 나아요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

ex.en: Please call my name.

부르다.nuance: 부르다 chiefly means to call/summon someone to come (택시를 부르다, 친구를 부르다), to call out a name (이름을 부르다), and — a key idiom — to sing (노래를 부르다, the standard phrase, not 노래를 하다). Don't confuse it with 전화하다, which is 'to phone': 친구를 불러요 means call your friend over to where you are, while 친구한테 전화해요 means ring them up. It's a textbook 르-irregular: before an 아/어 ending the final ㅡ drops and an extra ㄹ appears, so 부르 + 어요 → 불러요 and past → 불렀어요, but before consonant endings it stays whole (부르고, 부를 거예요, 부릅니다). Two traps: first, learners say 부르어요 — wrong, it must be 불러요. Second, beware the homonym 부르다 'to be full' (배가 부르다), a completely different adjective; 배가 불러요 means 'I'm full', not 'the stomach calls'. Also note honorific contexts: to summon a superior you'd soften with 모시다 ('escort/bring respectfully') rather than bluntly 부르다.
부르다.explanation: 부르다 (bureuda) = "to call". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 불러요 plus one useful sentence like 택시를 부르다 ("to call a taxi"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 부르고 싶어요 for what you want, 부를 수 있어요 for what you can, 못 불러요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
부르다.shortExplanation: 부르다 means "to call" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 부르다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 불러요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 부르어요 — 부르다 is 르-irregular, so the 요-form is 불러요 (ㅡ drops, ㄹ doubles) and the past is 불렀어요.
Using 노래를 하다 for 'sing a song' — the fixed collocation is 노래를 부르다; 노래하다 exists but 노래를 하다 sounds off.
Mixing up 부르다 'call' with the adjective 부르다 'full' — 배가 불러요 ('I'm full') is unrelated to summoning someone.

That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.body: 부르다 has an irregular stem (르 irregular). Memorize its polite form 불러요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

ex.en: Your face is red.

빨갛다.nuance: 빨갛다 is the vivid, pure 'red' of an apple, a stop light, or a blushing face. Among red words, contrast it with 붉다, which is the more literary, darker 'reddish/crimson' used for blood, sunsets, and emotion (붉은 노을), while 빨갛다 is the bright everyday red a child would point at. As an adjective it describes a STATE, so the thing that is red takes 이/가 (얼굴이 빨개요), never 을/를. The biggest trap for English speakers is the ㅎ-irregular: the stem-final ㅎ vanishes AND the vowel fuses, so it is never 빨갛아요 but 빨개요, and the noun-modifying form is 빨간 (빨간 사과), not 빨갛은. To say something 'turns red,' use 빨개지다, because 빨갛다 alone is a static quality, not a change. Note 빨간색 is the noun 'the color red.'
빨갛다.explanation: 빨갛다 (ppalgata) = "to be red". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 사과가 빨개요 ("The apple is red") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 빨갛다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
빨갛다.shortExplanation: 빨갛다 means "to be red" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 빨갛아요 — the ㅎ-irregular deletes ㅎ and fuses the vowel, so the correct polite form is 빨개요.
Using the modifier 빨갛은 사과 — drop the ㅎ for the modifier too: it is 빨간 사과.
Saying 사과를 빨개요 with 을/를 — a color is a state, so use 이/가: 사과가 빨개요.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, not 을/를
빨간색 = the noun 'red color'
빨개지다 = become red, change of state
빨간 = the modifier that sits before a noun

examples.en: This apple is red
examples.note: the most basic 요-form: 빨갛다 → 빨개요

examples.en: The evening sky was dyed red
examples.note: 빨갛게 = the adverb 'redly', + 물들다 'to be dyed'

examples.en: I got embarrassed so my face turned red

ex.en: The sky is blue today.

파랗다.nuance: 파랗다 is the bright blue of a clear sky and the sea, and in Korean it famously also covers what English calls 'green' for traffic lights and fresh leaves (파란불 'the green light,' 파란 잔디 'green grass') — a real surprise for learners. The neighboring word 푸르다 is more poetic and leans 'verdant/azure,' used for 푸른 산 'green mountains' and 푸른 하늘 in songs, while 파랗다 is the plain everyday blue. Being an adjective, the blue thing takes 이/가 (하늘이 파래요), not 을/를. The ㅎ-irregular is the key pitfall: never 파랗아요 but 파래요, and the modifier is 파란 (파란 바다), not 파랗은. Use 파래지다 for 'turn blue,' and 파란색 for the noun 'the color blue.'
파랗다.explanation: 파랗다 (parata) means "to be blue". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 하늘이 파래요 ("The sky is blue"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 파랗다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
파랗다.shortExplanation: 파랗다 means "to be blue" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 파랗아요 — the ㅎ deletes and the vowel fuses, giving 파래요 as the polite form.
Forming the modifier as 파랗은 바다 — it must be 파란 바다 with the ㅎ dropped.
Assuming 파랗다 only means 'blue' — for a traffic 'go' light Koreans say 파란불, so it can map to English 'green.'

usagePhrases.note: the classic blue thing, state with 이/가
파란색 = the noun 'blue', sits before another noun
파랗게 = adverb 'bluely' + 칠하다 'paint'
새- prefix intensifies the shade

examples.en: The sky is blue today
examples.note: basic 요-form: 파랗다 → 파래요

examples.en: The sea is really blue, isn't it
examples.note: -네요 adds a tone of fresh observation

examples.en: My lips went blue (from cold/fear)
examples.note: 파랗게 질리다 is a set phrase for going pale/blue

ex.en: The banana is yellow.

노랗다.nuance: 노랗다 is the cheerful pure yellow of a banana, a chick, or a school bus. Korean color adjectives like this come in a 'bright vs dark' vowel-harmony pair: 노랗다 (bright, with ㅗ/ㅏ) feels light and vivid, while its darker partner 누렇다 (with ㅜ/ㅓ) means a dull, dingy, faded yellow like old paper or unhealthy skin — choosing the wrong one changes the whole feeling. As an adjective it takes 이/가 on the yellow thing (잎이 노래요), not 을/를. Watch the ㅎ-irregular: it is 노래요, never 노랗아요, and the modifier is 노란 (노란 우산), not 노랗은. There is also a vivid set phrase 눈앞이 노래지다 'to feel faint/hopeless,' literally 'the front of the eyes turns yellow.' The noun is 노란색.
노랗다.explanation: "to be yellow" is 노랗다 (norata). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 바나나가 노래요 ("The banana is yellow"). Watch the particle attached to 노랗다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
노랗다.shortExplanation: 노랗다 means "to be yellow" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 노랗아요 — ㅎ drops and the vowel fuses to 노래요 for the polite form.
Writing the modifier as 노랗은 우산 — the correct modifier is 노란 우산.
Mixing up 노랗다 and 누렇다 — 노랗다 is bright/fresh yellow, 누렇다 is dull/sickly yellow, so they are not interchangeable.

usagePhrases.note: state with 이/가, describing a fruit
노란색 = noun 'yellow' before another noun
노랗게 = adverb + 익다 'ripen', a natural pair
샛- prefix intensifies the yellow

examples.en: This banana is yellow
examples.note: basic 요-form: 노랗다 → 노래요

examples.en: In autumn the ginkgo leaves turn yellow
examples.note: 노랗게 물들다 = 'be dyed yellow'

examples.en: After starving for days my vision went yellow (I felt faint)
examples.note: 눈앞이 노래지다 is an idiom for dizziness/despair

ex.en: How is this method?

어떻다.nuance: 어떻다 is the question-adjective 'to be how / to be what-like,' the root behind a whole family Koreans use constantly. Learn its three faces: 어때(요)? = 'How is it? / How about it?' (asking a state or making a soft suggestion — 이거 어때요?), 어떤 = the modifier 'what kind of' before a noun (어떤 음악 'what kind of music'), and 어떻게 = the adverb 'how / in what way' for asking method (어떻게 해요? 'how do you do it?'). Do not confuse 어떻다 with 어떡하다, the contraction of 어떻게 하다 'to do how,' which gives the very common cry 어떡해! 'what do I do?!' As an irregular ㅎ adjective, the polite/question form is 어때요, never 어떻아요, and the past is 어땠어요. The single most frequent learner error is choosing the wrong family member — using 어떤 where 어떻게 is needed, or vice versa.
어떻다.explanation: "to be how" is 어떻다 (eotteota). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 날씨가 어때요? ("How is the weather?"). Watch the particle attached to 어떻다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
어떻다.shortExplanation: 어떻다 means "to be how" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 어떻아요 — 어떻다 is ㅎ-irregular, so the question form is 어때요 (past 어땠어요).
Mixing 어떤 and 어떻게 — 어떤 + noun = 'what kind of' (어떤 색), but 어떻게 + verb = 'how' (어떻게 가요).
Writing 어떻해 for 'what do I do' — the set phrase is 어떡해 (from 어떻게 해), not 어떻해.

usagePhrases.note: asking about a state with 이/가
어떤 = the modifier 'what kind of'
어떻게 = the adverb 'how/in what way'
어떻게 해 contracted, a panicked reaction

examples.en: How's this outfit? / What do you think?
examples.note: 어때요 also means 'how about it?' to suggest

examples.en: How was the movie yesterday?
examples.note: past form: 어떻다 → 어땠어요

examples.en: How do you get to Seoul?
examples.note: 어떻게 = the adverb for asking the manner

ex.en: It is okay to bring detergent as a housewarming gift.

선물.nuance: 선물 can be the thing given, received, bought, or prepared. In this chapter, focus on the particle around the person and the particle attached to 선물 itself.
선물.explanation: "gift; present" is 선물 (seonmul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 친구에게 선물을 줬어요. ("I gave a gift to a friend."). Watch the particle attached to 선물 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
선물.shortExplanation: 선물 means "gift; present" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 에게 with objects instead of people. Say 친구에게 선물을 줬어요, not 선물에게.
Forgetting that 도 and 만 can replace 을/를: 선물도 줬어요, 선물만 샀어요.

usagePhrases.en: I gave a gift to a friend.
usagePhrases.note: 에게 marks the receiver.

usagePhrases.en: I also gave a gift to the teacher.
usagePhrases.note: 께 is honorific; 도 means also.

examples.en: It would be good to prepare at least a small gift.
examples.note: 이라도 gives the sense of at least.

ex.en: I also need to send the teacher an email.

이메일.nuance: 이메일 is the everyday loanword (from English 'e-mail') for electronic mail, used freely at work and in daily life; the Sino alternative 전자우편 (電子郵便 'electronic post') exists but sounds stiff and bureaucratic, mostly seen on official forms. Crucially, 이메일 ≠ paper mail: a physical letter is 편지, and the postal-mail system is 우편, so 'I got your letter' about a posted envelope is 편지를 받았어요, not 이메일. It collocates with 보내다 (send), 받다 (receive), 확인하다 (check), 첨부하다 (attach a file), 답장하다 (reply). The English-speaker pitfall is the recipient particle — a person who receives mail takes 에게/한테 (동료에게 이메일을 보내요), and don't drag the English verb 'do' over: you 이메일을 보내다 or 쓰다, never 이메일하다.
이메일.explanation: 이메일 (imeil) = "email". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이메일을 보내다. ("to send an email.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 이메일, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.
이메일.shortExplanation: 이메일 means "email" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 이메일 for a posted paper letter — that is 편지 (a letter) or 우편 (postal mail); 이메일 is only the electronic kind.
Marking the recipient with 을/를 (동료를 이메일 보냈어요) — the person gets 에게/한테 and the email is the object: 동료에게 이메일을 보냈어요.
Saying 이메일했어요 to mean 'I emailed' — Korean doesn't verb it that way; say 이메일을 보냈어요 or 이메일을 썼어요.

usagePhrases.note: 보내다 'send' is the core verb; the message takes 을/를 as the object.
Incoming mail is the subject of 오다; 이메일이 왔어요 = 'an email came.'
확인하다 'verify/check' is the standard verb for reading your inbox.
Compound noun; 주소 'address' attaches directly with no particle.

examples.en: What is your email address?
examples.note: Beginner exchange; 뭐예요? asks for the information directly.

examples.en: I sent an email to my coworker.
examples.note: Human recipient takes 에게 (written/neutral) — to a machine/place you'd use 에.

examples.ko: 참고로 아까 보낸 이메일에 자료 첨부했으니까 확인 부탁드려요.
examples.romanization: chamgoro akka bonaen imeire jaryo cheombuhaesseunikka hwagin butakdeuryeoyo.
examples.en: FYI, I attached the file to the email I sent earlier, so please check it.
examples.note: Workplace email register: 첨부하다 'attach', 확인 부탁드려요 'please check' are the real formulas.

ex.en: I gave a gift to a friend.

주다.nuance: 주세요 comes from 주다 and is one of the most important polite request endings.
주다.explanation: 주다 (juda) means "to give". Start from the polite form 줘요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 주다. A strong first sentence is 물 주세요 ("Please give me water."); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 주다 also becomes 주고 싶어요 (want), 줄 수 있어요 (can), and 못 줘요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about basic everyday communication, then bend it.
주다.shortExplanation: 주다 means "to give" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 주다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 줘요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Do not say 줘 주세요 for a normal request. Use 주세요 by itself.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 주다 becomes 줄 수 있어요 ("can") and 줄 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
Essential request.

examples.en: Please give me some water.
examples.note: Request.

examples.en: Please give me a receipt.
examples.note: Shopping.

examples.en: I will help you.
examples.note: Related giving-help pattern.

ex.en: We need four chairs.

개.nuance: 개 is the Sino-Korean general counter for inanimate objects, 個/箇, the catch-all you use when no more specific counter fits (it won't do for people, animals, or flat/long things, which have their own counters). It REQUIRES native Korean numbers, and the first four plus 20 shorten before any counter: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무 (so 한 개, 두 개, 세 개, 네 개, 스무 개). Word order is fixed as noun + number + 개 (사과 세 개), unlike English 'three apples'. Habitual partners: 한 개에 (price per item), 몇 개, 여러 개 'several', 개수 'the count'. The headline English-speaker pitfall is using Sino numbers with 개 — 일 개, 이 개 is wrong; counters like 개/명/마리 take native numbers (한 개), even though money/minutes take Sino. A second trap is English order: don't say 세 사과 개 or 개 세 사과; it's 사과 세 개. Note the contrast with 명/분 (people) and 마리 (animals): 개 is strictly for things.
개.explanation: 개 (gae) means "counter for things". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 한 개 ("one (item)"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 개 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.
개.shortExplanation: 개 means "counter for things" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using Sino numbers: 일 개, 이 개 — the counter 개 takes native numbers: 한 개, 두 개.
Forgetting the number-shortening: 하나 개, 둘 개 — before a counter they shorten to 한 개, 두 개 (also 세, 네, 스무).
Copying English order (세 사과 / three-apples) — Korean is noun + number + counter: 사과 세 개.

usagePhrases.note: native number 하나→한 + 개
native 둘→두 + 개
noun + native number + counter order
question word 몇 + 개

examples.en: Three apples, please.
examples.note: basic: noun–number–counter, object 를 often dropped when ordering

examples.en: How much is this per one?
examples.note: everyday: 한 개에 = 'per item', price-per-unit 에

examples.en: How many packs of ramyeon are left?
examples.note: real-situation: 몇 개 asking quantity + 남다 'be left'

ex.en: Three students are coming.

명.nuance: 명 is the Sino-Korean counter for people, 名 'name/person', and like all counters it takes native numbers: 한 명, 두 명, 세 명 (with the usual shortening 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무). The crucial register contrast is 명 vs 분: 분 is the honorific people-counter for guests, elders, customers, or anyone you respect, so a waiter asks 몇 분이세요? and you describe esteemed visitors as 세 분이 오셨어요, while 명 is the plain, neutral count fine for friends, students, or stating numbers factually (학생 세 명). Using 명 for a venerable elder can sound curt; using 분 for yourself sounds odd. Habitual partners: 몇 명/몇 분, 한 명도 없다 'not a single person', 인원 'headcount'. The top English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the all-purpose 개 to count people — 개 is for things only; people must be 명 (or honorific 분), never 사람 세 개. A second trap is Sino numbers (이 명); counters take native (두 명).
명.explanation: "counter for people" is 명 (myeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한 명 ("one person"). Watch the particle attached to 명 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.
명.shortExplanation: 명 means "counter for people" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting people with 개: 사람 세 개 — people take 명 (or honorific 분): 세 명 / 세 분.
Using neutral 명 for respected guests or elders — switch to the honorific counter 분: 손님 세 분, 할머니 한 분.
Using Sino numbers: 이 명, 삼 명 — the counter 명 takes native numbers: 두 명, 세 명.

usagePhrases.note: native number 한 + 명
native 두 + 명
noun + native number + 명
question word 몇 + 명

examples.en: There are five students.
examples.note: basic: subject 이 on the noun, count after it

examples.en: How many (people) are you? / For how many?
examples.note: everyday: a server's set phrase at a restaurant

examples.en: Five people (honored) came to the meeting.
examples.note: real-situation: honorific 분 + 오시다 replaces 명 for respected guests

ex.en: They say they are bringing one dog too.

마리.nuance: 마리 is the universal counter for animals — dogs, cats, fish, birds, insects, livestock, and even a whole cooked chicken or fish on the table. Crucially it is size-independent: the same word counts an ant (개미 한 마리) and an elephant (코끼리 한 마리). 마리 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. Its single most important contrast is with 명, the counter for PEOPLE: animals are 마리, humans are 명, and crossing that line matters socially. 마리 is also distinct from 분, the honorific people-counter. The big English-speaker pitfall is using 마리 for people because English says 'two' for both — but calling a person 한 마리 is insulting or mocking (treating them like an animal); always use 명 (or honorific 분) for humans. A second slip is the generic 개 for animals, which sounds wrong — creatures take 마리.
마리.explanation: 마리 (mari) means "counter for animals". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 강아지 한 마리 ("one puppy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 마리 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
마리.shortExplanation: 마리 means "counter for animals" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting people with 마리. People take 명 (or honorific 분); 마리 for a human is rude or mocking.
Using 개 for animals. Living creatures take 마리 (강아지 한 마리), not the generic object counter 개.
Saying 일 마리, 이 마리 with Sino-Korean numbers. Use native numbers: 한 마리, 두 마리, 세 마리.

usagePhrases.note: 마리 counts every kind of animal: pets, fish, birds, insects, livestock.
Native numbers go before 마리: 한, 두, 세 마리.
The quantity question for any creature.
A whole (cooked) chicken is counted with 마리 too.

examples.en: I want to raise one puppy.
examples.note: Basic: [animal] + 한 마리. 키우다 = 'to raise/keep (a pet)'.

examples.ko: 우리 집 어항에는 금붕어가 세 마리 있어요.
examples.romanization: uri jip eohangeneun geumbungeoga se mari isseoyo.
examples.en: There are three goldfish in our fish tank.
examples.note: 세 마리 counts the fish; even tiny creatures take 마리, regardless of size.

examples.ko: 배고픈데 치킨 한 마리 시켜 먹을까요?
examples.romanization: baegopeunde chikin han mari sikyeo meogeulkkayo?
examples.en: I'm hungry — shall we order a whole chicken?
examples.note: 한 마리 counts the chicken; 시켜 먹다 = 'order in and eat'. Classic fried-chicken line.

ex.en: I will prepare four cups of coffee.

잔.nuance: 잔 is the counter for a serving of liquid held in a cup or glass — it counts the POURED drink, not the container itself. Its near-rivals are 병 (a whole bottle) and 컵 (the physical cup as an object), and the dividing line is what you're measuring: 맥주 한 병 is a full bottle, 맥주 한 잔 is one glass poured from it. The hanja is 盞 ('small cup'), though it feels fully native in use and always takes native-Korean numbers (한, 두, 세 잔), never Sino-Korean 일/이. Watch two traps: 한잔하다 written together is a VERB ('go for a drink') and is idiomatic, so don't read it as a literal count; and English 'a cup of coffee' tempts learners to reach for 컵, but the natural measure word for the drink itself is 잔.
잔.explanation: 잔 (jan) means "glass; cup (counter for drinks)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 커피 한 잔 ("one cup of coffee"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 잔 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
잔.shortExplanation: 잔 means "glass; cup (counter for drinks)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 일 잔, 이 잔 with Sino-Korean numbers. Counters of servings take native numbers: 한 잔, 두 잔, 세 잔.
Using 잔 to count bottles. A sealed/whole bottle is 병 (맥주 두 병); 잔 is only the glass poured out.
Writing the drink-verb as two words '한 잔 하다' when you mean the idiom 'grab a drink' — the set verb is 한잔하다, one word.

usagePhrases.note: The everyday default: 잔 covers any served drink — coffee, tea, water, beer, soju.
Bar shorthand for another round; you'll hear this constantly while drinking together.
Written as ONE word, this is a verb meaning 'go have a (casual) drink', not literally one glass.
Spacing matters: number + space + 잔 (세 잔), never 세잔.

examples.en: One glass of water, please.
examples.note: Simplest form: [noun] + [native number] + 잔. The counter comes AFTER the number, before the verb.

examples.ko: 저는 하루에 커피를 세 잔씩 마셔요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun harue keopireul se janssing masyeoyo.
examples.en: I drink three cups of coffee each day.
examples.note: Note 씩 ('each/per') after the counter — '세 잔씩' = three cups apiece per day, a natural habit phrase.

examples.ko: 딱 한 잔만 더 하고 갈게요.
examples.romanization: tta kan janman deo hago galgeyo.
examples.en: I'll have just one more drink and then go.
examples.note: Real bar line: 딱...만 = 'just exactly one', and 한 잔 하다 here means 'have a drink', not eat.

ex.en: Please give me just two guide books too.

권.nuance: 권 is the counter for anything BOUND into a spine — novels, textbooks, notebooks, magazines, and each separate volume of a multi-volume series. Its critical contrast is with 장, which counts a single loose SHEET: 종이 한 장 is one sheet of paper, but the whole bound book made of many sheets is 책 한 권. The hanja is 卷, originally 'a scroll/roll', which is why it now measures a complete bound work. It always takes native-Korean numbers and is among the most frequent counters when you talk about reading or studying. The classic English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to the all-purpose 개 ('책 두 개') because English just says 'two books' — but printed/bound works specifically take 권; a related slip is using 권 for a single page, when one page is 한 장.
권.explanation: 권 (gwon) means "counter for books and volumes". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 책 한 권 ("one book"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 권 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
권.shortExplanation: 권 means "counter for books and volumes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 개 for books. 개 is for generic objects; bound books and volumes specifically take 권 (책 한 권).
Counting loose pages with 권. A single sheet/page is 장 (종이 한 장); the whole book is 권.
Counting a multi-volume set as 한 권 when you mean the whole series. Each volume is its own 권 (전 5권 = '5 volumes total').

usagePhrases.note: 권 counts bound things: books, notebooks, magazines, comic volumes.
Native numbers go before 권: 한, 두, 세 권.
The standard quantity question for anything bound.
Each volume of a series is counted separately as a 권.

examples.en: One notebook, please.
examples.note: Basic: [bound item] + 한 권. Notebooks count with 권 just like books.

examples.ko: 한 달에 책을 두 권 정도 읽어요.
examples.romanization: han dare chaegeul du gwon jeongdo ilgeoyo.
examples.en: I read about two books a month.
examples.note: 두 권 정도 = 'about two'; 정도 turns an exact count into an estimate.

examples.ko: 도서관에서 빌린 책 세 권을 오늘 반납해야 해요.
examples.romanization: doseogwaneseo billin chaek se gwoneul oneul bannapaeya haeyo.
examples.en: I have to return the three library books I borrowed today.
examples.note: 세 권을 marks the books as the object; 반납하다 = 'to return (borrowed items)'.

ex.en: Ten sheets of paper are enough.

장.nuance: 장 counts flat, thin items — sheets of paper, tickets, photographs, banknotes, stickers, postcards, and even thin foods like a sheet of dried seaweed (김) or a slice of cheese. Its sharpest contrast is with 권: 장 is the single loose SHEET, whereas many sheets bound together become 책 한 권 (a book). The hanja is 張, meaning 'to stretch/spread out flat', which captures exactly the flatness it measures. It always takes native numbers and is one of the most-used counters in daily errands — at ticket counters, copy machines, and photo booths. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 개 (a generic count) for tickets and photos because English says 'two tickets'; the natural, expected counter is 장. A second trap is using 장 for a whole magazine or book, which is 권, since those are bound, not loose.
장.explanation: "counter for flat/thin sheets (paper, tickets)" is 장 (jang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 종이 한 장 ("one sheet of paper"). Watch the particle attached to 장 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
장.shortExplanation: 장 means "counter for flat/thin sheets (paper, tickets)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting a bound book with 장. 장 is a single sheet; a whole bound book is 권 (책 한 권).
Using 개 for tickets or photos. Flat items take 장 (표 두 장, 사진 한 장), not the generic 개.
Mixing up 장 with 잔 (a glass of drink). They are different words and counters — 종이 한 장 vs 커피 한 잔.

usagePhrases.note: 장 counts flat, thin things: paper, tickets, photos, cards, banknotes.
Movie, concert, and transport tickets are counted with 장.
The quantity question for sheets, tickets, or photos.
Thin flat foods (김, a cheese slice) also use 장.

examples.en: Two movie tickets, please.
examples.note: Counter-window basic: [ticket] + 두 장 + 주세요. Tickets are flat, so 장.

examples.en: Could you give me just ten sheets of copy paper?
examples.note: 열 장만 = 'just ten sheets'; 만 caps the amount, and -시겠어요 makes it polite.

examples.ko: 가족사진을 한 장 인화하려고 사진관에 갔어요.
examples.romanization: gajoksajineul han jang inhwaharyeogo sajingwane gasseoyo.
examples.en: I went to a photo studio to print one family photo.
examples.note: 한 장 counts the photo; 인화하다 = 'to develop/print a photograph'.

ex.en: I packed only one set of clothes.

벌.nuance: 벌 counts clothing as a COMPLETE garment or a coordinated outfit, so a suit, dress, hanbok, or pajama set is 한 벌 even though it physically has several pieces — the counter measures the whole worn unit, not the parts. Its near-synonyms split by what they measure: 벌 is the full set, while 장 counts a single flat piece (티셔츠 한 장 — one tee) and 개 is the casual generic count. 벌 is native Korean (no hanja) and takes native numbers. The biggest English-speaker trap is logic-counting the pieces: a two-piece suit feels like 'two items', but the matching set is 한 벌, not 두 벌. A second trap is genre confusion — clothes are 벌, but the shoes that complete the look are 켤레, so don't say 신발 한 벌.
벌.explanation: 벌 (beol) = "counter for sets of clothing". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 옷 한 벌 ("one outfit/set of clothes") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 벌, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
벌.shortExplanation: 벌 means "counter for sets of clothing" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting a two-piece suit as 두 벌. The jacket-and-trousers set together is 한 벌 (one set).
Using 벌 for shoes. Footwear takes 켤레 (신발 한 켤레); clothing takes 벌.
Counting a single T-shirt as 한 벌 in casual speech. A flat single top is more naturally 티셔츠 한 장 or 한 개; 벌 leans toward full sets.

usagePhrases.note: 벌 counts a complete garment or coordinated set: a suit, a dress, pajamas, hanbok.
A suit (jacket + trousers) counts as a single 벌 — one set.
Asks the count of garments or sets.
Native numbers go before 벌: 한, 두, 세 벌.

examples.en: I'm planning to buy a set of pajamas.
examples.note: Simple: [clothing] + 한 벌. Pajamas (top + bottom) are one 벌, not two.

examples.ko: 출근용 정장을 한 벌 새로 맞췄어요.
examples.romanization: chulgeunyong jeongjangeul han beol saero matchwosseoyo.
examples.en: I had a new work suit custom-made.
examples.note: 맞추다 = 'have tailor-made'; 출근용 = 'for commuting/work'. The whole suit = 한 벌.

examples.ko: 이번 여행에는 갈아입을 옷을 세 벌만 챙겼어요.
examples.romanization: ibeon yeohaengeneun garaibeul oseul se beolman chaenggyeosseoyo.
examples.en: For this trip I packed only three changes of clothes.
examples.note: 세 벌만 = 'just three sets'; 갈아입다 = 'to change clothes'.

ex.en: We need one laptop.

대.nuance: 대 is the all-purpose counter for machines and vehicles — cars, motorcycles, bicycles, computers, phones, cameras, TVs, washing machines, and air conditioners — basically anything mechanical or electronic, so a resident reaches for it constantly when talking about appliances. The hanja is 臺 ('platform/stand'), historically the base a machine sat on, which is why it measures equipment. It contrasts with 채 (whole buildings) and 명 (people): the vehicle is 대, the people riding inside it are 명. It always takes native-Korean numbers. The main English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the generic 개 ('차 두 개') because English just says 'two cars'; machines and vehicles specifically take 대. A subtler trap is counting passengers with 대 — only the machine is 대, while the humans in it are counted with 명.
대.explanation: 대 (dae) = "counter for vehicles and machines". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 차 한 대 ("one car") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 대, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
대.shortExplanation: 대 means "counter for vehicles and machines" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 개 for cars, computers, or appliances. Machines and vehicles specifically take 대 (차 한 대, 노트북 한 대).
Counting the people riding in a vehicle with 대. People are 명 (세 명); only the vehicle itself is 대.
Saying 일 대, 이 대 with Sino-Korean numbers. Use native numbers: 한 대, 두 대, 세 대.

usagePhrases.note: 대 counts vehicles and machines: cars, bikes, phones, computers, ACs.
Native numbers go before 대: 한, 두, 세 대.
The quantity question for vehicles or appliances.
Home appliances and electronics count with 대.

examples.ko: 우리 집에 차가 한 대 있어요.
examples.romanization: uri jibe chaga han dae isseoyo.
examples.en: There's one car in our household.
examples.note: Basic existence: [thing]이/가 한 대 있어요. 차가 한 대 있어요 = 'have one car'.

examples.en: There are as many as five computers in the office.
examples.note: 다섯 대나 — the 나 after the counter adds the surprised nuance 'as many as'.

examples.ko: 오래된 에어컨을 한 대 더 설치하기로 했어요.
examples.romanization: oraedoen eeokeoneul han dae deo seolchihagiro haesseoyo.
examples.en: We decided to install one more old air conditioner.
examples.note: 한 대 더 = 'one more unit'; -기로 하다 = 'decide to'. Appliances take 대.

번.en: counter for times or number labels

ex.en: I have already tried it three times.

번.nuance: 번 (한자 番) is the counter for an assigned, ordered number — bus and route numbers, subway exits, exam questions, list items, jersey and seat numbers — and in this ID sense it always takes Sino-Korean numbers: 삼 번 출구, 오 번 버스, never 세 번 출구. Its tricky twin is the homograph 번 meaning 'times/occasions', which takes NATIVE numbers: 세 번 (three times), 다섯 번 (five times). The dividing line is meaning, not spelling: does 번 label a thing (use Sino) or count repetitions (use native)? A near-synonym for the labelling sense is 호(號), but 호 attaches to rooms and issue/model numbers (302호, 창간호) while 번 covers routes, exits, and questions. The English-speaker pitfall is the Sino/native split inside a single counter: learners who have just mastered '세 번 = three times' over-apply native numbers to bus and exit numbers, producing 세 번 버스 — which a Korean parses as 'the bus, three times', not 'bus number 3'. Anchor it with the contrast pair 삼 번 (No. 3) vs. 세 번 (3 times).
번.explanation: 번 (beon) means "number (in a sequence)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 번 ("number / No."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 번 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
번.shortExplanation: 번 means "number (in a sequence)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using native numbers for an ID (세 번 버스, 세 번 출구) — labelling 번 takes Sino, so it is 삼 번 버스 / 삼 번 출구.
Using Sino numbers for repetitions (삼 번 갔어요) — 'times' 번 takes native, so 'went three times' is 세 번 갔어요.
Swapping 번 and 호 — rooms and issues use 호 (302호), while routes, exits, and questions use 번 (삼 번).

usagePhrases.note: 番: counter for an assigned position or ID, with Sino numbers
list items, exam questions, jersey or seat numbers
asking for a bus, room, exit, or question number
the standard subway-exit phrasing

examples.en: What number is this?
examples.note: Simplest use: 몇 번 asking the assigned number of an item.

examples.ko: 저는 지하철 삼 번 출구에서 기다릴게요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun jihacheol sam beon chulgueseo gidarilgeyo.
examples.en: I'll wait at subway exit number 3.
examples.note: Everyday meet-up; 삼 번 출구 names a specific exit with Sino 삼.

examples.ko: 오 번 버스를 타고 두 번 갈아탔어요.
examples.romanization: o beon beoseureul tago du beon garatasseoyo.
examples.en: I took bus number 5 and transferred twice.
examples.note: Real situation: one sentence shows both 번s — ID 오 번 (Sino) and 'twice' 두 번 (native).

ex.en: They say they are bringing one dog too.

강아지.nuance: 강아지 literally means a puppy (the young of 개 'dog'), but in real Korean life it is the warm, default word people use for any beloved pet dog regardless of age — saying 우리 강아지 about a ten-year-old dog is completely normal and conveys affection, much like English 'puppy' or 'doggy' used fondly. The neutral, technical word for a grown dog is 개, which is what you use in formal writing, signs (개 조심 'beware of dog'), and breed talk; bare 개 can also sound blunt or even appear in insults (이 개 같은...), so 강아지 is the gentler everyday choice. As an endearment, calling a child 우리 강아지 means 'my little darling'. The English-speaker pitfall is register: in a report or formal context use 개, but in warm daily speech 강아지 is right. It ends in a vowel, so it takes 가/를.
강아지.explanation: 강아지 (gangaji) = "puppy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 강아지가 귀여워요 ("the puppy is cute") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 강아지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
강아지.shortExplanation: 강아지 means "puppy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 강아지 in formal or technical writing where 개 is expected. For documents, signs, and neutral statements the word is 개 (e.g., 개 조심 'beware of dog'); 강아지 is the affectionate everyday term.
Counting with 개 the object-counter, as in 강아지 두 개. Confusingly 개 is also 'dog', but as a counter it is for objects — animals take 마리, so say 강아지 두 마리.
Assuming 강아지 can only mean a baby dog. Koreans call adult pet dogs 강아지 too out of affection; age is not implied — use 새끼 강아지 if you specifically mean a newborn.

usagePhrases.note: 귀엽다 (a ㅂ irregular → 귀여워요) is the go-to adjective; subject 가
키우다 'to raise a pet', with object 를
counted with the animal counter 마리
산책 (walk); 강아지 산책시키다 'take the dog for a walk' is everyday

examples.en: There is a puppy in our house.
examples.note: simple: location 에 + existence 있어요 with subject 가

examples.en: I want to get a puppy.
examples.note: everyday: object 를 with 키우다 + -고 싶어요 'want to'

examples.en: Our dog is already five years old.
examples.note: real situation: a grown pet still called 강아지 out of affection

ex.en: How many sheets of paper do we need?

종이.nuance: 종이 is a pure native Korean word for paper, both as the material (made from 나무/pulp) and as a sheet of it. The crucial point is its counter: flat, thin things are counted with 장 (종이 한 장, 두 장) — the same 장 used for tickets (표 한 장), photos (사진 한 장), and pizza slices, so learning 종이 anchors the whole 'flat-sheet' counter family. Distinguish the raw material 종이 from finished paper products that have their own names: a 신문 (newspaper), a 책 (book), a 공책/노트 (notebook), and a filled-out 서류 (document) are all made of 종이 but are never just called 종이. Useful collocations: 종이에 쓰다/적다 (write on paper), 종이를 접다 (fold paper), 종이를 자르다/찢다 (cut/tear paper). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: defaulting to 개 instead of 장 to count sheets, and using 종이 for a form you must complete — that is 서류 (paperwork) or the document's specific name.
종이.explanation: "paper" is 종이 (jongi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 종이가 있어요 ("There is paper"). Watch the particle attached to 종이 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.
종이.shortExplanation: 종이 means "paper" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting sheets with 개 — say 종이 한 장 (one sheet), not 종이 한 개; flat things take the counter 장.
Calling a form or official document 종이 — the paper you fill in is 서류 (paperwork) or the named form; 종이 is the blank material.
Writing 'on paper' with the wrong particle, e.g. 종이를 써요 for 'write on paper' — use the surface particle 에: 종이에 써요 (종이를 쓰다 would mean 'use up paper').

usagePhrases.note: 종이 + 이/가 있어요
종이 + 장 (counter for flat things)
종이 + 에 + 쓰다
종이 + 를 + 접다

examples.en: Just give me one sheet of paper, please.
examples.note: 장 counts flat sheets; 만 = just/only

examples.ko: 여기 종이에 이름하고 전화번호를 써 주세요.
examples.romanization: yeogi jongie ireumhago jeonhwabeonhoreul sseo juseyo.
examples.en: Please write your name and phone number on this paper here.
examples.note: 종이에 = onto the paper, filling a form

examples.en: The printer is out of paper.
examples.note: 다 떨어지다 = run out completely

ex.en: We need four chairs.

의자.nuance: 의자 is Sino-Korean 椅子 ('chair') and covers any seat with legs — dining chairs, office chairs (사무용 의자 or 사무 의자), folding chairs (접이식 의자). The single most common English-speaker error is the particle with 앉다: sitting DOWN is reaching a resting position, so it must be 의자에 앉아요 (에 = destination), not 의자에서 앉아요 — even though English 'sit ON the chair' tempts you toward a location particle. Compare with standing up, which is motion away and DOES take 에서: 의자에서 일어나요. Distinguish 의자 (chair, you sit on it) from 소파 (sofa/couch, plush multi-seat) and 책상 (desk) — beginners sometimes pair them loosely. The set phrase for offering someone a seat is 의자를 빼 드리다 (pull the chair out for them). Register is neutral.
의자.explanation: "chair" is 의자 (uija). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 의자에 앉다 ("to sit on the chair"). Watch the particle attached to 의자 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests first, then vary one word.
의자.shortExplanation: 의자 means "chair" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 의자에서 앉아요 for 'I sit on the chair.' 앉다 reaches a resting point, so it takes destination 에 (의자에 앉아요). Use 에서 only for leaving the chair (의자에서 일어나요).
Calling a sofa 의자. A plush multi-seat couch is 소파; 의자 is a single hard-ish chair.
Using 위에 redundantly: 의자 위에 앉아요 sounds odd for normal sitting. Just say 의자에 앉아요 — 위에 is for objects placed on top of the seat.

usagePhrases.note: resting destination 에 with 앉다, never 에서

usagePhrases.en: to stand up from the chair
usagePhrases.note: starting point of the motion 에서
collocation 빼다 (pull out) for offering a seat
편하다 (comfortable) is the natural modifier

examples.en: Please have a seat on this chair.
examples.note: 앉다 + -으세요 honorific; 에 marks where you come to rest

examples.en: After the meeting I stood up from my chair.
examples.note: 에서 = the point you rise from; motion away

examples.en: This chair is plush and comfortable.
examples.note: 푹신하다 (soft/plush) + 편하다 collocate for seating

ex.en: 국밥 sounds like [국빱].

국밥.nuance: 국밥 is literally 국 'soup' + 밥 'rice' — a hot bowl in which rice is either pre-mixed into the broth (토렴) or served alongside to add yourself, eaten fast and cheap as a complete one-bowl meal. It differs from a plain 국 in that 국밥 is a whole meal (rice included), whereas 국 is just the soup component of a larger spread. The defining verb to learn is 말다 'to put/swirl rice into soup' — 밥을 국에 말다 — which has no clean English equivalent and trips learners up. 국밥 is the classic 해장 'hangover-cure' food, and Busan's 돼지국밥 (pork) is nationally famous. Pitfall: even though it looks like soup, you say 국밥을 먹다 'eat gukbap', not 마시다 'drink', because the rice makes it food, not a beverage — and don't forget the counter 그릇 when ordering a single bowl.
국밥.explanation: "gukbap; soup with rice" is 국밥 (gukbap). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 국밥을 먹다 ("to eat gukbap"). Watch the particle attached to 국밥 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.
국밥.shortExplanation: 국밥 means "gukbap; soup with rice" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 국밥 as just soup and forgetting the 밥 'rice' — the word literally bundles rice and soup into one complete meal.
Saying 국밥을 마셔요 'I drink gukbap' — the rice content means it takes 먹다 'eat'; 마시다 is only for pure liquid.
Ordering '국밥 하나' and stopping there in a sit-down place; the natural, polite phrasing uses the bowl counter: 국밥 한 그릇 주세요.

usagePhrases.note: 먹다 'eat', not 마시다 — even though it's soupy, the rice makes it a meal you eat
뜨겁다 = hot to the touch/temperature, the typical comment on a steaming bowl
그릇 counts a bowl/serving
돼지 'pig' + 국밥; the Busan specialty

examples.en: One bowl of gukbap, please.
examples.note: simplest ordering line; 그릇 is the natural counter

examples.ko: 술 마신 다음 날엔 국밥이 최고예요.
examples.romanization: sul masin daeum naren gukbabi choegoyeyo.
examples.en: The day after drinking, gukbap is the best.
examples.note: everyday hangover context — 해장 culture

examples.en: Mix the rice into the broth and eat.
examples.note: real server's tip; 말다 'to put rice into soup' is the exact verb

국민.en: citizens; the people of a nation

ex.en: 국민 sounds like [궁민].

국민.nuance: 국민 (國民, 國 'nation' + 民 'people' — 'the people of the nation') means the people as citizens of a particular country: a civic, collective term bound up with rights (권리), duties (의무), and the state. Distinguish it from two neighbors. Against 사람들 ('people' in general): 국민 is people specifically as a national citizenry, so '거리에 사람들이 많아요' (lots of people on the street) could never be 국민. Against 시민 (市民, 'citizens'): 시민 leans toward city residents or civil society (시민 단체 = civic groups, 서울 시민 = Seoul residents), while 국민 frames people in relation to the nation and government. Use 국민 whenever the context is national identity, elections, law, or the state's relationship to its population.
국민.explanation: 국민 (gungmin) means "the people; citizens of a nation". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 국민의 권리 ("the rights of the people"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 국민 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
국민.shortExplanation: 국민 means "the people; citizens of a nation" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 국민 to mean 'people' in a general, casual sense. For an unspecified crowd use 사람들 — '사람들이 많아요', not '국민이 많아요'.
Confusing 국민 with 시민. 국민 = citizens of a nation (national level); 시민 = city residents / civil society (서울 시민, 시민 단체).

usagePhrases.note: 국민 pairs with 권리 ('rights') and 의무 ('duties') in civic contexts.
전 ('whole') + 국민 = everyone in the country (전 국민이 = all citizens [as subject]).
Fixed compound written as one word; a direct vote by all citizens.
뽑다 ('choose, pick, elect') is the natural verb in election contexts.

examples.en: The people elect the president.
examples.note: Simple civic frame: 국민이 (subject) + 뽑다; 뽑다 is the everyday verb for 'elect/choose'.

examples.ko: 이 정책은 전 국민에게 영향을 줘요.
examples.romanization: i jeongchaegeun jeon gungminege yeonghyangeul jwoyo.
examples.en: This policy affects all citizens.
examples.note: 전 국민에게 uses 에게 for the people affected; 영향을 주다 = 'have an effect on'.

examples.ko: 국가는 국민의 안전과 행복을 위해 일해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gukganeun gungminui anjeongwa haengbogeul wihae ilhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: The state should work for the safety and happiness of its citizens.
examples.note: 국가 + 국민, the classic civic pairing; 의 links 국민 to 안전과 행복.

ex.en: 입학 sounds like [이팍].

입학하다.nuance: 입학하다 is Sino-Korean 入學 — 入 'enter' + 學 'learning/school' — literally 'enter into learning', i.e. be admitted to and begin a school. Its exact opposite is 졸업하다 (卒業). Here is a beautiful particle trap that mirrors its opposite: 입학하다 uses 에 ('enter INTO' a school — 대학에 입학하다), whereas 졸업하다 uses 를 (대학을 졸업하다). English 'enroll IN' luckily matches the 에 here, but learners who memorized 졸업하다's 를 wrongly carry it over. Don't confuse 입학하다 with 등록하다 'to register': 입학하다 is the once-in-a-school-career act of being admitted, while 등록하다 is the recurring paperwork of signing up (for a term, a course). As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (입학해요, 입학했어요, formal 입학합니다); negative and impossible split the noun (입학 안 해요, 입학 못 해요). Note the pronunciation: 입학 sounds like [이팍], the ㅂ and ㅎ fusing to ㅍ.
입학하다.explanation: 입학하다 (iphakada) means "to enroll in school". Start from the polite form 입학해요 — it is safe with almost anyone, so use it before the dictionary form 입학하다. A strong first sentence is 대학교에 입학하다 ("to enter / enroll in university"); once that feels natural, swap the noun, place, or time and reuse the verb everywhere. Korean changes the ending rather than the word, so the same 입학하다 also becomes 입학하고 싶어요 (want), 입학할 수 있어요 (can), and 입학 못 해요 (cannot). Say one true sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then bend it.
입학하다.shortExplanation: 입학하다 means "to enroll in school" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 입학하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 입학해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 대학교를 입학해요 by analogy with 대학교를 졸업해요 — the two opposites take opposite particles: enter uses 에 (대학교에 입학해요), graduate uses 를.
Using 입학하다 for re-registering each semester — that is 등록하다. 입학하다 is the one-time admission/start.
Writing the negative as 안 입학해요 — split: 입학 안 해요 (impossible = 입학 못 해요).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 입학하다 becomes 입학할 수 있어요 ("can") and 입학할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not enroll in school.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to enroll in school.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to enroll in school.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
the school takes 에 (entered-into), NOT 를: 대학교에 입학해요

examples.en: My younger sibling is starting middle school.
examples.note: School entered = 에: 중학교에 입학해요

examples.en: I want to get into a good university.
examples.note: ~고 싶어요 = want to; 좋은 대학 = a good university

examples.ko: 성적이 낮아서 그 학교에 입학 못 해요.
examples.romanization: seongjeogi najaseo geu hakgyoe ipang mo taeyo.
examples.en: My grades are low, so I can't get into that school.
examples.note: Reason ~아서 + impossible form split: 입학 못 해요

ex.en: 축하해요 sounds like [추카해요].

축하해요.nuance: 축하해요 congratulates someone on genuinely HAPPY news. 축하(祝賀) is Sino-Korean — 祝 'to wish, to celebrate' + 賀 'to congratulate' — and it conjugates as a 하다-verb: 축하하다 → 축하해요 (polite) → 축하합니다 (formal) → 축하해 (casual). The structural pattern is [occasion noun] + 축하해요: 결혼 축하해요, 합격 축하해요, 생일 축하해요, 출산 축하해요. Register is critical: toward a senior, use the humble 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다 (드리다 'to give humbly'), NOT plain 축하해요, because you are offering the congratulation upward as a gift rather than stating it. The English-speaker pitfall is using 축하해요 like the broad English 'congratulations' — in Korean, 축하 is strictly for joyful milestones. For someone going through hardship (failed exam, difficult project, loss) you never 축하; you say 힘내세요 ('stay strong'), 고생했어요 ('you worked hard'), or offer 수고 language. Also, don't conflate with 화이팅 — 화이팅 cheers someone ON before they face a challenge; 축하해요 celebrates AFTER the good outcome has arrived.
축하해요.explanation: 축하해요 (chukahaeyo) = "Congratulations.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 축하해요 ("congratulations"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
축하해요.shortExplanation: 축하해요 is a practical expression meaning "Congratulations.".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 축하해요 for difficult or sorrowful situations — it is only for genuinely happy news; for someone who went through hardship say 힘내세요 or 고생했어요 instead.
Saying plain 축하해요 to a clearly senior person — toward elders, bosses, or respected seniors, the humble form 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다 is expected and its omission can seem disrespectful.
Mixing it up with 화이팅 — 화이팅 cheers someone on BEFORE a challenge; 축하해요 celebrates AFTER the good outcome has arrived. Using 축하해요 before someone takes an exam would be bizarre and presumptuous.

usagePhrases.note: warm, friendly-polite (해요체) — for peers and acquaintances on happy news
formal occasions: award ceremonies, company announcements, official events
toward a senior or elder — 드리다 'to give (humbly)' shows deference
highest register of sincerity: 진심으로 ('from the heart') + humble 드립니다

examples.ko: A: 시험에 합격했어요! / B: 정말요? 축하해요! 고생했어요.
examples.romanization: A: siheome hapgyeokaesseoyo! / B: jeongmaryo? chukahaeyo! gosaenghaesseoyo.
examples.en: A: I passed the exam! / B: Really? Congratulations! You worked so hard.
examples.note: immediate spontaneous reaction to good news — 고생했어요 acknowledges the effort behind the achievement

examples.ko: 졸업 축하해요! 앞날이 더 빛날 거예요.
examples.romanization: joreop chukahaeyo! amnari deo binnal geoyeyo.
examples.en: Congratulations on your graduation! Your future will be even brighter.
examples.note: occasion word 졸업 fronts the phrase — the standard [occasion] + 축하해요 pattern; warm wish follows

examples.ko: 부장님, 승진을 진심으로 축하드립니다. 앞으로도 잘 부탁드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: bujangnim, seungjineul jinsimeuro chukadeurimnida. apeurodo jal butakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: Director, I offer my sincere congratulations on your promotion. I look forward to your continued guidance.
examples.note: humble 축하드리다 toward a clearly senior person; followed by 잘 부탁드리겠습니다 to reinforce deference

ex.en: 못해요 sounds like [모태요].

한국어를 잘 못해요.nuance: 한국어를 잘 못해요 = 한국어 (Korean language) + 를 (object marker) + 잘 (well) + 못하다 (to be unable to do well). The key interpretive point: 잘 못하다 means 'can't do it well' (ability is limited), while 안 하다 means 'I don't do it' (by choice). Using 안 하다 — 한국어를 안 해요 — implies you are refusing or unwilling, which is not what you mean. The 잘 softens the claim from 'I can't speak Korean at all' (한국어 못해요) to 'I'm not good at it', which is more accurate and humble. 한국어 is the neutral/formal word for the language, while 한국말 is more colloquial and warm; both are correct. The classic follow-up toolkit: 천천히 말씀해 주세요 ('please speak slowly'), 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요? ('could you say that again?'), and 영어 하시는 분 계세요? ('is there anyone who speaks English?'). English speakers most often get the particle wrong (한국어가 잘 못해요 — the language is the object, not the subject) or write 잘못해요 as one word, which means 'to do something wrong/make a mistake' — a completely different word.
한국어를 잘 못해요.explanation: "I'm not good at Korean." — that is 한국어를 잘 못해요 (hangugeoreul jal motaeyo). It is a fixed expression you use as a chunk, like 한국어를 잘 못해요 ("I'm not good at Korean"). Match it to the right moment and the right listener; the examples show when it fits and what usually comes next.
한국어를 잘 못해요.shortExplanation: 한국어를 잘 못해요 is a practical expression meaning "I'm not good at Korean.".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Saying 한국어를 안 해요.
안 하다 = 'choose not to do'. To say you lack ability, use 못하다: 한국어를 잘 못해요.
Using the subject particle: 한국어가 잘 못해요.
The language is the object of 못하다: 한국어를 잘 못해요.
Splitting 못해요 wrongly or writing 잘못해요.
Here 못 means 'cannot' (잘 못해요 = can't do well). 잘못하다 as one word means 'to do wrong / make a mistake' — a different meaning.

usagePhrases.note: 존댓말, the standard polite way to flag your limited Korean to any stranger
반말 to a friend or peer your age

usagePhrases.en: I do not speak Korean well
usagePhrases.note: 격식 -습니다; 한국말 is the slightly more colloquial word for the language
The essential follow-up request — always pair this with 잘 못해요 when asking someone to accommodate you

examples.en: I'm sorry, I'm not good at Korean.
examples.note: The most natural opener; 죄송해요 cushions the admission and invites the other person's patience

examples.ko: A: 주문하시겠어요? / B: 저 한국어를 잘 못해요. 혹시 영어 되세요? / A: 조금요!
examples.romanization: A: jumunhasigesseoyo? / B: jeo hangugeoreul jal motaeyo. hoksi yeongeo doeseyo? / A: jogeumyo!
examples.en: A: Are you ready to order? / B: I'm not good at Korean. Do you happen to speak English? / A: A little!
examples.note: Real A/B restaurant exchange; 혹시 영어 되세요? is a natural, gentle way to ask

examples.ko: 한국어를 잘 못해요. 죄송한데 조금만 천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: hangugeoreul jal motaeyo. joesonghande jogeumman cheoncheonhi malsseumhae jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: I'm not good at Korean. Sorry, but could you speak just a bit more slowly?
examples.note: Real scene; 조금만 ('just a little') + 천천히 + 말씀해 주시겠어요 is the full polite request to slow down

ex.en: We grill the meat and the garlic together too.

고기.nuance: In everyday speech 고기 by default means red land meat — usually 돼지고기(pork) or 소고기(beef) — so 고기 먹으러 가자 implies a BBQ, not seafood. To be specific you compound the animal onto 고기: 닭고기(chicken), 소고기(beef), 돼지고기(pork). The words to contrast are 생선(fish as food) and 해산물(seafood), which Koreans do NOT file under 고기; chicken sits on the edge, so people usually say 닭고기 rather than bare 고기 for it. The set cooking verb is 굽다, a ㅂ-irregular that becomes 구워요/구웠어요 (not 'gubeoyo'). The English-speaker pitfall is the English umbrella sense of 'meat' that includes fish and poultry — in Korean, unmarked 고기 leans strongly toward pork/beef, and you should name the animal when you mean otherwise.
고기.explanation: 고기 (gogi) means "meat (esp. pork or beef)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 고기를 먹어요 ("I eat meat"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 고기 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.
고기.shortExplanation: 고기 means "meat (esp. pork or beef)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming bare 고기 covers fish or chicken — Koreans say 생선 for fish and usually 닭고기 for chicken; unmarked 고기 ≈ pork/beef.
Conjugating 굽다 as 'gubeoyo' regularly — it is ㅂ-irregular: 굽다 → 구워요, 구웠어요.
Using 고기 for seafood at a restaurant — order 회 (raw fish) or 해산물 (seafood); 고기 sets up the wrong dish.

usagePhrases.note: object marker 를
subject marker 가 to describe texture
-고 싶다 = want to; attaches to 먹다
굽다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 구워요; the verb for Korean BBQ

examples.en: I want to eat meat tonight.
examples.note: simple desire with -고 싶어요

examples.ko: 고기가 좀 질긴데 더 익혀 주세요.
examples.romanization: gogiga jom jilginde deo ikyeo juseyo.
examples.en: The meat is a bit tough — please cook it more.
examples.note: everyday line; 질기다(tough) vs 부드럽다(tender)

examples.ko: 우리 회식인데 소고기로 구울까, 돼지고기로 할까?
examples.romanization: uri hoesiginde sogogiro guulkka, dwaejigogiro halkka?
examples.en: It's our team dinner — shall we grill beef, or go with pork?
examples.note: real situation; 소고기 vs 돼지고기 specified for clarity

ex.en: I cannot eat it because I have an allergy.

알레르기.nuance: 알레르기 gives a concrete outside reason. In Korean this often makes 못 sound appropriate because the limit is physical or medical, not a preference.
알레르기.explanation: 알레르기 (allereugi) = "allergy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 알레르기가 있어서 못 먹어요. ("I cannot eat it because I have an allergy.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 알레르기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
알레르기.shortExplanation: 알레르기 means "allergy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 안 먹어요 when the reason is a medical restriction and you need 못 먹어요.
Using 알레르기 like an adjective. Say 알레르기가 있어요 or 우유 알레르기가 있어요.

usagePhrases.en: I cannot eat it because I have an allergy.
usagePhrases.note: 못 marks a real restriction.
있다 marks the presence of the allergy.

examples.ko: 고기는 싫어서 안 먹는 게 아니라 알레르기가 있어서 못 먹어요.
examples.romanization: gogineun sireoseo an meongneun ge anira allereugiga isseoseo mon meogeoyo.
examples.en: It is not that I avoid meat because I dislike it; I cannot eat it because of an allergy.
examples.note: Contrasts 안 먹다 with 못 먹다.

ex.en: It is not that I do not want to go.

싫다.nuance: 싫어요 can sound strong. For polite refusal, 고 싶지 않아요 can be softer.
싫다.explanation: 싫다 (silta) means "to dislike / to be undesirable". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 싫어요 ("I do not like it."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 싫다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
싫다.shortExplanation: 싫다 means "to dislike / to be undesirable" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Do not use 싫어요 for every polite refusal; sometimes 괜찮아요 or 안 해도 돼요 is softer.

conjugationTips.title: Describing a noun: ㄴ/은 vs ㄹ/을
conjugationTips.body: To put 싫다 in front of a noun, use the ㄴ/은 form for how something is right now: 싫은 것 ("a dislike / to be undesirable thing"). The ㄹ/을 form points to something that will or might become that way later. So 뜨거운 물 is water that is hot now, but 뜨거울 물 is water that will be hot — same adjective, different time feeling. For everyday description, reach for the ㄴ/은 form.

usagePhrases.note: Polite.
Direct.
Gerund phrase.
Preference.

examples.en: I dislike spicy food.
examples.note: Preference.

examples.en: I dislike waiting.
examples.note: Feeling.

examples.en: I do not like that.
examples.note: Direct.

ex.en: I am an employee, but I am not the person in charge.
ex.note: Useful for soft background with 인데요.

직원.nuance: 직원 (職員, 'duty-personnel') is the plain, everyday word for anyone who works at a company, shop, bank, or office — the person on the other side of the counter helping you. The synonym contrast to nail: 직원 is generic 'staff' regardless of rank, while 사원 (社員) specifically names the entry-level rung on the corporate ladder, and 종업원 sounds older/more clerical (waitstaff, hired help). In daily life 직원 is overwhelmingly the natural choice — 직원한테 물어보세요 (ask a staff member) is a sentence you'll use weekly. Register is neutral and safe for everyone. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, don't call the customer a 직원 — the 직원 is the one who WORKS there, not the visitor (that's 손님); second, English says 'I asked the staff' with no particle, but Korean must mark the person with 한테/에게: 직원에게 물어봤어요.
직원.explanation: 직원 (jigwon) = "employee; staff member". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 회사 직원 ("a company employee") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 직원, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.
직원.shortExplanation: 직원 means "employee; staff member" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a customer a 직원 — the 직원 is the worker; the customer is a 손님. Mixing these reverses who serves whom.
Dropping the particle: 직원 물어봤어요 is wrong. You must mark the person you asked with 한테/에게 → 직원한테 물어봤어요.
Assuming 직원 means a high-ranked person. It's rank-neutral; the boss is 사장 or 상사, not just 직원.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 sits in front as a noun modifier; no particle needed between them.
한테 marks the human recipient of the question; 에게 is its formal twin.
Place + 직원 names the staff of a specific business.
뽑다 literally 'to pull/pick out' is the everyday verb for hiring.

examples.en: I am a bank employee.
examples.note: Workplace + 직원 + 이에요 states your role simply.

examples.en: Please ask a staff member.
examples.note: You hear this constantly in shops; 한테 + 물어보다 = ask (a person).

examples.en: The staff at this shop are kind.
examples.note: 직원이 + adjective; Korean keeps it singular even for 'the staff' collectively.

ex.en: This year I am an office worker.
ex.note: Pairs naturally with 작년 when comparing past and present identity.

올해.nuance: 올해 is the native Korean word for the present calendar year and slots straight in front of a verb, normally WITHOUT 에: 올해 졸업해요 (I graduate this year), not 올해에. It anchors the three-year set 작년 (last year) – 올해 (this year) – 내년 (next year). There is a Sino-Korean synonym 금년 (今年, 'present year'), but it is stiff and limited to formal writing or speeches; in conversation 올해 is the only natural choice. Two English-speaker pitfalls stand out. First, the 에 habit: because English says 'in this year' learners over-add 에, but native usage drops it after 올해. Second, the look-alike trap with 오늘 ('today') — both start with 오, yet 올해 is a whole year and 오늘 is a single day, so 'I'm twenty this year' is 올해 스무 살이에요, never 오늘.
올해.explanation: 올해 (olhae) means "this year". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 올해 ("this year"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 올해 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
올해.shortExplanation: 올해 means "this year" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Adding 에 — 올해 갔어요 is natural, 올해에 갔어요 sounds off; 올해 normally takes no particle before the verb.
Confusing 올해 (this year) with 오늘 (today) — same 오- start, but one is a year and one is a day.
Reaching for 금년 in speech — it is formal-written; say 올해 when talking.

usagePhrases.note: the current calendar year
는 marks topic/contrast with other years
말 = the closing part/end
안에 = within, before the year is out

examples.en: I came to Korea this year.
examples.note: no 에 — 올해 sits straight before the verb

examples.en: This year is really busy.
examples.note: 는 contrasts it with calmer years

examples.en: I want to graduate within this year.
examples.note: 올해 안에 = before this year ends

ex.en: Because it is a weekday, I cannot do it for long.
