ex.note: Useful contrast with 주말 for schedule-based reasons.

평일.nuance: 평일 is Sino-Korean 平日 (平 'flat/ordinary' + 日 'day'), literally an 'ordinary day' — Monday through Friday, the regular working days, set against 주말 (weekend) and 휴일 (holiday/day off). The dividing line vs 주중 (週中, 'inside the week'): 평일 simply names the ordinary days as a category, while 주중 frames those same days as the span 'during the week' and pairs naturally with 주말 as a matched contrast (주중에는 바쁘고 주말에는 쉬어요). 평일 is neutral and used by everyone in any register, from a weather report to a friend's text. It habitually appears as 평일 + time-of-day (평일 아침/낮/저녁) and with 에/에는. The English-speaker pitfall: 'weekday' in English can mean 'any single working day' OR the whole work portion of the week, but in Korean 평일 leans toward the category of ordinary days, so for a duration like 'during the week I'm busy' Koreans more often say 주중에는 바빠요; also don't write the near-homophone 휴일 (rest day) by mistake.
평일.explanation: 평일 (pyeongil) means "weekday". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 평일에 ("on a weekday"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 평일 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
평일.shortExplanation: 평일 means "weekday" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 평일날 to mean 'on a weekday' is redundant — 일(日) already means 'day', so 날 doubles it; just say 평일에.
Writing 주말 (weekend) when you mean 평일 — they are exact opposites, so 평일에 일해요 (work on weekdays) vs 주말에 쉬어요 (rest on weekends).
Forgetting 에 in time phrases: not 평일 갔어요 but 평일에 갔어요, because a point-in-time noun needs the locative-time particle 에.

usagePhrases.note: Add 에 for 'on'; 평일에 갔어요 = went on a weekday
No particle: 평일 sticks directly to the next noun to modify it
Common slot for off-peak hours, doctor visits, quiet cafes
After-work time; 평일 저녁에 운동해요 = I work out on weeknights

examples.en: On weekdays I go to school.
examples.note: Topic 은 makes a 'weekdays, as for them' contrast with weekends

examples.en: On weekdays there are fewer people.
examples.note: 에는 = 에(on) + 는(contrast), the natural way to set the scene

examples.en: It's hard to make time on a weekday.
examples.note: Real-life 직장인 complaint: 시간(을) 내다 = to make/spare time

ex.en: There are four people in my family.
ex.note: Core word for polite family introductions.

저희.nuance: 저희 is not colder than 우리; it is socially careful. Use it when the listener is outside your group and the situation is polite. Use 우리 with close friends, family, and many natural everyday phrases like 우리 엄마.
저희.explanation: 저희 (jeohui) means "our / my (humble, polite)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 저희 가족은 네 명이에요. ("There are four people in my family."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 저희 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
저희.shortExplanation: 저희 means "our / my (humble, polite)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 제 가족은 too mechanically. It is possible, but 저희 가족은 sounds more natural in polite introductions.
Using 저희 for the listener's family. 저희 lowers your own side, not the other person's side.
Forgetting that 저희 pairs naturally with 가족 and 부모님 in formal or semi-formal introductions.

usagePhrases.en: There are four people in my family.
usagePhrases.note: Polite family introduction to someone outside the family.
Humble 우리 with respectful family noun 부모님.

examples.ko: 회사 동료에게는 '저희 가족은 네 명이에요'라고 말해요.
examples.romanization: hoesa dongnyoegeneun 'jeohui gajogeun ne myeongieyo'rago malhaeyo.
examples.en: To a coworker, say 'There are four people in my family.'
examples.note: 저희 fits polite outside-the-family introductions.

ex.en: How many people are in your family?
ex.note: Pairs with 명 for family size.

가족.nuance: 가족 is the Sino-Korean word 家族 ('house' 家 + 'clan/group' 族), so it names the whole family unit as a collective, never a single relative — for one member you must say 가족 한 명 or name the relationship (형, 누나). The near-synonym 식구 also means family but literally means 食口 'mouths to feed', stressing the people who live and eat under one roof, so 식구 feels warmer and more domestic ('우리 식구 다섯이에요') while 가족 is the neutral standard term that also covers relatives living apart. Register is neutral and safe in any setting. The big English-speaker trap is two-fold: 'big/small family' is 가족이 많다/적다 (many/few), never 가족이 크다 (that sounds like physically large bodies); and Koreans say 우리 가족 ('our family') where English forces 'my family', so the 우리 is idiomatic, not a mistake.
가족.explanation: 가족 (gajok) means "family". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우리 가족 ("my family"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 가족 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
가족.shortExplanation: 가족 means "family" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 가족이 커요 for 'I have a big family' — 크다 describes physical size, so it sounds like your relatives are huge; use 가족이 많아요 (many members).
Using 가족 to point at one person ('그 가족이 제 형이에요') — 가족 is a group word; for a single relative say 가족 중 한 명 or just 제 형.
Dropping 우리 and saying only 가족 for 'my family' in conversation — natural Korean fronts it as 우리 가족, even when the meaning is singular 'my'.

usagePhrases.note: 우리 (our) is the default possessive Koreans use even for 'my' family
literally 'family is many' — use 많다, not 크다, for member count
two nouns stacked directly, no 의 needed
과 is the bookish 'with'; 하고/랑 are the casual ones

examples.en: My family has four people.
examples.note: 명 is the counter for people; say the number + 명, not just the number

examples.en: I really love my family.
examples.note: 가족 takes the object particle 을 here because 사랑하다 acts on it

examples.en: On weekends I eat with my family.
examples.note: 주말에는 fronts the time with 에 + 는 for 'as for weekends'

ex.en: My father is coming too.

아버지.nuance: 아버지 is the respectful, neutral word for 'father,' used in polite conversation, in writing, and whenever you speak about your dad to others. Its near-synonym 아빠 is the warm home word ('dad/daddy'): children and many adults call him 아빠 to his face, while 아버지 sounds more grown-up, dignified, or formal — the gap is exactly the English 'dad' vs 'father.' One step higher is 아버님, reserved for someone else's father or your father-in-law. Because a father is an elder, 아버지 naturally pulls honorific machinery: the subject marker 께서, the dative 께, and -(으)시- verb endings (읽으세요, 주무세요). Two English-speaker pitfalls: the copula is 아버지예요 (vowel-final 지 → 예요, not '아버지이에요'); and possession uses 우리 아버지 ('our father'), since 내 아버지 sounds oddly cold to Korean ears.
아버지.explanation: 아버지 (abeoji) means "father". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 아버지 ("father"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 아버지 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
아버지.shortExplanation: 아버지 means "father" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '아버지이에요' — after the vowel 지 the copula contracts to 아버지예요.
Using casual 아빠 in formal, business, or written contexts where the respectful 아버지 is expected.
Saying '내 아버지' for 'my father'; Koreans normally say 우리 아버지 ('our father').

usagePhrases.note: The standard, respectful word for one's father, in both speech and writing.
After the vowel-final 지 the copula is 예요, not '이에요': 아버지예요.
Honorific subject marker 께서 replaces 이/가 to elevate the elder.
Extra-honorific 아버지 + 님; used for another person's father or one's father-in-law.

examples.en: My father is an office worker.
examples.note: Note 우리 ('our') for 'my' family member — Koreans rarely say 내 아버지.

examples.en: I respect my father.
examples.note: 아버지 as object with 를; pairs with the humble self-pronoun 저.

examples.en: My father is reading the newspaper.
examples.note: Full honorific chain: subject 께서 + the honorific verb ending -으세요.

ex.en: My mother came.

어머니.nuance: 어머니 is the respectful, neutral word for 'mother,' used in polite speech, in writing, and when talking about your mom to others. Its near-synonym 엄마 is the affectionate home word ('mom/mommy') that people usually call her directly at home, while 어머니 carries more formality and respect — the same distance as English 'mom' vs 'mother.' The higher honorific 어머님 is for someone else's mother or your mother-in-law. As an elder, 어머니 routinely takes honorific particles and endings: 께서 for the subject, 께 for 'to,' and -(으)시- verbs (하세요, 주무세요). Watch two English-speaker traps: the copula contracts to 어머니예요 after the vowel 니 (not '어머니이에요'); and you give things to her with the honorific 어머니께 ... 드리다, not the plain 어머니한테 ... 줘요. Possession is likewise 우리 어머니, since 내 어머니 sounds unnaturally distant.
어머니.explanation: "mother" is 어머니 (eomeoni). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어머니 ("mother"). Watch the particle attached to 어머니 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
어머니.shortExplanation: 어머니 means "mother" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying '어머니이에요' — after the vowel 니 the copula contracts to 어머니예요.
Using casual 엄마 in formal or written settings where the respectful 어머니 is expected.
Saying '어머니한테 줘요' to an elder; politely it is 어머니께 드려요 (honorific 께 + humble 드리다).

usagePhrases.note: The standard, respectful word for one's mother, in both speech and writing.
After the vowel-final 니 the copula is 예요, not '이에요': 어머니예요.
Honorific subject marker 께서 replaces 이/가 to elevate the elder.
Extra-honorific 어머니 + 님; for another person's mother or one's mother-in-law.

examples.en: My mother is a teacher.
examples.note: Again 우리 ('our') for one's own mother, the natural choice over 내 어머니.

examples.en: I gave my mother a present.
examples.note: Honorific dative 께 (not 한테) plus the humble give-verb 드리다.

examples.en: My mother is cooking.
examples.note: Real scene: subject 께서 + honorific 하세요 to respect the elder.

ex.en: I have one older brother.

형.nuance: 형 (Sino-Korean 兄 'elder brother') is the word a MALE uses for an older brother, and crucially it is also a warm address term a younger man uses for any slightly-older male he is close to — an older friend, schoolmate, or colleague — so '민수 형' can mean 'Minsu, my big-brother-figure', not a blood relative. The matched set is gendered by speaker: a female says 오빠 for the same older-brother relationship, while 누나/언니 cover older sisters — so the single word leaks the speaker's gender, something English's flat 'older brother' never does. Register is casual-but-respectful: 형 is itself an honorific address (you call him 형, never his bare name), and you speak up to him. The dominant English-speaker pitfall is gender: a woman must never call her older brother 형 — that is 오빠 — and second, don't assume 형 always means kin; in daily life it is most often the affectionate title for an older male friend.
형.explanation: "older brother (male speaker)" is 형 (hyeong). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우리 형 ("my older brother"). Watch the particle attached to 형 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
형.shortExplanation: 형 means "older brother (male speaker)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
A female speaker using 형 for her older brother — women say 오빠; 형 is strictly male-to-male.
Assuming 형 only ever means a blood brother — a younger man also calls a close older male friend 형 (e.g. 동수 형).
Calling your older brother by his bare first name instead of 형 — Korean requires the title 형 as both address and reference for elders.

usagePhrases.note: said only by a male; the word itself signals the speaker is male
있다 = 'have/exist'; 형 takes 가→이 after a consonant
한테 is the casual dative used among close family
친 (親, 'blood/real') distinguishes him from a 사촌 or 의형

examples.en: I have one older brother.
examples.note: 명 counts people; one says 한 명, never 일 명

examples.en: I play games with my older brother.
examples.note: 하고 (casual 'with') + 같이 is the everyday combo for 'together with'

examples.en: My older brother is taller than me.
examples.note: 보다 = 'than'; literally 'than me, height is big' = taller

ex.en: I have one older brother.

오빠.nuance: 오빠 is the word a FEMALE uses for an older brother, and it is the most socially loaded kinship term in Korean: a woman also calls a close older male friend, a senior, or especially a boyfriend 오빠, so '오빠' on its own can mean 'my big brother', 'my guy friend', or 'babe' depending on context — hence 친오빠 exists to specify the actual sibling. Its gendered counterpart is 형, used by a MALE for the same older-brother relationship, so 오빠 vs 형 splits by speaker, and the word instantly reveals the speaker is a woman. Register is casual and affectionate, used with -요 forms, and 오빠 is itself the address term (never his bare name). The major English-speaker pitfall is gender — a man must say 형, never 오빠 — and the cultural trap: because 오빠 also means 'boyfriend' in romantic use, calling a male friend 오빠 can imply flirtation, so learners should know the connotation before using it freely.
오빠.explanation: 오빠 (oppa) means "older brother (female speaker)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우리 오빠 ("my older brother"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 오빠 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
오빠.shortExplanation: 오빠 means "older brother (female speaker)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
A male speaker using 오빠 for his older brother — men say 형; 오빠 is used only by females.
Not realizing 오빠 can mean 'boyfriend' — a woman calling any older man 오빠 may signal romantic interest, so use it knowingly.
Saying 친오빠 when you mean a boyfriend — 친오빠 specifically means a blood older brother; for a boyfriend just say 남자친구.

usagePhrases.note: said only by a female; the word signals the speaker is female
있다 'have'; 오빠 ends in a vowel so it takes 가
한테 is the casual dative among close people
친 (親 'real') separates him from a boyfriend or cousin called 오빠

examples.en: I have one older brother.
examples.note: 명 counts people; 한 명 = one (person)

examples.en: My older brother is coming to pick me up.
examples.note: 데리러 오다 = come in order to fetch a person; -러 marks purpose

examples.en: I watch a movie with my older brother.
examples.note: 보다 'watch' → 봐요; 하고 같이 = 'together with'

ex.en: I have one older sister.

누나.nuance: 누나 is the word a MALE uses for an older sister, and like 형 it doubles as a warm address title a younger man uses for any older woman he is close to — an older female friend, senior student, or, famously, a beloved older woman ('누나' in K-pop). Its gendered partner is 언니, which a FEMALE uses for the very same older-sister relationship, so 누나 vs 언니 is split purely by who is speaking, and the word betrays the speaker's gender in a way English 'older sister' cannot. Register is casual but deferential: 누나 is itself a respectful address (you call her 누나, not her name) and you speak up to her with -요 forms. A very natural collocation is 도와주다 'help (as a favor)'. The headline English-speaker pitfall is gender: a man must say 누나 and a woman 언니 for an older sister — swapping them is an immediate giveaway — and remember 누나 is also how a younger man fondly addresses an older woman, not only a sibling.
누나.explanation: 누나 (nuna) = "older sister (male speaker)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리 누나 ("my older sister") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 누나, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
누나.shortExplanation: 누나 means "older sister (male speaker)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
A female speaker using 누나 for her older sister — women say 언니; 누나 is strictly used by males.
Confusing 누나 (male→older sister) with 언니 (female→older sister) — the choice depends entirely on the SPEAKER's gender, not the sister's.
Addressing your older sister by her bare name rather than 누나 — Korean expects the kinship title 누나 for someone older.

usagePhrases.note: said only by a male; the word marks the speaker as male
있다 'have'; 누나 ends in a vowel so it takes 가
한테 is the casual dative for close family
친 (親 'real/blood') marks her as a full sister, not 사촌

examples.en: I have two older sisters.
examples.note: 명 counts people; 두 명 = two (people)

examples.en: My older sister often helps me.
examples.note: 도와주다 (돕다 + 주다, ㅂ-irregular) = do the favor of helping

examples.en: I go to a cafe with my older sister.
examples.note: 하고 'with' + 같이; 에 marks the destination 카페

ex.en: I have one older sister.

언니.nuance: 언니 is the word a FEMALE uses for an older sister, and it extends warmly to any close older woman — an older female friend, a senior at school or work — and is also the friendly way younger women address a female shopkeeper or restaurant server ('언니, 여기요!'), so it ranges from blood sister to polite stranger. Its gendered counterpart is 누나, used by a MALE for the same older-sister bond, so 언니 vs 누나 splits purely by the speaker's gender, and the word reveals that the speaker is a woman — a distinction English 'older sister' simply lacks. Register is casual and affectionate, used with -요 endings, and 언니 itself serves as the address (you say 언니, not her name). The chief English-speaker pitfall is gender: a man must say 누나, never 언니, for an older sister; and don't be surprised to hear women call a saleswoman 언니 — it is friendly social lubricant, not a claim of kinship.
언니.explanation: "older sister (female speaker)" is 언니 (eonni). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우리 언니 ("my older sister"). Watch the particle attached to 언니 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
언니.shortExplanation: 언니 means "older sister (female speaker)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
A male speaker using 언니 for his older sister — men say 누나; 언니 is used only by females.
Confusing 언니 (female→older sister) with 누나 (male→older sister) — the form depends on the SPEAKER's gender.
Thinking 언니 always means a relative — women also use 언니 to address an older female friend or even a shop assistant.

usagePhrases.note: said only by a female; the word marks the speaker as female
있다 'have'; 언니 ends in a vowel so it takes 가
한테 is the casual dative for close family
친 (親 'real') distinguishes her from a cousin or older female friend

examples.en: I have two older sisters.
examples.note: 명 counts people; 두 명 = two (people)

examples.en: My older sister often lends me clothes.
examples.note: 빌려주다 (빌리다 + 주다) = lend; the favor flows from her to me

examples.en: I go shopping with my older sister.
examples.note: 쇼핑을 하다 = to shop; 하고 같이 = 'together with'

ex.en: I have one younger sibling.
ex.note: Works regardless of the speaker's gender.

동생.nuance: 동생 (Sino-Korean 同生 'born of the same' parents) means a younger sibling and, unlike the older-sibling words, is NOT split by speaker gender and does NOT itself reveal whether the sibling is male or female — to specify you prepend 남 (男) for 남동생 'younger brother' or 여 (女) for 여동생 'younger sister'. It also extends to any younger person you are close to (a junior at work or school), mirroring how 형/오빠/누나/언니 work upward; the system is asymmetric — elders get gendered, speaker-dependent titles, while juniors share the one neutral 동생. Register: unlike the older-sibling titles, 동생 is NOT used as a direct address — you call a younger sibling by name, and 동생 is only how you refer to them. The key English-speaker pitfall is assuming 동생 means 'younger brother'; it is sex-neutral, so without 남/여 it could be either, and you should never address someone as '동생' the way you'd say '형' — call them by name instead.
동생.explanation: 동생 (dongsaeng) = "younger sibling". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리 동생 ("my younger sibling") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 동생, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
동생.shortExplanation: 동생 means "younger sibling" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 동생 means only 'younger brother' — it is sex-neutral; add 남 (남동생) or 여 (여동생) to specify, or it stays ambiguous.
Using 동생 as a direct address ('동생, 이리 와') — unlike 형/누나, you call a younger sibling by name, not by the word 동생.
Writing 일 명 / 이 명 to count siblings — people use native numbers with 명: 한 명, 두 명.

usagePhrases.note: works for a younger brother OR sister, any speaker
있다 'have'; 동생 ends in a consonant so it takes 이
남 (男 'male') specifies the sex of the sibling
여 (女 'female') specifies the sex of the sibling

examples.en: I have one younger sibling.
examples.note: 명 counts people; 동생 doesn't reveal the sex on its own

examples.en: I often take care of my younger sibling.
examples.note: 돌보다 'look after' → 돌봐요; 동생 takes object 을 here

examples.en: My younger brother is tall.
examples.note: 키가 크다 = 'height is big' = tall; 남동생 makes the sex explicit

ex.en: My grandfather is coming.

할아버지.nuance: 할아버지 is your grandfather on either side, and casual speech uses it for both the father's and the mother's father; 외할아버지 (maternal) or 친할아버지 (paternal) pin down the side when it matters. It is 할- (a prefix for the generation above) + 아버지 'father', and like 할머니 it can respectfully address any elderly man you know. The spelling trips beginners because of the liaison: it is one solid word, 할아버지, written together — never 할 아버지 — and the ㄹ slides onto the next syllable so it sounds like 하라버지. The deeper pitfall for English speakers is honorifics: a grandfather outranks you, so the verb climbs to the honorific level (읽으세요, 주무세요, 진지 드세요), and 밥 politely becomes 진지. Say 우리 할아버지, mirroring 우리 할머니, rather than the textbook-literal 제 할아버지.
할아버지.explanation: "grandfather" is 할아버지 (harabeoji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 우리 할아버지 ("my (our) grandfather"). Watch the particle attached to 할아버지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
할아버지.shortExplanation: 할아버지 means "grandfather" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 할아버지이에요. After the vowel 지 it must contract to 할아버지예요.
Splitting it as 할 아버지. Grandfather is a single lexical word, 할아버지, and the liaison even makes it sound like 하라버지.
Saying 할아버지가 밥을 먹어요 for your own grandfather. Raise it: 할아버지께서 진지를 드세요 — honorific subject 께서, honorific noun 진지, honorific verb 드세요.

usagePhrases.note: use 우리, the inclusive 'our', for family
noun + 예요 because 지 ends in a vowel
께 is the honorific of 에게/한테 for an elder
께서 honors the elder as the subject

examples.en: Grandfather, please eat (your meal).
examples.note: 진지 is the honorific word for 밥, and 드세요 honors the eating

examples.en: Grandfather reads the newspaper.
examples.note: the honorific 읽으세요 (not 읽어요) raises the grandfather

examples.en: Grandfather told me old stories.
examples.note: 께서 + 주셨어요 (honorific of 줬어요) show layered respect

ex.en: Please send my regards to your grandmother.
ex.note: 께 marks a respected receiver; 께서 marks a respected subject.

할머니.nuance: 할머니 is your grandmother on either side, and in plain conversation Koreans use it for both the father's and the mother's mother; add 외- (외할머니) or 친- (친할머니) only when you must mark the side. It is built from 할- (an old prefix meaning a generation above) + 어머니 'mother', and it doubles as a warm, respectful way to address ANY elderly woman you feel close to, much like English 'grandma' for a kindly neighbor. The big trap for English speakers is grammar of respect, not vocabulary: a grandmother is a high-status elder, so the verb itself must be honorific — say 할머니는 사세요 / 주무세요 / 드세요, never the flat 살아요 / 자요 / 먹어요. Pair it with 우리 할머니 ('our grandmother'), not 제 할머니, because Korean treats family as shared. Compared with the polite stranger-address 아주머니/아주머님 (a middle-aged woman), 할머니 implies real old age, so misjudging the age can sting.
할머니.explanation: 할머니 (halmeoni) means "grandmother". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 우리 할머니 ("my (our) grandmother"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 할머니 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
할머니.shortExplanation: 할머니 means "grandmother" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 할머니이에요. After a vowel (니) the copula contracts to 할머니예요; 이에요 is only for nouns ending in a consonant.
Saying 할머니가 집에 있어요 about your own grandmother. For an elder you should raise the verb: 할머니께서 집에 계세요 (계세요, the honorific of 있어요).
Calling a middle-aged woman 할머니 to be polite. It signals old age and can offend; use 아주머니 unless she is genuinely elderly.

usagePhrases.note: Koreans say 우리 (our), not 제 (my), for close family
noun + 예요 because 니 ends in a vowel
께 replaces 에게/한테 to honor an elder
께서 is the honorific of 가, raising the elder

examples.en: Grandmother, sleep well (good night).
examples.note: 안녕히 주무세요 is the honorific bedtime greeting to an elder

examples.en: My grandmother lives in the countryside.
examples.note: the honorific verb ending 사세요 (not 살아요) raises the grandmother

examples.en: Grandmother made the kimchi herself.
examples.note: 께서 + the honorific past 담그셨어요 mark deep respect

ex.en: My parents are coming to the wedding too.
ex.note: A natural event where family members are introduced politely.

결혼식.nuance: 결혼식 is the wedding CEREMONY (식 = 式 'ceremony/rite'), as opposed to 결혼 (結婚, 'tie + marry'), which is the marriage or the act of getting married — so 결혼했어요 means 'I got married,' while 결혼식에 갔어요 means 'I attended a wedding.' That 결혼/결혼식 split is the #1 trap for English speakers, since English 'wedding' blurs both. Compared with the everyday synonym 예식 (禮式, 'ceremony of courtesy'), 결혼식 is the plain default and 예식 sounds slightly more formal/venue-flavored (hence 예식장). The ceremony itself is famously short (30–60 minutes); the socially weighty part is the buffet meal afterward, which your cash gift 축의금 helps cover. Habitual collocations: 결혼식에 가다/참석하다, 결혼식을 올리다, 결혼식장. Take 에 for attendance — 결혼식을 가다 is a common particle error.
결혼식.explanation: 결혼식 (gyeolhonsik) = "wedding (ceremony)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 결혼식에 가다 ("go to a wedding") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 결혼식, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
결혼식.shortExplanation: 결혼식 means "wedding (ceremony)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.

Don't confuse 결혼식 (the ceremony you attend) with 결혼 (the marriage): '결혼했어요' means YOU got married, so saying it when you only went to a friend's wedding wrongly announces your own marriage. Use 결혼식에 갔어요.
Avoid 결혼식을 가다 — 'go' targets a destination, so the natural particle is 에: 결혼식에 가다. The 을/를 here sounds like you're somehow 'doing' the wedding.
Don't say 결혼식을 하다 for the couple holding it; the idiomatic verb is 올리다 (결혼식을 올리다) or simply 결혼하다.

usagePhrases.note: Take the particle 에 (destination/event), never 을 — you go TO the event
Set idiom for the couple having their ceremony; 올리다 (lit. 'raise/offer up') sounds more elevated than 하다
Add 場 (-장, 'place') for the building; 예식장 (禮式場) is the equally common synonym
You receive a 청첩장 (invitation); 초대받다 = 'be invited' in passive

examples.en: There's a wedding next week.
examples.note: Simple 있다 existence sentence — note 결혼식이, the subject marker, not 결혼식을

examples.en: There are so many weddings every weekend that it's a bit of a financial burden.
examples.note: 마다 = 'every'; weekend weddings + 축의금 are a real money pressure Koreans joke about

examples.ko: 부장님 딸 결혼식이라 회사 사람들이 다 같이 갔어요.
examples.romanization: bujangnim ttal gyeolhonsigira hoesa saramdeuri da gachi gasseoyo.
examples.en: It was our manager's daughter's wedding, so everyone from the office went together.
examples.note: Shows the workplace-obligation register: attending a boss's family wedding is near-mandatory

ex.en: When did the symptoms start?

증상.nuance: 증상(症狀)은 '병 증(症)' + '모양 상(狀)', 즉 '병의 모양·꼴'이라는 뜻으로, 병 때문에 몸에 드러나는 기침·열·통증 같은 '겉 신호'를 가리킨다. 헷갈리기 쉬운 이웃 단어가 둘 있다. 하나는 병 자체인 질병(disease)으로, 증상은 그 질병이 밖으로 내보이는 표시일 뿐이다. 또 하나는 통증(pain)인데, 통증은 아픈 느낌 하나를 가리키고 증상은 통증·발열·기침을 모두 아우르는 더 넓은 말이다. 말투는 격식·비격식을 가리지 않는 중립어라 환자도 의사도 똑같이 쓰며, 병원에서는 '어떤 증상이 있으세요?'가 첫 질문일 만큼 핵심어다. 영어 화자의 함정은 'I feel a symptom'을 직역해 '증상을 느끼다'만 고집하는 것인데, 한국어에서는 '증상이 있다 / 나타나다 / 심해지다 / 사라지다'처럼 증상을 주어로 세워 변화를 말하는 어법이 훨씬 자연스럽다.
증상.explanation: "symptom" is 증상 (jeungsang). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 증상이 나타나다 ("symptoms appear"). Watch the particle attached to 증상 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.
증상.shortExplanation: 증상 means "symptom" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
증상과 질병을 같은 말로 쓰는 것 — 증상은 밖으로 드러나는 신호이고, 질병은 그 신호를 일으키는 병 자체다. '감기 증상'은 감기라는 병이 보이는 표시라는 뜻이다.
'증상을 느끼다'만 쓰는 것 — 영어 feel을 직역한 어색한 어법이다. '증상이 있다, 증상이 나타나다, 증상이 심하다'처럼 증상을 주어로 말하는 게 한국어답다.
증상과 통증을 똑같이 보는 것 — 통증은 아픈 느낌 하나, 증상은 발열·기침·통증을 모두 포함하는 더 넓은 상위 개념이다.

usagePhrases.note: 나타나다와 자주 짝을 이룸
악화를 말할 때 흔한 표현
병명+증상 복합어로 자주 씀
병원에서 꼭 쓰는 표현

examples.en: What symptoms do you have?
examples.note: 병원 접수·진료실에서 가장 먼저 듣는 질문

examples.ko: 약을 먹었는데도 증상이 전혀 나아지지 않아요.
examples.romanization: yageul meogeonneundedo jeungsangi jeonhyeo naajiji anayo.
examples.en: Even though I took medicine, the symptoms aren't getting better at all.
examples.note: 진료실에서 경과를 설명 — 증상을 주어로 쓰는 자연스러운 어법

examples.ko: 초기에는 증상이 가벼워서 그냥 넘어가기 쉬운데, 그때 병원에 가는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: chogieneun jeungsangi gabyeowoseo geunyang neomeogagi swiunde, geuttae byeongwone ganeun ge joayo.
examples.en: In the early stage symptoms are mild, so it's easy to let them slide, but that's exactly when you should see a doctor.
examples.note: 초기 증상 = early symptoms, 조언을 담은 실제 상황 문장

ex.en: I take the prescription to the pharmacy.

약국.nuance: 약국 is where medicine is dispensed or sold. 병원 is where you see the doctor; 약국 is where you usually receive the medicine afterward.
약국.explanation: 약국 (yakguk) = "pharmacy". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 약국에 가다 ("to go to the pharmacy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 약국, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
약국.shortExplanation: 약국 means "pharmacy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 병원 for the pharmacy step. After receiving a prescription, you usually go to 약국.
Saying 약국에서 가요 for destination. Use 약국에 가요.
Forgetting that the pharmacist is 약사, not 의사.

usagePhrases.note: Destination takes 에.

usagePhrases.en: to receive medicine at the pharmacy
usagePhrases.note: The action place takes 에서.
Common everyday phrase.

examples.en: I take the prescription to the pharmacy.
examples.note: Clinic-to-pharmacy flow.

examples.en: I checked the medicine schedule at the pharmacy.
examples.note: Pharmacy context for instructions.

examples.en: The pharmacy is next to the clinic.
examples.note: Existence location uses 에.

ex.en: My throat hurts.
ex.note: In symptom talk, 목 often means throat.

목.nuance: 목 covers both the neck and the throat, so 목이 아프다 most often means a sore throat from a cold, NOT neck pain — assuming it only means 'neck' is the main English-speaker pitfall (for true neck/shoulder stiffness Koreans more often say 목이 뻐근하다 or specify 목덜미). Thirst is the fixed phrase 목이 마르다 ('the throat dries'), where 마르다 is 르-irregular → 말라요, 말랐어요; do not invent 목이 건조하다. A swollen throat is 목이 붓다 (ㅅ-irregular → 부어요), the same swelling verb as 발이 붓다, and going hoarse is 목이 쉬다 (lit. 'the throat rests'). Idiomatically 목이 빠지게 기다리다 means to wait so eagerly your neck stretches out ('wait with bated breath'). A throat/neck symptom marks the part with 가 (목이 아파요).
목.explanation: 목 (mok) means "neck; throat". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 목이 아프다 ("to have a sore throat"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 목 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.
목.shortExplanation: 목 means "neck; throat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 목이 아파요 only means a stiff neck — it usually means a sore throat from a cold; clarify with context if you mean the neck.
Conjugating 마르다 as 마르요 — it is 르-irregular, so 'I'm thirsty' is 목이 말라요.
Saying 목이 목말라요, doubling the word — the set phrase is simply 목이 말라요 (or colloquially just 목말라요).

usagePhrases.note: the standard cold symptom, not just neck pain
fixed phrase; 마르다 is 르-irregular: 말라요
붓다 is ㅅ-irregular: 부어요

usagePhrases.en: to lose one's voice / be hoarse
usagePhrases.note: from shouting or a cold; 'the throat rests'

examples.en: My throat hurts.
examples.note: survival sentence; usually means sore throat from a cold

examples.en: Please give me some water, I'm thirsty.
examples.note: everyday; 목이 마르다 → 말라요 (르-irregular)

examples.en: I lost my voice from cheering.
examples.note: real situation; 목이 쉬다 = go hoarse

ex.en: My stomach hurts.
ex.note: Most natural first sentence for stomach pain.

배.nuance: 배 means the belly/stomach (the body region), and the same syllable also means 'pear' and 'boat/ship' — three homonyms split only by context. Hunger and fullness are locked set phrases that ALWAYS keep 배: 배가 고프다 (hungry) and 배가 부르다 (full); you cannot say 나는 고파요 alone, which is the top beginner error. Both adjectives are irregular: 고프다 is ㅡ-irregular (고파요, 고팠어요) and 부르다 is 르-irregular (불러요, 불렀어요). Note 배 here is the colloquial stomach for aches and hunger, distinct from the Sino-Korean 위 (胃, the actual stomach organ) used in medical contexts like 위염 (gastritis). A culturally important idiom: 배가 아프다 also figuratively means to be jealous of someone's good fortune ('my stomach hurts' = green with envy), so context decides literal pain vs. envy.
배.explanation: "belly; stomach" is 배 (bae). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 배가 아프다 ("one's stomach hurts"). Watch the particle attached to 배 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.
배.shortExplanation: 배 means "belly; stomach" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 나는 고파요 for 'I'm hungry' — the set phrase requires 배, so it must be 배가 고파요.
Conjugating 부르다 as 부르요 — it is 르-irregular, so 'I'm full' is 배가 불러요.
Saying 배가 차다 for being full — fullness is 배가 부르다; 차다 ('be filled') is not used this way for the stomach.

usagePhrases.note: the everyday stomachache; also idiom for jealousy
fixed phrase; 고프다 is ㅡ-irregular: 고파요
fixed phrase; 부르다 is 르-irregular: 불러요
describing a protruding stomach

examples.en: My stomach hurts.
examples.note: survival sentence; the go-to stomachache line

examples.en: I'm so hungry right now.
examples.note: everyday; spoken as one word 배고파요

examples.en: I ate a lot so I'm full.
examples.note: real situation; 부르다 → 불러요 (르-irregular)

ex.en: I have had a fever since this morning.
ex.note: Use 열이 나다 for having a fever.

열.nuance: 열 (熱, the hanja for 'heat') is a fever, and the must-learn collocation is 열이 나다, where 나다 literally means '(something) comes out/arises' — Korean conceives a fever as heat 'coming out' of the body, so you never say 열을 가지다 ('have/possess a fever'), a direct translation of English 'have' that sounds completely unnatural. You can also say 열이 있다 ('there is fever') as a calmer alternative. The level of a fever is described with 높다/낮다 (열이 높다 = high fever), not 크다/작다, and once treated, 열이 내리다 ('the fever comes down') is the natural way to say it subsides — paralleling how prices or temperature 내리다. To take someone's temperature is 열을 재다 (재다 = to measure), the same verb as 키를 재다 (measure height). Don't confuse this 열 with the homonym 열 meaning 'ten' (열 개 = ten items); context separates them.
열.explanation: 열 (yeol) = "fever". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 열이 나다 ("to have a fever") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 열, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
열.shortExplanation: 열 means "fever" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 열을 가지다 for having a fever — this English-style 'have' is unnatural; use 열이 나요 or 열이 있어요.
Describing a high fever as 열이 커요 — fever level uses 높다, so it is 열이 높아요.
Saying 열이 떨어지다 vs the idiom — while understandable, the standard expression for a fever subsiding is 열이 내리다.

usagePhrases.note: fixed phrase; 나다 lit. '(it) comes out'
높다, not 크다, for fever level
재다 = measure; with a thermometer
내리다 = come down, after medicine

examples.en: I have a fever.
examples.note: survival sentence; 열이 나다 is the core phrase

examples.en: My child has a high fever so I'm worried.
examples.note: everyday; 열이 높다, not 크다

examples.en: After taking medicine the fever went down a bit.
examples.note: real situation; 열이 내리다 = fever subsides

ex.en: I could not sleep because of the cough.

기침.nuance: 기침 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean), and it works in two equally natural patterns that differ subtly in viewpoint: 기침이 나다 frames the cough as something that 'comes out' on its own — built with 나다, the same verb in 열이 나다(run a fever), 콧물이 나다(runny nose), 재채기가 나다(sneeze) — stressing it's involuntary; whereas 기침을 하다 frames it as an action you perform, useful when you mean someone coughs deliberately or repeatedly. English speakers raised on 'have a cough' often try 기침을 가지다 ('possess a cough'), which is flatly wrong — Korean never 'has' a symptom with 가지다; symptoms either 나다 (come out) or you 하다 (do) them. Don't confuse 기침 with 재채기 (a sneeze): 기침 is a throat/chest cough, 재채기 is the explosive nose sneeze, and they are not interchangeable. For severity use 심하다 (기침이 심하다 = a bad cough), not 크다.
기침.explanation: "cough" is 기침 (gichim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 기침이 나요 ("a cough comes on"). Watch the particle attached to 기침 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.
기침.shortExplanation: 기침 means "cough" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기침을 가지고 있어요 from English 'I have a cough': symptoms use 나다 or 하다, so say 기침이 나요 / 기침을 해요.
Confusing 기침 with 재채기: a throat cough is 기침; the nose sneeze is 재채기.
Saying 기침이 커요 for a bad cough: severity is 심하다, so it must be 기침이 심해요.

usagePhrases.note: 나다 = the cough 'comes out' involuntarily
하다 = perform the act of coughing
심하다 for a severe, persistent cough
멈추다 (intransitive) = it ceased

examples.en: My throat is itchy, so I keep coughing.
examples.note: Simple: cause 목이 간지럽다 + 기침이 나다, the involuntary frame.

examples.ko: 회의 중에 자꾸 기침을 해서 미안했어요.
examples.romanization: hoeui junge jakku gichimeul haeseo mianhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I kept coughing during the meeting, so I felt sorry.
examples.note: Everyday: 기침을 하다 (active) + 자꾸 (repeatedly) in a social setting.

examples.ko: 기침이 2주 넘게 안 멈추면 병원에 가 보세요.
examples.romanization: gichimi 2ju neomge an meomchumyeon byeongwone ga boseyo.
examples.en: If a cough doesn't stop for over two weeks, go see a doctor.
examples.note: Real-situation: 안 멈추다 + 가 보다 (go and see), giving health advice.

ex.en: I came to the clinic because of a cold.
ex.note: Common named cause in clinic talk.

감기.nuance: 감기 (感氣, 'feeling/affecting + air/energy') is the Sino-Korean word for a common cold, the everyday illness with cough, runny nose, and sore throat — distinct from the heavier 독감 (毒感, 'poison-cold' = influenza/the flu), which is a serious, feverish illness, so don't call the flu just 감기. The critical grammar point is the particle: you 'catch' a cold with 감기에 걸리다, using 에, because 걸리다 ('get caught by/hung on') takes a location-like target — 감기를 걸리다 with 을 is the number-one English-speaker error. Cold medicine is taken with 먹다 (감기약을 먹다, lit. 'eat medicine'), never 마시다 ('drink'), even for liquid syrup. The phrase 감기 조심하세요 ('be careful of cold') is a warm, very common parting line when the weather turns cold, much like 'stay warm / don't catch a cold.'
감기.explanation: "a cold; illness" is 감기 (gamgi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 감기에 걸리다 ("to catch a cold"). Watch the particle attached to 감기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.
감기.shortExplanation: 감기 means "a cold; illness" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Saying 감기를 걸리다 — 걸리다 requires the particle 에, so it is 감기에 걸리다.
Calling the flu 감기 — the flu is 독감 (a far more severe illness); 감기 is an ordinary cold.
Saying 감기약을 마시다 — medicine is 'eaten' in Korean, so use 감기약을 먹다 even for liquid medicine.

하루.nuance: 하루 is the native Korean word for a single 24-hour day and lives inside several fixed phrases you should memorise as chunks: 하루 종일 (all day long), 하루에 ... 번 (... times a day), and the doubled 하루하루 (day by day, one day at a time). Here 하루 is pure native counting, which is why it heads the irregular native day-count series 하루(1)·이틀(2)·사흘(3)·나흘(4) rather than taking 일(日) the way calendar dates do. Two English-speaker pitfalls. First, the rate construction: 'once a day' is 하루에 한 번, with 에 carrying the 'per' meaning — never 하루 번. Second, do not let 하루 drift into meaning 'today'; 하루 is 'a day' as a length or an unspecified day ('one day...'), whereas 'today' is the separate word 오늘. So 'I worked all day today' combines both: 오늘 하루 종일 일했어요.
하루.explanation: 하루 (haru) means "one day, a day". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 하루 종일 ("all day long"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 하루 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
하루.shortExplanation: 하루 means "one day, a day" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Using 하루 to mean 'today' — 하루 is 'a day' as a span; 'today' is 오늘.

약사.nuance: 약사 (藥師) combines 藥 'medicine/drug' with the professional 師 'master' (the same dignified 師 in 의사 doctor, 교사 teacher) — literally 'a medicine-master', the licensed pharmacist who dispenses drugs and counsels on dosage at a 약국 (藥局, 'medicine bureau'). A culturally important point for English speakers: in Korea the 약사 actively recommends over-the-counter remedies, so walking into a 약국 and asking the 약사 directly is a normal first move for a headache, cold, or upset stomach — you don't always need a doctor. Keep the obvious pairs straight: 의사 (醫師) diagnoses and writes the 처방전 'prescription', then the 약사 fills it; both share 師 but they are different jobs. Also distinguish the person 약사 from 약 'medicine' and 약국 'pharmacy'. Habitual verbs: 약을 짓다 'fill/compound medicine', 약을 추천받다 'get a medicine recommended', 약사한테 물어보다. English-speaker pitfall: the vowel-final stem takes 약사예요, not 약사이에요; and don't say 약사를 만나다 for routine advice — 약사한테 물어보다 (ask the pharmacist) is the natural collocation.
약사.explanation: "pharmacist" is 약사 (yaksa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 저는 약사예요. ("I'm a pharmacist."). Watch the particle attached to 약사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations first, then vary one word.

Saying 약사이에요 — the vowel-final stem contracts to 약사예요; 이에요 follows consonants only.
Confusing 약사 (pharmacist) with 의사 (doctor): the 의사 diagnoses and prescribes, the 약사 dispenses; they aren't interchangeable.
Mixing up the person and the place — 약사 is the pharmacist, 약국 is the pharmacy: 약국한테 물어봤어요 should be 약사한테 물어봤어요.

관리비.nuance: 관리비 is Sino-Korean: 管理費, literally 管理 'management' + 費 'expense', i.e. 'management/maintenance fee'. It is the monthly building-upkeep charge covering shared costs — cleaning, security (경비), the elevator (엘리베이터), corridor lighting, and very often part of the utilities (수도세, 난방비, sometimes 인터넷) — and crucially it is billed ON TOP OF 월세 (monthly rent), which blindsides many newcomers. Always ask what the 관리비 covers and whether it's 포함 (included) or 별도 (別途, 'separate'), because a temptingly cheap 월세 can hide a fat 관리비. Like other recurring charges it 나오다 (comes out) and you 내다 (pay) it. Pitfalls for English speakers: first, do not confuse 관리비 (the monthly, non-refundable maintenance fee) with 보증금 (保證金, the large refundable deposit you get back when you leave) — they are completely different money. Second, do not assume rent already includes it the way some Western 'all-bills-included' rents do; in Korea 관리비 is usually a separate line. Third, distinguish 관리비 (shared building costs) from the individually-metered 공과금 like personal 전기세 — though some 관리비 bills bundle a portion of utilities, so reading the 관리비 고지서 (statement) itemization matters.
관리비.explanation: 관리비 (gwallibi) = "maintenance fee (for an apartment/building)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 관리비를 내다 ("to pay the maintenance fee") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 관리비, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.
관리비.shortExplanation: 관리비 means "maintenance fee (for an apartment/building)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 관리비 (recurring monthly maintenance fee, non-refundable) with 보증금 (the large refundable deposit). You pay 보증금 once and get it back; 관리비 you pay every month and never recover.
Assuming the advertised 월세 already includes 관리비. In Korea it is typically billed separately (별도), so always ask 관리비 포함이에요, 별도예요? before signing.
Treating 관리비 as a fixed number. It fluctuates — heating-heavy winters make it 확 올라가다 (jump), so budget for a seasonal swing rather than the summer figure.

거실.nuance: 거실 is the shared 'living/common' room of a Korean home — the social hub where the family relaxes together and where guests are received, almost always centred on a 소파 and a TV. It is Sino-Korean: 居室, literally 居 'to dwell/reside' + 室 'room', so the feel is 'the room you live in (together)'. Contrast it with 응접실 (應接室, a formal parlour for receiving visitors), which sounds old-fashioned and upper-class today, and with 방, the generic word for any closed 'room/bedroom'; 거실 specifically names the open central area. Register is fully neutral — children and adults alike say 거실. The big English-speaker pitfall is location particles: because a TV simply sits there you say 거실에 텔레비전이 있어요 (에 = existence), but because you *do* something there you switch to 거실에서 쉬어요 (에서 = action). Mixing these up (거실에서 텔레비전이 있어요) is the single most common error.
거실.explanation: 거실 (geosil) = "living room". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 거실이 넓어요. ("The living room is spacious.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 거실, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.
거실.shortExplanation: 거실 means "living room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 거실에서 소파가 있어요 to mean 'there is a sofa in the living room'. Existence/location of a thing takes 에 (거실에 소파가 있어요); 에서 only marks the place where an action occurs.
Calling the living room 방. 방 means a closed private room (often a bedroom); the open central area is specifically 거실. Use 거실, not 방, for the family room.
Treating 거실 as 'house' and saying 거실에 가요 for 'I'm going home'. To go home you say 집에 가요; 거실 is just one room inside the 집.

부엌.nuance: 부엌 is the warm, native-Korean everyday word for the room where you cook and wash dishes — the heart of the home where the smell of food lives. Its nearest synonym is the Sino-Korean 주방 (廚房, 'cooking-room'): 주방 is the neutral, technical label you see on apartment floor plans, restaurant signs, and in compounds like 주방용품 (kitchen goods), whereas 부엌 carries a homier, more personal feeling — 우리 집 부엌 sounds natural, 우리 집 주방 sounds like a brochure. Both are everyday and polite; there's no status caution. It collocates with 요리하다, 치우다, and 부엌 살림. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the final consonant: it ends in ㅋ (부엌), so the spelling is fixed even though it's pronounced [부억] before a pause — never write 부억. The second trap is particle choice: use 부엌에서 for an action happening there, but 부엌에 for where something simply sits (부엌에 냉장고가 있어요).
부엌.explanation: 부엌 (bueok) means "kitchen". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 부엌에서 요리하다 ("cook in the kitchen"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 부엌 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests, then change a single part.
부엌.shortExplanation: 부엌 means "kitchen" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 부억 instead of 부엌 — it is pronounced [부억] before a pause, but the correct final letter is always ㅋ, so the spelling never changes.
Saying 부엌에 요리해요 for the action of cooking — an action done in a place needs 에서, so it must be 부엌에서 요리해요; 에 only marks where something exists.
Calling a restaurant or floor-plan kitchen 부엌 in a formal label — there the neutral word 주방 (주방용품, 공용 주방) is expected; 부엌 sounds like a cozy home kitchen.

usagePhrases.note: 부엌 takes 에서 because cooking is a dynamic action done there

살림 = household goods & housekeeping; a very natural pairing

공인중개사.nuance: 공인중개사 (公認仲介士) is a long but transparent compound: 公認 'officially recognized' (公 public + 認 acknowledge) + 仲介 'mediation/brokerage' (仲 go-between + 介 intermediary) + 士 certified professional — so literally 'an officially-licensed brokerage professional', the agent who arranges 전세, 월세, and home sales, and the person you inevitably deal with when renting in Korea. The number-one English-speaker confusion is place vs person: 부동산 (不動産, lit. 'immovable property') colloquially names the agent's office or the property itself, so 부동산에 가다 = 'go to the agent's office', but the human is the 공인중개사 — never call the person 부동산. The 공인 'officially licensed' prefix matters in formal/contractual contexts; dropping it to just 중개사 is loose. In everyday speech people also warmly say 중개사님 or 사장님 to the agent's face. Collocations: 공인중개사 사무소 'realtor office', 공인중개사 자격증 'realtor license', 집을 구하다 'find a home'. Note 공인중개사 ends in a vowel, so it would be 공인중개사예요, not 공인중개사이에요.
공인중개사.explanation: 공인중개사 (gonginjunggaesa) means "licensed real estate agent". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 공인중개사한테 묻다 ("to ask a licensed agent"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 공인중개사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.
공인중개사.shortExplanation: 공인중개사 means "licensed real estate agent" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling the person 부동산 — 부동산 is the office/property; the licensed human is the 공인중개사 (or politely 중개사님/사장님 to their face).
Dropping 공인 to say just 중개사 in formal or contract settings — the official title is 공인중개사; 중개사 alone is loose.
Saying 공인중개사이에요 instead of the contracted 공인중개사예요, which the vowel ending requires.

일기예보.nuance: 일기예보 is the official weather forecast you get from the news or an app (日氣豫報, literally 일기 'the day's air = weather' + 예보 'fore-report'), so it names the prediction itself, not the weather. Contrast it with plain 날씨, which is the actual weather happening now: you say 날씨가 좋아요 for today's nice weather but 일기예보가 좋아요 only when the predicted outlook is good. Koreans habitually 일기예보를 보다 (watch/read it) and judge it as 맞다 right or 틀리다 wrong, and they quote it with 일기예보에서 ~고 했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a verb ('to forecast') — it is a noun, so attach a verb like 보다 or 확인하다, and use 에서 (the source particle) rather than 에 when reporting what it announced.
일기예보.explanation: "weather forecast" is 일기예보 (ilgiyebo). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 일기예보를 보다 ("to check the forecast"). Watch the particle attached to 일기예보 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.
일기예보.shortExplanation: 일기예보 means "weather forecast" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 듣다 by default (일기예보를 들었어요) because English says 'hear the forecast'; the unmarked verb is 보다 since people watch or read it.
Saying 일기예보를 했어요 as if it were a verb; it is a noun, so say 일기예보를 봤어요/확인했어요.
Marking the source with 에 (일기예보에 ~고 했어요); the quoting source particle is 에서: 일기예보에서 비가 온다고 했어요.

usagePhrases.note: forecasts are watched/read with 보다, not 듣다 by default
맞다 = turn out correct; opposite 틀리다
quote source with 에서 + 고 하다
주간 weekly, 오늘/내일 일기예보 for the day

examples.en: I check the weather forecast every morning.
examples.note: habit with 마다 + 보다

examples.en: The forecast was right, so I grabbed an umbrella.
examples.note: 맞다 as result + practical action

examples.en: The forecast said it would snow tomorrow.
examples.note: reported speech with 에서 ... 고 하다

ex.en: Let's book again when the weather clears.

맑다.nuance: 맑다 means CLEAR or CLEAN in the sense of pure and transparent — clear see-through water (맑은 물), a cloudless sky (맑은 하늘 = sunny), fresh unpolluted air (맑은 공기), a clear ringing sound or a clear alert mind (정신이 맑다). Its opposite is 흐리다 (cloudy/murky). The key English-speaker pitfall is using 맑다 for a tidy ROOM: English 'clean' covers both purity and tidiness, but a clean, tidy room is 깨끗하다 (방이 깨끗하다), not 맑다. Reserve 맑다 for natural clearness/transparency (water, sky, air, sound) and use 깨끗하다 for cleanliness/neatness of objects and spaces. As a weather word it pairs with 날씨 and 하늘 and is the standard term in forecasts: 내일은 맑겠습니다 (it will be clear/sunny tomorrow). Pronunciation: the ㄺ surfaces as g before a vowel, so 맑아요 is 'malg-a-yo' and 맑게 is 'mak-ge.' As a descriptive adjective it never takes 있다: 물이 맑아요, not 맑아 있어요.
맑다.explanation: 맑다 (malkda) = "to be clear; to be clean/sunny". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 하늘이 맑다 ("the sky is clear/sunny") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 맑다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
맑다.shortExplanation: 맑다 means "to be clear; to be clean/sunny" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 맑다 for a tidy room — cleanliness/neatness of a space is 깨끗하다 (방이 깨끗해요), not 맑아요.
Saying 맑은 날씨예요 is fine, but for 'a clear/cloudless sky' remember the noun pairing 맑은 하늘; don't substitute 깨끗한 하늘.
Mispronouncing the ㄺ cluster — 맑아요 is 'malg-a-yo' (the g sounds before the vowel), not 'mal-a-yo.'

usagePhrases.note: the everyday weather collocation
see-through, clean water
맑은 공기 = crisp, clean air

눈.nuance: 눈 is the eye, but the identical spelling also means 'snow'; the two are split by pitch (eye = short/low, snow = long/high) and above all by context, so listeners rarely confuse them. Korean treats the pair of eyes as one uncountable 눈, so you never pluralize it. The big English-speaker trap is eyesight: vision is rated with 좋다 (good) and 나쁘다 (bad) — 눈이 좋아요 / 눈이 나빠요 — never with 'strong/weak' (강하다/약하다), which would sound bizarre. Note that 눈을 감다 uses the same 감다 as washing hair but means 'close', and the related verb 보다 ('see/look') is what the eye does, while 만나다 ('meet') is for people, so don't blend them.
눈.explanation: "eye" is 눈 (nun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 눈이 아파요 ("my eyes hurt"). Watch the particle attached to 눈 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs first, then vary one word.
눈.shortExplanation: 눈 means "eye" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 눈이 강해요/약해요 for eyesight — vision uses 좋다/나쁘다, so it must be 눈이 좋아요 or 눈이 나빠요.
Pluralizing as 눈들이 아파요 — the pair of eyes stays singular, so say 눈이 아파요.
Confusing 눈 (eye) with 눈 (snow) when out of context — rely on the surrounding words; 눈이 와요 = snow falls, 눈이 아파요 = eyes hurt.

vision is 좋다/나쁘다, never 강하다/약하다

go-to compliment about appearance

ex.en: It looks like a typhoon may come, so the plane might be late.

태풍.nuance: 태풍 is a typhoon, the large tropical storm system that strikes Korea mainly in late summer and early autumn (颱風, literally 태 'typhoon' + 풍 'wind'). Even though the second character means wind, 태풍 is conceived as a moving body of weather, so it travels with 오다 come, 지나가다 pass, and the news verb 북상하다 move north — it does not 'blow.' That is the key contrast with plain 바람 wind, which 불다 blows: you must not say 태풍이 불어요. Distinguish it too from 폭풍 (a general violent storm, including at sea) and 돌풍 (a sudden gust); 태풍 specifically names the seasonal tropical cyclone, each one given an official name. Strength is described with 강하다/세다. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'the wind blows' onto 태풍 and producing 태풍이 불어요 — say instead 태풍이 와요 / 태풍이 지나가요.
태풍.explanation: 태풍 (taepung) means "typhoon". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 태풍이 오다 ("a typhoon comes"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 태풍 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.
태풍.shortExplanation: 태풍 means "typhoon" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 태풍이 불어요 because in English 'the wind blows'; a typhoon is a moving system, so 태풍이 와요/지나가요, while only 바람 불다.
Confusing 태풍 with 바람; ordinary wind is 바람, and 태풍 is the named seasonal storm — 바람이 불어요 vs 태풍이 와요.
Using 폭풍 loosely for any typhoon; 폭풍 is a generic violent storm, whereas 태풍 is specifically the tropical cyclone the forecast names.

usagePhrases.note: 태풍 moves, so it uses 오다/지나가다/북상하다
지나가다 = pass by, leaving calm after
영향권 = the affected zone forecasters mention

ex.en: The yellow dust is bad today.

황사.nuance: 황사 is Sino-Korean, 黃沙 'yellow + sand', and names the seasonal haze of desert sand carried on the wind from China and Mongolia, peaking in spring. The crucial contrast is with 미세먼지 ('fine dust', fine particulate air pollution): 황사 is coarse natural desert sand, a centuries-old phenomenon, whereas 미세먼지 is man-made fine pollution measured as PM10/PM2.5 — news reports list them together but they are different things, and conflating them is the classic learner error. Note also that 황사 is described with 심하다 (severe) and the wind verb 불다/불어오다, not with 많다 or 오다. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the 황사/미세먼지 mix-up, is reaching for 황사가 와요; in news-register Korean 황사가 심해요 or 황사가 불어와요 sounds far more natural.
황사.explanation: 황사 (hwangsa) = "yellow dust". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 황사가 심하다 ("the yellow dust is severe") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 황사, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
황사.shortExplanation: 황사 means "yellow dust" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Treating 황사 and 미세먼지 as synonyms. 황사 is coarse desert sand blown in seasonally; 미세먼지 is fine man-made particulate pollution measured year-round — they are different phenomena.
Saying 황사가 많아요. Intensity of dust/haze is rated with 심하다: 황사가 심해요.
Saying 황사가 와요 in a forecast. Because it rides the wind, the natural verb is 불다: 황사가 불어와요, or simply 황사가 심해요.

usagePhrases.note: describe intensity with 심하다, not 많다
compound for the protective mask people wear
불어오다 = blow in on the wind, natural verb

미세먼지.nuance: 미세먼지 is not ordinary dust in your room. It refers to air pollution particles reported in forecasts and apps.
미세먼지.explanation: 미세먼지 (misemeonji) means "fine dust; particulate air pollution". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 미세먼지가 심하다 ("the fine dust is bad"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 미세먼지 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Translating it as simple 먼지 when the topic is air quality. Use 미세먼지.
Forgetting that 미세먼지 often changes outdoor plans in Korea.
Using 좋다/나쁘다 without context; 미세먼지가 심하다 is the clearest beginner phrase.

ex.ko: 장마라서 비가 많이 올 텐데 우산 챙기세요.
ex.en: It is rainy season, so it will probably rain a lot. Bring an umbrella.

장마.nuance: 장마 is Korea's long early-summer monsoon, the roughly three-to-four-week stretch around late June and July when a stationary rain front parks over the peninsula and brings steady, humid rain day after day. It is a whole climatic period, not a single rainfall, so it contrasts sharply with 비 (one instance of rain) and with 소나기 (a sudden short downpour): you can have 비 during 장마, but 장마 names the season. The word is treated as native Korean (it is not a hanja compound), and it lives in fixed phrases — 장마가 시작되다/끝나다 and the compound 장마철 'rainy-season time'. The pitfall for English speakers is calling any rainy day 장마; reserve it for the seasonal monsoon, and note that 장마 takes 시작되다/끝나다 rather than the falling verbs 오다/내리다 that plain rain uses.
장마.explanation: 장마 (jangma) = "rainy season". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 장마가 시작되다 ("the rainy season begins") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 장마, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
장마.shortExplanation: 장마 means "rainy season" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a single rainy day 장마 (오늘 장마예요 for one wet afternoon); 장마 is the multi-week season — for one rain say 비가 와요.
Saying 장마가 와요 / 장마가 내려요 by analogy with rain; the season 시작되다 begins and 끝나다 ends, while only 비 오다/내리다.
Dropping 철 when you mean 'during the rainy season'; say 장마철에 rather than just 장마에 for the time frame.

usagePhrases.note: set inchoative 시작되다 / opposite 끝나다, 물러가다
철 = season; 장마철에 = during the rainy season
전선 = the weather front that brings it
마른장마 = a dry spell with little rain

examples.en: The rainy season begins in summer.
examples.note: season + inchoative 시작되다

examples.en: This year the rainy season is long, so I am worried about mold.
examples.note: real-life worry: humidity and mold

ex.ko: 기온이 영하로 떨어질 텐데 따뜻하게 입으세요.
ex.en: The temperature will probably drop below zero, so dress warmly.

영하.nuance: 영하(零下) is Sino-Korean — 零 'zero' + 下 'below' — meaning below 0°C. Its exact opposite is 영상(零上, 'above zero'), used for plus temperatures (영상 3도 = +3°C). The crucial structural fact, opposite to English, is word order: the marker comes BEFORE the number, so 'minus five degrees' is 영하 5도 (literally 'below-zero five degrees'), never 5도 영하. English speakers also say 'negative five' / 'minus five,' but Korean does not use 마이너스 in weather speech — it is always 영하. 영하 most often appears in winter forecasts and pairs with 떨어지다 (plunge below) and 내려가다 (drop), plus the handy forecaster word 영하권 (the subzero range). The pitfalls: (1) putting the number first (5도 영하 ✗); (2) confusing 영하 (below zero) with 영상 (above zero) — they look and sound similar but are opposites; (3) saying 마이너스 5도 in everyday weather talk, which sounds like a math/English calque rather than natural 영하 5도.
영하.explanation: 영하 (yeongha) = "below zero". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 영하 5도 ("minus five degrees") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 영하, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
영하.shortExplanation: 영하 means "below zero" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Putting the number before 영하, e.g. 5도 영하. Korean states the zone first: 영하 5도 (below-zero, five degrees).
Confusing 영하 (below zero) with 영상 (above zero). 하=below, 상=above. They are direct opposites, easy to mix up by sound.
Saying 마이너스 5도 for the weather. That's an English-style calque; natural Korean weather speech is 영하 5도.

usagePhrases.note: 영하 comes BEFORE the number
떨어지다 (plunge) is more vivid than 내려가다 for crossing zero
영하 + -의 + noun to modify
-권 (zone/range) for 'down in the minuses'

examples.en: This morning it's minus five degrees.
examples.note: Word order to memorize: 영하 + number + 도. Never 5도 영하.

examples.en: The temperature dropped below zero.
examples.note: 영하로 떨어지다 = the reading plunges past zero; 로 marks the endpoint.

examples.en: Subzero cold is coming tomorrow.
examples.note: 영하권 (the subzero zone) is how forecasters frame a cold snap.

ex.en: I think the temperature will drop.

기온.nuance: 기온 is the air temperature expressed as a number of degrees (氣溫, 기 'air/atmosphere' + 온 'warmth'), so it is the measurable reading the forecaster gives, whereas 날씨 is the whole overall feel of the weather (sunny, humid, windy) and 온도 is the neutral word for the temperature of any object or liquid like 물 온도 water temperature or 체온 body temperature. Use 기온 only for outdoor air. It pairs with 높다 high and 낮다 low, and with the motion verbs 오르다 rise and 떨어지다 fall; the big English-speaker trap is reaching for 크다/작다 (big/small) the way English lets you say a 'big' difference, but a temperature itself is 높다/낮다, and only the gap 일교차 or 차이 can be 크다.
기온.explanation: 기온 (gion) means "temperature". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 기온이 높아요 ("the temperature is high"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 기온 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs, then change a single part.
기온.shortExplanation: 기온 means "temperature" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 기온이 커요 to mean a high temperature; size words do not apply, say 기온이 높아요.
Using 온도 for the weather outside (온도가 높아요 about the sky); for outdoor air use 기온, and reserve 온도 for objects or water.
Saying 기온이 내려가요 by translating 'go down'; the idiomatic verb for the reading is 기온이 떨어지다.

usagePhrases.note: air temperature takes 높다/낮다, never 크다
fixed phrase: 기온은 떨어지다/오르다, not 내려가다 in forecasts
일교차 means the daily high-low gap
영하 = below zero, 영상 = above zero

ex.ko: 안개 때문에 앞이 잘 안 보여요.
ex.en: I cannot see well ahead because of the fog.

안개.nuance: 안개 is fog or mist — the cloud of tiny water droplets near the ground that cuts visibility. Its defining grammar is the verb 끼다, the same verb used for clouds 구름이 끼다, meaning the haze 'settles in,' so 안개가 끼다 is the standard way to say it gets foggy and 안개가 걷히다 that it lifts. Density is expressed with 짙다 thick and 옅다 thin — never the physical-thickness word 두껍다 — and a thick fog is 짙은 안개. 안개 is a native Korean noun (no hanja), and a close relative is 안개비 'misty drizzle.' The crucial pitfall for English speakers is the verb: do not say 안개가 와요 (treating fog like rain) and do not say 안개가 두꺼워요 by translating 'thick fog' literally; say 안개가 끼다 and 안개가 짙다.
안개.explanation: 안개 (angae) = "fog". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 안개가 끼다 ("it becomes foggy") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 안개, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about saying what hurts, asking for rest, and explaining basic health needs and swap just one element to make it yours.
안개.shortExplanation: 안개 means "fog" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 안개가 와요 because rain 'comes'; fog settles, so the verb is 끼다 — 안개가 꼈어요.
Saying 안개가 두꺼워요 by translating 'thick fog'; physical thickness 두껍다 is wrong here — use 짙다: 안개가 짙어요.
Saying 안개가 가요 for fog clearing; the set verb is 걷히다 or 사라지다 — 안개가 걷혔어요.

usagePhrases.note: 끼다 'settle in' is the set verb for fog/clouds
density is 짙다 thick / 옅다 thin, not 두껍다
걷히다/사라지다 = clears away; opposite of 끼다
앞이 안 보이다 = can't see ahead

examples.en: It got foggy in the morning.
examples.note: past tense of the set verb 끼다 (꼈어요)

examples.ko: 안개가 짙어서 앞이 잘 안 보여요.
examples.romanization: angaega jiteoseo api jal an boyeoyo.

examples.note: density 짙다 + everyday consequence

examples.en: Once the fog lifts, driving is much easier.
examples.note: conditional 면 + 걷히다 in a real situation

ex.en: The plane was late because of the typhoon.

비행기.nuance: 비행기 (飛行機, literally 'fly-go-machine') is the everyday spoken word for an airplane — the aircraft you board for trips abroad or across the country. Its near-synonym 항공기 means the same machine but is a stiffer, technical/news register ('aircraft'), and the ticket has its own formal twin: spoken 비행기 표 vs. written/official 항공권. It collocates with 타다 (board), 표/항공권 (ticket), 예약하다 (reserve), 연착되다 (be delayed), 환승하다 (transfer), and 공항 (airport). As with all vehicles, the pitfall is the particle: 'get on the plane' tempts 비행기에 타요, but Korean wants the object marker — 비행기를 타요. A second subtle trap is 타다 vs 내리다: you board with 비행기를 타다 (object) but disembark with 비행기에서 내리다 (source), so the particle flips between getting on and getting off.
비행기.explanation: "airplane" is 비행기 (bihaenggi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 비행기를 타요 ("I take the airplane"). Watch the particle attached to 비행기 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.
비행기.shortExplanation: 비행기 means "airplane" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 비행기에 타요 to mean 'board the plane' — Korean uses the object marker, so the natural form is 비행기를 타요.
Using 비행기에서 가요 for 'go by plane' — the means takes 로, giving 비행기로 가요; 에서 only marks the place you are in.
Treating 항공권 as casual speech — in conversation Koreans usually say 비행기 표; save 항공권 for booking sites and formal writing.

usagePhrases.note: board = 을/를 + 타다, not 에
로 marks the means of travel
항공권 is the formal ticket word
놓치다 = miss a departure

examples.note: Simple sentence; 날다 (to fly) is the verb that goes with it.
