셔츠.nuance: 셔츠 is the loanword for a collared upper-body shirt; the general Sino-Korean cover term for any top is 상의 (上衣, 'upper garment'), and a knit pullover is 티셔츠/티. Because a shirt covers the torso it ALWAYS takes 입다 ('put on the body'), the same family of dressing verbs that splits by body zone in Korean: 입다 for trunk and legs, 신다 for feet, 쓰다 for the head/face, 끼다 for hands. The single biggest English-speaker pitfall is treating 'wear' as one verb the way English does — you cannot say 셔츠를 써요 or 셔츠를 신어요. Register is neutral and the word fits any politeness level. Natural collocations: 셔츠를 입다/벗다 (put on/take off), 셔츠를 다리다 (iron a shirt), 셔츠가 (안) 맞다 (it does (not) fit). Note that to take a shirt off you switch to 벗다, not a negated 입다.
셔츠.explanation: 셔츠 (syeocheu) means "shirt". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 셔츠를 입어요 ("I wear a shirt"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 셔츠 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.
셔츠.shortExplanation: 셔츠 means "shirt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 셔츠를 써요 by mapping English 'wear' onto 쓰다 — 쓰다 is only for things on the head/face (hats, glasses); a shirt must use 입다.
Counting with 개 (셔츠 한 개). Clothing uses the counter 벌, so it is 셔츠 한 벌.
Using a negated 입다 for taking it off (셔츠를 안 입어요 to mean 'I take it off'). Removing clothing is its own verb 벗다: 셔츠를 벗어요.

usagePhrases.note: upper-body clothing always takes 입다
흰 is the modifier form of 희다 placed before the noun

usagePhrases.en: the shirt is a bit big
usagePhrases.note: subject marker 가; 좀 softens the complaint
clothing is counted with 벌, never 개

examples.en: I wear a shirt.
examples.note: Bare basics: the verb for putting on body clothing is 입다.

examples.en: This shirt fits me well.
examples.note: 잘 맞다 = to fit; the size partner-verb is 맞다, not 좋다.

examples.ko: 면접 때문에 깔끔한 셔츠 한 벌 샀어요.

examples.en: I bought one neat shirt for the interview.
examples.note: Real situation: 깔끔하다 (neat/crisp) is the go-to adjective for dress shirts.

ex.en: I often wear T-shirts in summer.

티셔츠.nuance: 티셔츠 is a direct loanword from English 'T-shirt' (named for its T shape), and it specifically means a pull-over knit top — most often short-sleeved cotton. The key contrast English speakers miss is 티셔츠 vs 셔츠: in Korean 셔츠 by itself implies a button-up collared shirt (a dress shirt / 와이셔츠), so a casual tee must keep the 티 to stay distinct. Sleeve length is built right into the noun phrase: 반팔 티셔츠 (half-sleeve) vs 긴팔 티셔츠 (long-sleeve). Register is casual and neutral. The pitfalls: (1) the verb is 입다, never 신다; (2) thin tees are frequently counted with 장 ('흰 티 한 장' = one plain white tee), though 벌 also works for an outfit; and (3) Koreans clip it to 티 in speech (흰 티, 검은 티), so don't be thrown when the 셔츠 disappears.
티셔츠.explanation: 티셔츠 (tisyeocheu) means "t-shirt". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 티셔츠를 입어요. ("I wear a t-shirt."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 티셔츠 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.
티셔츠.shortExplanation: 티셔츠 means "t-shirt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying just 셔츠 for a casual tee. 셔츠 alone suggests a button-up dress shirt; keep 티셔츠 (or 티) for a pull-over t-shirt.
Saying 티셔츠를 신어요 — 신다 is footwear only. A top takes 입다: 티셔츠를 입어요.
Forcing English plural 'two t-shirts' as a plural noun. Say 티셔츠 두 장 / 두 벌 — Korean marks number with a counter, not a plural ending.

usagePhrases.note: tops take 입다; 를 marks the object
반팔 'half-sleeve' specifies sleeve length, vs 긴팔 'long-sleeve'
thin flat tops are often counted with 장, the counter for flat sheet-like things
A에 B names the classic paired casual outfit

examples.en: In summer I often wear t-shirts.
examples.note: 은 contrasts summer with other seasons; 자주 'often' marks the habit

examples.en: The t-shirt shrank, so I gave it to my younger sibling.
examples.note: 줄어들다 'shrink'; -아서 reason; 주다 'give' takes the recipient with 에게/한테 (here dropped casually)

examples.en: The neckline of this t-shirt has stretched out.
examples.note: 목 here = the collar/neckline; 늘어나다 'stretch out' is the opposite of 줄어들다

ex.en: The pants look a little big.

바지.nuance: 바지 covers the lower body, so despite English treating 'pants' as plural, Korean treats it as a single uncountable garment: there is no plural ending, no 'a pair' built into the word, and the verb is 입다 just like a shirt. The dividing line with footwear matters — legs use 입다 but the feet that stick out below use 신다, so you 입다 your 바지 but 신다 your 양말. Jeans are 청바지 (靑—, 'blue-color pants'), shorts are 반바지 ('half pants'), and dress slacks are often just called 슬랙스. The classic English-speaker error is the literal plural reflex — saying 바지들이 길어요 sounds as odd as saying 'pantses'. Natural collocations: 바지를 입다/벗다, 바지를 갈아입다 (change into other pants), 바지 길이를 줄이다 (shorten), 바지가 끼다 (the pants are tight). Note 끼다 here means 'feel tight', a different sense from putting gloves on.
바지.explanation: "pants" is 바지 (baji). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 바지를 입어요 ("I wear pants"). Watch the particle attached to 바지 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.
바지.shortExplanation: 바지 means "pants" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Adding a plural marker (바지들) because English 'pants' is plural — 바지 is always singular in Korean; the noun never pluralizes.
Saying 바지를 신어요 by lumping pants with shoes. 신다 is feet-only; legs take 입다, so it is 바지를 입어요.
Inventing '한 켤레' for pants by analogy with shoes. Pants are counted 한 벌, since 켤레 is reserved for paired footwear and gloves.

usagePhrases.note: legs are body clothing, so 입다 (not 신다)
긴 is the adnominal form of 길다 before a noun
subject marker 가; 바지 stays singular
counted with 벌, and treated as one item

examples.en: I wear pants.
examples.note: Even though English is plural, 바지 is grammatically singular in Korean.

examples.en: These pants are too long for me.
examples.note: -한테 marks the person a measurement is judged against ('for me').

examples.en: I had the pants shortened at the tailor's.
examples.note: Real situation: 길이를 줄이다 (shorten the length) is the standard alteration phrase.

ex.en: These dress shoes go well with the skirt.

치마.nuance: 치마 is the native Korean word for a skirt and is purely neutral; the English loanword 스커트 exists but 치마 is what people actually say in daily life, and a traditional hanbok skirt is also 치마. Like all lower-body clothing it takes 입다, and to take it off you switch to 벗다 — never a negated 입다. The trap for English speakers is again the one-word-'wear' habit plus assuming a fancier loanword is more polite; here the plain native 치마 is the unmarked, fully appropriate choice in every register. A very useful partner verb is 어울리다 ('to suit/match'), used with the marker -이/가 for the item and -에게/한테 for the person: 그 치마가 너한테 잘 어울려. Natural collocations: 치마를 입다/벗다, 짧은/긴 치마 (short/long skirt), 치마가 어울리다, 치마를 갈아입다. Do not confuse 어울리다 (looks good on) with 맞다 (fits in size) — a skirt can 맞다 yet not 어울리다.
치마.explanation: 치마 (chima) = "skirt". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 치마를 입어요 ("I wear a skirt") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 치마, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.
치마.shortExplanation: 치마 means "skirt" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 신다 for a skirt because it hangs near the legs/feet. 신다 is strictly for feet; a skirt takes 입다.
Saying 치마가 나를 잘 어울려요. 어울리다 marks the wearer with -에게/한테, not the object marker: 치마가 나한테 잘 어울려요.
Reaching for the loanword 스커트 thinking it is more polite. 치마 is the natural, register-neutral default; the loanword carries no extra politeness.

짧은 is the adnominal of 짧다 before the noun
어울리다 = to look good on someone
counted with the clothing counter 벌

examples.en: I wear a skirt.
examples.note: Skirts use 입다, exactly like pants — both are lower-body garments.

examples.en: Isn't this skirt a bit short?
examples.note: -지 않아요? turns it into a soft, seeking-agreement question.

examples.ko: 결혼식에 갈 거라서 단정한 치마를 골랐어요.
examples.romanization: gyeolhonsige gal georaseo danjeonghan chimareul gollasseoyo.
examples.en: I picked a tidy skirt because I'm going to a wedding.
examples.note: Real situation: 단정하다 (tidy/proper) is the register word for formal dressing; 고르다 = to pick.

ex.ko: 이 원피스는 면접에는 조금 화려해 보여요.
ex.en: This dress looks a little flashy for an interview.

원피스.nuance: 원피스 is a loanword from English 'one-piece', and that literal sense is the whole point: it's a dress where top and skirt are a single connected garment, as opposed to a 투피스 ('two-piece', a matching top-and-skirt set). The sharp contrast English speakers must learn is 원피스 vs 드레스: everyday casual or work dresses are 원피스, while 드레스 in Korean is reserved for a formal gown — a wedding dress (웨딩드레스) or evening gown — so calling your sundress a 드레스 sounds like you're going to a gala. The word is essentially female-coded. Register is neutral. Pitfalls: (1) the verb is 입다; (2) compliment the fit with 어울리다 ('it suits you'), the single most useful clothes-shopping verb; (3) count with 벌, and (4) never split a 원피스 into separates — that's literally a 투피스.
원피스.explanation: 원피스 (wonpiseu) = "dress". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 원피스를 입어요. ("I wear a dress.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 원피스, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.
원피스.shortExplanation: 원피스 means "dress" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a casual dress a 드레스. 드레스 means a formal gown (wedding/evening); an everyday dress is 원피스.
Saying 원피스가 예뻐요 to mean 'it looks good on you'. 예쁘다 describes the dress itself; to say it suits the person use 어울리다 → 원피스가 잘 어울려요.
Using 개 to count: 원피스 한 개. Use the clothing counter 벌 → 원피스 한 벌.

usagePhrases.note: a one-piece garment takes 입다; 를 marks the object
무늬 'pattern' attaches to a noun: 꽃무늬 'flower pattern'
어울리다 'suit/match' is the standard compliment verb for clothes
season + garment is a fixed modifier pattern

examples.en: Today I wore a dress.
examples.note: 은 on 오늘 highlights today as different from usual; simple past with 입다

examples.ko: 이 원피스 너무 예쁜데 좀 비싸요.
examples.romanization: i wonpiseu neomu yeppeunde jom bissayo.
examples.en: This dress is so pretty, but it's a bit pricey.
examples.note: -는데 sets up the 'but'; 예쁘다 is the ㅡ-irregular adjective for 'pretty'

examples.en: I'm going to buy a dress to wear to the wedding.
examples.note: 입을 (future-modifier) + noun = 'a dress to wear'; -려고요 states the intention

ex.en: This coat looks expensive.

코트.nuance: 코트 is a loanword for a warm outer layer; the broader native umbrella term for any outerwear is 외투 (外套, 'outer wrap'), and a padded winter jacket is 패딩 or 점퍼. Even though it is the outermost layer, 코트 still takes 입다 because the rule keys off the body zone (trunk), not how many layers are underneath; you put it on with 입다 and take it off with 벗다. The English-speaker pitfall is pronunciation-driven spelling and the 'wear' reflex: 코트 is two clean syllables (ko-teu) and is never said with 쓰다 or 차다. A second subtlety: when you mean 'put a coat ON over other clothes' Koreans often say 코트를 걸치다 ('throw on lightly'), a nuance 입다 alone doesn't carry. Natural collocations: 코트를 입다/벗다, 코트를 걸치다 (drape on), 두꺼운/긴 코트, 코트 단추를 잠그다 (button up the coat). Note 걸치다 implies a casual, partial wearing, unlike the full 입다.
코트.explanation: 코트 (koteu) means "coat". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 코트를 입어요 ("I wear a coat"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 코트 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.
코트.shortExplanation: 코트 means "coat" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 코트를 써요 or 코트를 차요 from English 'wear'. A coat covers the body, so only 입다 works.
Spelling/saying it as one blurred syllable. It is 코트 (ko-teu), with the 으 vowel fully pronounced.
Assuming 입다 covers the casual 'throw it on' meaning. For draping a coat loosely over the shoulders, Koreans prefer 걸치다: 코트를 어깨에 걸쳤어요.

usagePhrases.note: outerwear is still body clothing, so 입다
두꺼운 is the adnominal of 두껍다 (ㅂ-irregular)
subject marker 가; 따뜻하다 describes warmth
counted with 벌 like other clothing

examples.en: I wear a coat.
examples.note: An overcoat is worn on the body, so the verb is 입다, same as a shirt.

examples.en: Since it's cold outside, put your coat on and go out.
examples.note: -고 links 'put on' then 'go'; the sequence verb 입고 means 'having put on'.

examples.ko: 올겨울에 입을 따뜻한 코트를 하나 장만했어요.
examples.romanization: olgyeoure ibeul ttatteutan koteureul hana jangmanhaesseoyo.
examples.en: I got myself one warm coat to wear this winter.
examples.note: Real situation: 장만하다 (acquire/get for oneself) is warmer and more natural than 사다 for a planned purchase.

ex.en: May I try on these sneakers too?

운동화.nuance: 운동화 (運動靴, 運動 'exercise/movement' + 靴 'shoe', literally 'exercise-shoe') means sneakers/trainers, and like all 신발 (footwear) it takes 신다, the foot-zone verb shared with socks; it never takes 입다. The near-synonym to keep straight is 구두 (dress/leather shoes): both are shoes and both use 신다 and 켤레, but 운동화 is casual/athletic while 구두 is formal — so the choice signals register, not grammar. A pair is counted with 켤레. The English-speaker pitfalls: the single-'wear' habit, and forgetting that the generic word for any shoe is 신발, with 운동화 being one specific type. To take shoes off — a daily act before entering Korean homes — you use 벗다 (신발을 벗다). Natural collocations: 운동화를 신다/벗다, 운동화 한 켤레, 운동화 끈을 묶다 (tie the laces), 운동화가 편하다/낡다 (comfy/worn out). Note 끈을 묶다 ('tie the laces') uses 묶다, and 낡다 ('wear out with age') is the adjective for worn shoes.
운동화.explanation: "sneakers" is 운동화 (undonghwa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 운동화를 신어요 ("I wear sneakers"). Watch the particle attached to 운동화 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.
운동화.shortExplanation: 운동화 means "sneakers" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 운동화를 입어요 with default 입다. Footwear takes 신다: 운동화를 신어요.
Counting with 개 (운동화 한 개). A pair of shoes uses 켤레: 운동화 한 켤레.
Confusing 운동화 with formal shoes. Athletic/casual shoes are 운동화; leather dress shoes are 구두 — both grammar-identical but different in register.

usagePhrases.note: footwear takes 신다
편한 is the adnominal of 편하다
subject marker 가; 편하다 = comfortable
paired footwear uses 켤레

examples.en: I wear sneakers.
examples.note: All footwear takes 신다 — never 입다, even for athletic shoes.

examples.ko: 발이 편한 운동화를 신고 많이 걸었어요.
examples.romanization: bari pyeonhan undonghwareul singo mani georeosseoyo.
examples.en: I walked a lot in comfortable sneakers.
examples.note: 발이 편하다 ('feet are comfortable') is the set phrase for comfy shoes.

examples.romanization: deungsaneun an hajiman undonghwaga pyeonhaeseo jaju sineoyo.
examples.en: I don't hike, but sneakers are comfy so I wear them often.
examples.note: Real situation: 신다 covers habitual wearing too; 자주 신다 = 'wear often'.

ex.ko: 면접에는 운동화보다 구두가 더 단정해 보여요.
ex.en: For an interview, dress shoes look more presentable than sneakers.

구두.nuance: 구두 is the native everyday word for formal leather shoes (often dress/heeled shoes), and like all footwear it takes 신다 and is counted with 켤레; it never takes 입다. The key contrast is with 운동화 (sneakers): grammatically identical — both 신다, both 켤레 — but 구두 carries a formal, dressed-up register (worn with a suit, 정장, to work or interviews) while 운동화 is casual and athletic, so picking the right noun signals the occasion. The broad cover term for any shoe remains 신발. English-speaker pitfalls: the 'wear = one verb' reflex, and assuming 'shoes' is one word — Korean forces you to choose 구두 vs 운동화 vs the generic 신발 by formality. Because Koreans remove shoes indoors, 벗다 (신발/구두를 벗다) is a verb you will use daily, and 갈아 신다 means swapping footwear. Natural collocations: 구두를 신다/벗다, 구두 한 켤레, 구두를 닦다 (polish dress shoes), 구두 굽 (the heel of the shoe). Note 닦다 ('shine/polish') pairs especially with leather 구두, and 굽 is the heel.
구두.explanation: 구두 (gudu) = "dress shoes". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 구두를 신어요 ("I wear dress shoes") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 구두, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.
구두.shortExplanation: 구두 means "dress shoes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 구두를 입어요 with default 입다. Shoes take 신다: 구두를 신어요.
Counting with 개. A pair of shoes uses 켤레: 구두 한 켤레.
Using 구두 for sneakers or casual shoes. 구두 specifically means formal leather shoes; everyday athletic shoes are 운동화 and the generic word is 신발.

usagePhrases.note: footwear takes 신다
검은 is the adnominal of 검다 ('black')
불편하다 = uncomfortable; subject marker 가
paired footwear uses 켤레

examples.en: I wear dress shoes.
examples.note: Formal leather shoes still take 신다, like every other shoe.

examples.ko: 발이 아파서 구두를 벗고 슬리퍼로 갈아 신었어요.
examples.romanization: bari apaseo gudureul beotgo seullipeoro gara sineosseoyo.
examples.en: My feet hurt so I took off the dress shoes and changed into slippers.
examples.note: 갈아 신다 ('change footwear') is the foot-specific 'change into' verb.

examples.ko: 정장에 맞춰 검은 구두를 신고 면접에 갔어요.
examples.romanization: jeongjange matchwo geomeun gudureul singo myeonjeobe gasseoyo.

examples.note: Real situation: 정장에 맞추다 ('match to a suit') shows 구두's formal register.

ex.en: Could you show me another color too?

색깔.nuance: 색깔 is the everyday, standalone word for 'color,' built on the Sino-Korean root 색 (色 'color') plus a native suffix that makes it feel fuller and more conversational. Its near-synonym is just 색: the dividing line is grammatical, not meaning — 색깔 stands on its own (색깔이 예뻐요, 무슨 색깔?), while 색 is the building block that fuses to a specific shade name (파란색 blue, 빨간색 red, 노란색 yellow). A more formal, technical synonym is 색상, common in design and shopping ('color option'). The main English-speaker pitfall is over-using 색깔 by sticking it onto shade names — '파란색깔' is wrong; the named colors take 색, giving 파란색. Also, to ask 'what color,' the natural question word is 무슨 색깔, not 어떤 색깔 (which leans toward 'what kind/sort of color').
색깔.explanation: 색깔 (saekkkal) means "color". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 색깔 ("color"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 색깔 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
색깔.shortExplanation: 색깔 means "color" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Attaching a shade directly to 색깔, e.g. '파란색깔'; named colors use 색, as in 파란색.
Asking '어떤 색깔' for 'what color' when 무슨 색깔 is the natural phrasing.
Forgetting 색깔 is for color only — for a person's complexion or facial expression use 안색 / 얼굴색, not 색깔.

usagePhrases.note: Everyday standalone word for color; feels fuller and warmer than the bare 색.
무슨 + 색깔 asks which color something is: 무슨 색깔이에요?
색깔 + 이 as subject with an adjective; 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular (예뻐요).
set collocation; 진하다 (deep) vs 연하다 (light) describe color intensity.

examples.en: What color is it?
examples.note: Simplest color question; 색깔 stands alone naturally as the subject.

examples.en: This bag has a pretty color.
examples.note: Double-subject pattern: 가방은 (topic) ... 색깔이 (subject) ... 예뻐요.

examples.en: My favorite color is blue.
examples.note: Real answer: 색깔 as topic, but a specific shade uses 색 inside 파란색.

ex.en: For an interview, a navy shirt looks neat and presentable.

남색.nuance: 남색 is the deep, near-ink blue of school uniforms, business suits, and dark denim. The 남 is Sino-Korean 藍 ('indigo', the dye plant), so the word literally means 'indigo-color' — a good reminder that it lives at the DARK end of blue, the opposite pole from 하늘색 (sky blue). Against everyday 파란색 (a saturated mid-blue), 남색 reads as more formal and 차분하다 ('calm, composed'), which is exactly why it dominates uniforms and interview wear; younger shoppers often just say the loanword 네이비. Two English-speaker pitfalls: first, don't merge 남색 with 파란색 — they are not interchangeable, and a navy suit described as 파란색 정장 will sound like a bright-blue suit. Second, when stating 'navy is more X', the comparison particle goes on the thing you compare against: 남색이 파란색보다 (navy, compared-to blue), not 남색보다 파란색이 unless you mean the reverse.
남색.explanation: "navy (deep blue)" is 남색 (namsaek). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 남색 ("navy / deep indigo-blue"). Watch the particle attached to 남색 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
남색.shortExplanation: 남색 means "navy (deep blue)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 파란색 for navy — 남색 is specifically the dark indigo end, so a 파란색 정장 sounds bright blue, not navy.
Confusing 남색 (navy) with 하늘색 (sky blue) — they're opposite ends of the blue range, dark vs pale.
Flipping the comparison: to say 'navy is calmer than blue', mark blue with 보다 → 남색이 파란색보다 차분해요, not 남색보다 파란색이…

사이즈.nuance: 사이즈 is the size label or fit. Use 맞다 for whether it fits, and 어울리다 for whether it looks good on someone.
사이즈.explanation: 사이즈 (saijeu) means "size". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 사이즈가 맞아요. ("The size fits."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 사이즈 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.
사이즈.shortExplanation: 사이즈 means "size" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 어울리다 for size. 사이즈가 맞아요 means it fits; 잘 어울려요 means it suits you.
Asking only 이거 있어요? when you need a size. Say 다른 사이즈 있어요?
Forgetting that shop staff may ask 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? to mean what size would you like?

usagePhrases.note: 맞다 is about size or correctness, not style.
A direct shop question.

examples.ko: 사이즈가 조금 커서 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: saijeuga jogeum keoseo han chisu jageun geotdo boyeo jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: The size is a little big, so could you show me one size smaller too?
examples.note: Combines size judgment with a polite staff request.

ex.ko: 한 치수 작은 것도 입어 봐도 돼요?
ex.en: May I try on one size smaller too?

치수.nuance: 사이즈 is the everyday label; 치수 is the size measurement or one-step comparison used in 한 치수 큰/작은.
치수.explanation: "size; measurement" is 치수 (chisu). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 한 치수 큰 거 ("one size larger"). Watch the particle attached to 치수 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.
치수.shortExplanation: 치수 means "size; measurement" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 더 작은 사이즈 only every time. 한 치수 작은 거 is compact and natural in clothing stores.
Confusing 치수 with 가격. 치수 is about size or measurement, not price.
Forgetting the modifier: 한 치수 작아요 describes a size, but 한 치수 작은 거 asks for the item.

usagePhrases.note: 큰 modifies 거 through the adjective modifier form.
작은 is the modifier form of 작다.

examples.ko: 한 치수 작은 것도 입어 봐도 돼요?
examples.romanization: han chisu jageun geotdo ibeo bwado dwaeyo?
examples.en: May I try on one size smaller too?
examples.note: Natural fitting-room sentence.

ex.en: The fitting room is on the right.

피팅룸.nuance: 피팅룸 is used in many stores, but 탈의실 also means changing room. For clothing shopping, 피팅룸 is natural and easy to understand.
피팅룸.explanation: 피팅룸 (pitingnum) = "fitting room". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 피팅룸이 어디예요? ("Where is the fitting room?") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 피팅룸, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options and swap just one element to make it yours.
피팅룸.shortExplanation: 피팅룸 means "fitting room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling staff with 피팅룸? alone. Make it a full question: 피팅룸이 어디예요?
Using 입다 without try-on meaning. 입어 봐도 돼요? asks permission to try it on.
Assuming every shop allows try-ons; ask first for cosmetics, innerwear, sale items, or delicate clothing.

usagePhrases.note: A practical store question.

usagePhrases.en: The fitting room is on the right.
usagePhrases.note: Likely staff answer.

examples.ko: 이 셔츠 입어 보고 싶은데 피팅룸이 어디예요?
examples.romanization: i syeocheu ibeo bogo sipeunde pitingnumi eodiyeyo?
examples.en: I want to try on this shirt. Where is the fitting room?
examples.note: Connects trying on with store navigation.

ex.en: The navy shirt looks neater.

단정하다.nuance: 단정하다 means neat, orderly, and socially appropriate. It is not the same as stylish or trendy; it is often safer for interviews, school, and work.
단정하다.explanation: 단정하다 (danjeonghada) means "to be neat; tidy; presentable". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 단정한 셔츠 ("a neat shirt"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 단정하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
단정하다.shortExplanation: 단정하다 means "to be neat; tidy; presentable" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 예쁘다 for every clothing compliment. 예쁘다 is pretty; 단정하다 is neat and appropriate.
Saying 단정 옷. Use the modifier form: 단정한 옷.
Confusing 단정하다 with 깨끗하다. 깨끗하다 is clean; 단정하다 is presentable and orderly.

usagePhrases.note: A-ㄴ/은 N modifier form.
Appearance judgment with -아/어 보이다.

examples.ko: 면접에는 이 셔츠보다 남색 셔츠가 더 단정해 보여요.
examples.romanization: myeonjeobeneun i syeocheuboda namsaek syeocheuga deo danjeonghae boyeoyo.
examples.en: For an interview, the navy shirt looks neater than this shirt.
examples.note: Connects interview clothing with comparison and appearance.

ex.en: Can I exchange it too?
ex.note: Linked to dictionary card word-ext-1971 and expression expr-765.

교환.nuance: 교환 means swapping a purchased item for a different size, color, or model of the same kind of product, from the hanja 交換 (交 'to cross/mutual' + 換 'to change'), literally 'mutually change.' The crucial shopping contrast is with 반품, a 'return' that gives your money back: 교환 keeps the transaction (you walk out with goods), 반품 undoes it (you walk out with a refund). Counters typically post '교환·반품 안내' together. Note 교환 is also used more broadly than shopping — 의견 교환 (exchanging opinions), 정보 교환 (exchanging information) — so the word isn't shop-only, but here it's the item-swap sense. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'exchange money' tempts a literal 돈을 교환하다, but currency exchange is 환전 (a different word). To swap into the replacement item, use 로/으로 (큰 사이즈로 교환), and remember the verb is 교환하다, so 'I want to exchange' is 교환하고 싶어요, not 교환을 싶어요.
교환.explanation: 교환 (gyohwan) means "exchange". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 교환하다 ("to exchange"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 교환 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options, then change a single part.
교환.shortExplanation: 교환 means "exchange" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 교환 (swap for another item) with 반품 (return for a refund). If you want your money back, that's 반품; 교환 means you leave with replacement goods.
Saying 돈을 교환하다 for changing currency. Money exchange is 환전(하다); 교환 is for swapping purchased items or, figuratively, opinions/information.
Marking the replacement with the wrong particle: '큰 사이즈에 교환해요.' Use 로/으로 for what you swap into — 큰 사이즈로 교환해요.

usagePhrases.note: 교환 + 하다 turns the noun into the verb 'to swap an item'
가능하다 (be possible) pairs with 이; the standard shop phrasing
로 marks what you swap into (the target size)
및 (and, formal) is the set sign wording at counters

examples.en: Can I exchange it?
examples.note: simple: 되다 here means 'is allowed/possible'

examples.ko: 이 옷을 큰 걸로 교환하고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: i oseul keun geollo gyohwanhago sipeoyo.
examples.en: I'd like to exchange this for a bigger one.
examples.note: everyday: 걸로 (= 것으로) marks the replacement; -고 싶다 = 'want to'

examples.en: You can exchange it only if you have the receipt.
examples.note: real situation: -아야 (only if) states the condition for 교환

ex.en: Can I get a refund too?
ex.note: Linked to dictionary card word-ext-143 and expression expr-764.

환불.nuance: 환불(還拂) is Sino-Korean — 還 'return/give back' + 拂 'pay out' — literally 'pay back', i.e. returning the buyer's money for a returned item. The contrast learners must nail is 환불 vs 교환: 환불 = money back, 교환(交換 'exchange') = swap for a different item/size/color, no money returned. A related word is 반품(返品) 'returning the goods' — the physical act of sending the product back, which usually triggers a 환불. So you 반품 the item and receive a 환불. Voice matters as with 할인: from your side you say 환불을 받다 ('receive a refund'); to request it you say 환불해 주세요 ('refund it for me'); about whether it's allowed you say 환불이 되다/환불되다 ('a refund is possible'). The English-speaker pitfall is wanting an exchange but saying 환불 — if you actually want a different size, ask 교환돼요? / 교환해 주세요, because 환불 will give you cash back, not a swap. Note Korean also uses 결제 (결제하다) for 'make a payment/settle by card', often in the same conversation. Collocations: 환불을 받다, 환불해 주다, 환불되다, 환불 정책 (refund policy), 환불 규정.
환불.explanation: "refund" is 환불 (hwanbul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 환불을 받아요 ("I get a refund"). Watch the particle attached to 환불 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about buying things, checking prices, quantities, and payment options first, then vary one word.
환불.shortExplanation: 환불 means "refund" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 환불 when you want an exchange. 환불 returns your money; to swap for another size/color say 교환해 주세요 or ask 교환돼요?. They are different transactions.
Reversing the giver/receiver: customers say 환불을 받다 (receive a refund); shops say 환불해 주다 (give a refund). 환불을 줘요 about yourself wrongly casts you as the one paying back.
Confusing 환불 (the money refund) with 반품 (physically returning the goods). You 반품 the product, and that leads to a 환불. Mixing them muddles 'send it back' with 'get money back'.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 'receive'; you, the buyer, get your money back
환불하다 + 주세요; what you say to request it
환불 + 되다 'be doable', about store policy
-(으)ㄹ 수 있다 to ask if it's allowed

examples.en: Can I get a refund on this?
examples.note: simple: 환불되다 as one verb to ask about policy

examples.ko: 영수증이 있으면 환불 받을 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: yeongsujeungi isseumyeon hwanbul badeul su isseoyo.
examples.en: If you have the receipt, you can get a refund.
examples.note: everyday: -(으)면 'if' condition + 받을 수 있다 'can receive'

examples.ko: 사이즈가 안 맞아서 환불하러 왔는데요, 카드로 결제했어요.
examples.romanization: saijeuga an majaseo hwanbulhareo wanneundeyo, kadeuro gyeoljehaesseoyo.
examples.en: I came to get a refund because the size doesn't fit; I paid by card.
examples.note: real situation: -러 오다 'come in order to' + explaining 결제 (payment) method

ex.en: Please give us two servings of samgyeopsal.

삼겹살.nuance: 삼겹살 literally breaks down as 삼(三, three) + 겹(layer) + 살(flesh) — 'three-layered meat' — naming the alternating stripes of fat and lean in pork belly, and it is the single most iconic Korean BBQ cut and a default casual group meal. Don't confuse it with 목살 (pork neck/collar, leaner) or 오겹살 (a five-layer belly cut with the skin on); waiters list these as separate menu lines. Register-wise the word itself is neutral, but the situation is firmly casual — friends, 회식 work dinners, late nights with soju — never a formal banquet. The pitfall for English speakers is the counter: 'a piece of pork belly' tempts you into 삼겹살 한 개, but you must order by 인분 (삼겹살 2인분), and you say 구워 먹다 (grill-and-eat) rather than the English 'have a barbecue,' because here you do the grilling yourself.
삼겹살.explanation: 삼겹살 (samgyeopsal) means "pork belly (grilled)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 삼겹살 2인분 주세요 ("Two servings of pork belly, please"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 삼겹살 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.
삼겹살.shortExplanation: 삼겹살 means "pork belly (grilled)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 삼겹살 한 개 — meat is counted by 인분 (serving), so the correct order is 삼겹살 1인분 / 2인분.
Calling any grilled pork 삼겹살 — 삼겹살 is specifically the belly cut; 목살 (neck) and 항정살 (jowl) are different lines on the menu.
Using 만들다 ('make') for grilling at the table — Koreans say 삼겹살 구워 먹다 (grill and eat), not 삼겹살 만들다.

usagePhrases.en: Two servings of pork belly, please
usagePhrases.note: Meat is ordered by 인분 (serving), never by piece — this is the core ordering phrase.

usagePhrases.en: Pork belly with a shot of soju
usagePhrases.note: 에 here marks the food you pair a drink with; the most iconic Korean food-and-drink combo.

usagePhrases.en: We grill and eat pork belly
usagePhrases.note: 굽다 → 구워 (ㅂ-irregular); you cook it yourself at the table-top grill.

usagePhrases.en: The fat renders right out, which is great
usagePhrases.note: 쫙 빠지다 is the set phrase Koreans use to praise well-grilled 삼겹살.

examples.en: Want to go eat pork belly?
examples.note: The everyday casual invite; 먹으러 가다 = go in order to eat.

examples.en: Is the pork belly fully cooked?
examples.note: 익다 = (food) to be cooked through; ask before you pick a piece off the grill.

examples.en: Pork belly only tastes right wrapped in a lettuce leaf.
examples.note: 쌈 = the lettuce/perilla wrap; -아야 제맛이다 = 'it's only truly good when…', a very natural food cliché.

ex.ko: 삼겹살 두 인분하고 공기밥 하나 주세요.
ex.en: Please give us two servings of samgyeopsal and one bowl of rice.

인분.nuance: 명 counts people; 인분 counts portions. 두 명 왔어요 says two people came, but 두 인분 주세요 orders two servings.
인분.explanation: "serving; portion for one person" is 인분 (inbun). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 삼겹살 두 인분 주세요. ("Please give us two servings of samgyeopsal."). Watch the particle attached to 인분 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.
인분.shortExplanation: 인분 means "serving; portion for one person" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 명 to order food. Say 삼겹살 두 인분, not 삼겹살 두 명.
Forgetting that some restaurants have a minimum order such as 2인분.
Treating 인분 as exactly the eater count. People can order more or fewer servings than the number of people.

usagePhrases.en: Please give us two servings of samgyeopsal.
usagePhrases.note: Core barbecue order.

usagePhrases.en: Please give us one more serving.
usagePhrases.note: Common extra order.

examples.ko: 삼겹살 두 인분하고 공기밥 하나 주세요.
examples.romanization: samgyeopsal du inbunhago gonggiba pana juseyo.
examples.en: Please give us two servings of samgyeopsal and one bowl of rice.
examples.note: Combines a serving counter and a rice order.

ex.en: Please give us one bowl of rice.

공기밥.nuance: 밥 can mean cooked rice or a meal. 공기밥 is the restaurant item, a separate bowl of rice.
공기밥.explanation: 공기밥 (gonggibap) = "bowl of rice". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 공기밥 하나 주세요. ("Please give me one bowl of rice.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 공기밥, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.
공기밥.shortExplanation: 공기밥 means "bowl of rice" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Ordering 밥 vaguely when the menu item is 공기밥.
Confusing 공기밥 with 볶음밥. 공기밥 is plain rice; 볶음밥 is fried rice.
Forgetting the counter: 공기밥 하나/두 개 is common.

usagePhrases.en: Please give me one bowl of rice.
usagePhrases.note: Simple restaurant request.

usagePhrases.en: We will add a bowl of rice.
usagePhrases.note: Common after ordering meat or stew.

examples.en: The seasoning is spicy, so I eat it with a bowl of rice.
examples.note: Reason plus food pairing.

ex.en: Please give us a little more side dishes too.

밑반찬.nuance: 밑반찬 is not the main dish. It refers to small supporting dishes such as kimchi, vegetables, or pickles served with the meal.
밑반찬.explanation: 밑반찬 (mitbanchan) means "basic side dishes". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 밑반찬 좀 더 주세요. ("Please give us a little more side dishes."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 밑반찬 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.
밑반찬.shortExplanation: 밑반찬 means "basic side dishes" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling every Korean side dish 밑반찬 in every context. On a menu, 반찬 or 사이드 may also appear.
Forgetting 좀 in refill requests. 밑반찬 좀 더 주세요 sounds softer.
Assuming refills are always unlimited; most ordinary restaurants refill, but special side dishes may not be free.

usagePhrases.en: Please give us a little more side dishes.
usagePhrases.note: Polite refill request.
Simple restaurant compliment.

examples.en: The side dishes are not enough, so please give us more.
examples.note: Uses -니까 before a request.

ex.en: We grill the meat and the garlic together too.

굽다.nuance: 굽다 is a ㅂ-irregular verb: the dictionary ㅂ becomes 우 before any vowel ending, so the 요-form is 구워요 (not the textbook-looking 굽어요), past 구웠어요, future 구울 거예요 — memorize the 요-form and the rest follows. Meaning-wise it is dry-heat cooking with direct radiant heat: grilling meat, roasting, AND oven-baking bread all fall under this one word, which surprises English speakers who keep three separate verbs. Contrast it sharply with its kitchen neighbours: 굽다 uses no water and little-to-no oil (just the surface), whereas 볶다 tosses food in a little oil and 튀기다 submerges it in lots of oil. It is the single most useful cooking verb for a foreigner here because 구이 (grilled dishes) and Korean BBQ are everywhere. The classic learner trap is writing 굽어요/굽었어요 by analogy with regular verbs — say 구워요/구웠어요.
굽다.explanation: "to grill / to roast / to bake" in Korean is 굽다 (gupda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 구워요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 굽다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 고기를 굽다 ("to grill meat") — then reshape the same stem into 굽고 싶어요 (desire), 구울 수 있어요 (ability), and 구울 수 없어요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
굽다.shortExplanation: 굽다 means "to grill / to roast / to bake" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 굽다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 구워요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Conjugating it as a regular verb: 굽어요/굽었어요. It's ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ→우 gives 구워요/구웠어요.
Using 굽다 for boiling or deep-frying. Boiling a solid is 삶다, boiling a liquid is 끓이다, and deep-frying is 튀기다 — 굽다 is dry direct heat only.
Forgetting the ㅂ drops before consonant endings too in the future/modifier: it's 구울 거예요 and 구운 고기, not 굽을 거예요/굽은 고기.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 굽다 becomes 구울 수 있어요 ("can") and 구울 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 굽다 has an irregular stem (ㅂ). Memorize its polite form 구워요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

usagePhrases.en: I grill / to roast / to bake.
usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.

usagePhrases.en: I do not grill / to roast / to bake.
usagePhrases.note: Short everyday negative.

usagePhrases.en: I want to grill / to roast / to bake.
usagePhrases.note: Useful for choices and plans.

usagePhrases.en: I can grill / to roast / to bake.
usagePhrases.note: Ability or possibility.

usagePhrases.en: I have to grill / to roast / to bake.
usagePhrases.note: Requirement or obligation.
The default verb at Korean BBQ — at a 고깃집 you 고기를 구워 먹어요 (grill it on the table and eat it yourself).

examples.en: I'm baking bread.
examples.note: Simplest possible frame — note the form is 구워요, never 굽어요; the dictionary ㅂ is already gone.

examples.en: Is the meat all grilled?
examples.note: The constant question at the table. 구웠어요 is the ㅂ-irregular past — it is NOT 굽었어요.

examples.en: I'll grill the pork belly, you stay seated.
examples.note: 구울게요 (ㅂ→우 + ㄹ게요) volunteers you for grill duty; said warmly to elders so they don't work.

ex.en: The meat is cooked now, so please cut it.

익다.nuance: 익다 is intransitive: 고기가 익어요. 익히다 is transitive: 고기를 익혀요, to cook something through.
익다.explanation: "to be cooked; to ripen" is 익다 (ikda). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 고기가 익었어요. ("The meat is cooked."). Watch the particle attached to 익다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.
익다.shortExplanation: 익다 means "to be cooked; to ripen" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 고기를 익어요. Use 고기가 익어요 because the meat becomes cooked.
Confusing 익다 with 굽다. 굽다 is the cooking action; 익다 is the result.
Using 익다 only for fruit. It also works for meat, rice, and other food becoming cooked.

자르다.nuance: 자르다 means to cut THROUGH and separate something with a blade or scissors — paper, hair, cake, rope, nails — i.e. to sever into pieces. Distinguish it from 썰다, which is 'to slice' food into many pieces on a board (양파를 썰다, 'chop an onion'), and from 끊다, which is 'to cut off / break' a connection, line, or supply (전화를 끊다 'hang up', 담배를 끊다 'quit smoking') — note 머리를 자르다 (cut hair) but never 머리를 끊다. There's also 깎다 for shaving/peeling/paring (사과를 깎다 'peel an apple', 수염을 깎다 'shave'). It's a 르-irregular: 자르 + 아요 → 잘라요 (ㅡ drops, ㄹ doubles), past 잘랐어요, but consonant endings keep it whole (자르고, 자를게요, 자릅니다). The big pitfall is 자르아요 (wrong) instead of 잘라요. Also, English 'cut prices' or 'cut down' does not map to 자르다 — reducing an amount is 줄이다, and cutting off a service is 끊다.
자르다.explanation: "to cut" in Korean is 자르다 (jareuda). In real conversation you will lean on the polite form 잘라요, so make that your default and leave the bare dictionary form 자르다 for study notes. Grow outward from one concrete line — 머리를 자르다 ("to cut/get a haircut") — then reshape the same stem into 자르고 싶어요 (desire), 자를 수 있어요 (ability), and 못 잘라요 (a real limit) as the moment needs. The stem stays put; only the ending moves.
자르다.shortExplanation: 자르다 means "to cut" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 자르다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 잘라요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Saying 자르아요 — being 르-irregular it becomes 잘라요 (ㅡ drops, ㄹ doubles), past 잘랐어요.
Using 자르다 for 'hang up the phone' or 'quit smoking' — severing a connection/habit is 끊다 (전화를 끊다, 담배를 끊다), not 자르다.
Confusing 자르다 with 썰다 when chopping food — slicing veggies on a board is 썰다 (양파를 썰다); 자르다 is a single cut-through.

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 자르다 becomes 자를 수 있어요 ("can") and 자를 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 자르다 has an irregular stem (르 irregular). Memorize its polite form 잘라요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

마늘.nuance: 마늘 is a native Korean word for garlic, and few foods are more central to Korean cooking — it's the aromatic base (with 양파 and 파) of countless dishes, eaten raw with grilled meat, pickled, or 다지다 (minced) into almost everything. Crucially, a single clove is counted with 쪽 (마늘 한 쪽), while a whole bulb/head is 마늘 한 통 — using 개 for garlic sounds wrong, so learn 쪽 (clove) vs 통 (head). It ends in ㄹ, so particles are 마늘을 / 마늘이, and say it as two clean syllables 'ma-neul.' The English-speaker pitfall is the counter (defaulting to 개 instead of 쪽/통), pronouncing 맵다 regularly (the correct form is 마늘이 매워요, ㅂ-irregular), and over-pluralizing (no 마늘들). It collocates with 다지다 (mince), 까다 (to peel a clove), 넣다 (add), and 빻다 (to crush/pound).
마늘.explanation: "garlic" is 마늘 (maneul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 마늘을 먹어요 ("I eat garlic"). Watch the particle attached to 마늘 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.
마늘.shortExplanation: 마늘 means "garlic" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Counting garlic with 개. A clove is 마늘 한 쪽 and a whole head is 마늘 한 통; 개 is unnatural.
Conjugating 맵다 as 맵어요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 마늘이 매워요.
Using 를/가 after 마늘. It ends in ㄹ, so the correct particles are 마늘을 / 마늘이.

상추.nuance: 상추 is the soft, floppy leaf lettuce used to wrap grilled meat as 쌈 — and the sharp line to draw is 상추 vs 양배추 vs 양상추: 상추 is the tender wrapping lettuce, 양배추 is the round head cabbage, and 양상추 is crunchy iceberg/head lettuce for salads. They are different vegetables, so the 양- prefix (a 'Western/foreign' marker, as in 양파 onion, 양식 Western food) is doing real work — 상추 vs 양상추 is not just casual vs formal, it's two distinct plants. Register is plain everyday vocabulary; the only social note is the BBQ ritual phrase. The single most useful collocation a resident learns is '상추 좀 더 주세요' — refills of 상추 are free at almost every 고깃집, so this one line earns its keep nightly. Other collocations: 상추쌈, 상추를 씻다, 상추가 아삭하다/싱싱하다. English-speaker pitfall: 'lettuce' in English defaults to the crunchy salad iceberg, but 상추 is the soft wrap leaf, so don't expect a Caesar-salad crunch; and English speakers often hesitate to ask for more because in many countries refills cost extra — in Korea, just say 더 주세요. 상추 is a native Korean word, no hanja.
상추.explanation: 상추 (sangchu) means "lettuce (for wrapping)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 상추 한 봉지 ("one bag of lettuce"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 상추 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together, then change a single part.
상추.shortExplanation: 상추 means "lettuce (for wrapping)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Mixing up 상추 (soft wrap lettuce), 양상추 (crunchy iceberg for salad), and 양배추 (round head cabbage) — the 양- prefix marks genuinely different vegetables, not a register difference.
Not asking for refills with '상추 좀 더 주세요' — at a 고깃집 the lettuce refill is free, so it's normal and expected to ask.
Expecting iceberg-style crunch — 상추 is tender leaf lettuce meant for wrapping (쌈), not a crisp salad base.

쌈장.nuance: 쌈장 is not the same as 고추장. It is a mixed paste commonly used for wraps with grilled meat.
쌈장.explanation: 쌈장 (ssamjang) = "ssamjang; thick sauce for wraps". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 쌈장 조금만 주세요. ("Please give me just a little ssamjang.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 쌈장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.
쌈장.shortExplanation: 쌈장 means "ssamjang; thick sauce for wraps" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling every red sauce 고추장. 쌈장 is a specific wrap sauce.
Using too much without tasting; 쌈장 can be salty.
Forgetting that 쌈장 often goes with 상추, 마늘, and grilled meat.

짜다.nuance: 짜다 means having a strong salt taste, and the practical contrast for cooking is 짜다 vs 간이 맞다: 짜다 says there is too much salt, while 간이 맞다 means the seasoning is just right (and 싱겁다 means too little). The salty thing takes 이/가 (국이 짜요). Conjugation is regular for an ㅏ-stem: 짜 + 아요 contracts to 짜요 (not 짜아요), past 짰어요. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, never write 짜아요. Second, 짜다 has a very common figurative meaning — 'stingy / tightfisted' — so 그 사람 진짜 짜 means 'that person is so cheap', nothing to do with food; English 'salty' meaning 'bitter/annoyed' does NOT transfer to Korean 짜다, so do not use it that way. When you want to talk about how salty you eat in general, use the adverb 짜게 (짜게 먹다), which health advice constantly repeats.
짜다.explanation: "to be salty" is 짜다 (jjada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 짠맛이 나다 ("to taste salty"). Watch the particle attached to 짜다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
짜다.shortExplanation: 짜다 means "to be salty" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Writing 짜아요 for the polite form; the ㅏ-stem contracts to 짜요.
Using 짜다 to mean emotionally 'salty/annoyed' as in English — in Korean that figurative sense is 'stingy', so the English idiom does not carry over.
Saying '이 국을 짜요' — the dish is the subject: 이 국이 짜요.

양념.nuance: 양념 is the native-Korean word for a whole blend of seasonings — soy sauce, garlic, sesame oil, sugar, chili — mixed to flavor a dish, NOT a single spice. This is the key contrast: one spice is a 향신료 or just its name (소금, 후추), but the prepared mixture you rub or pour on is 양념. The word also signals a style: 양념치킨 is chicken coated in sweet-spicy 양념 sauce, opposite 후라이드 (plain fried). 양념 collocates with 만들다 (make), 무치다 (toss/dress vegetables in it), 재우다 (marinate), 바르다 (brush on), and the verb 양념하다 (to season). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 양념 = one spice; if you only added salt, that's not really 양념 — 양념 implies a composed blend, and you marinate IN it with 에 (양념에 재우다).
양념.explanation: "seasoning; marinade" is 양념 (yangnyeom). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 양념을 만들어요 ("I make the seasoning"). Watch the particle attached to 양념 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together first, then vary one word.
양념.shortExplanation: 양념 means "seasoning; marinade" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Thinking 양념 means a single spice. It's a blended seasoning/marinade; one spice is its own name (소금, 후추).
Saying 양념을 재워요. You marinate the food IN seasoning: 닭고기를 양념에 재워요.
Forgetting the verb form 양념하다 (to season), distinct from just naming the noun 양념.

국물.nuance: 국물 (국 'soup' + 물 'water') is the liquid part of a soup or stew, as opposed to the 건더기 (the solid pieces) — that pair is the contrast to know. Its most famous quirk is the word 시원하다: applied to a steaming hot broth, 시원해요 does NOT mean cold — it means the hot liquid feels refreshing, clearing, soothing, the way a hot bath or a sip of hot soup makes you exhale 'ahh'. 국물 collocates with 마시다 (drink — you drink broth, you don't 먹다 it), 우러나다 (flavor steeps out), 진하다 (rich/concentrated), and 시원하다/뜨겁다. The headline English-speaker pitfall is hearing 시원한 국물 and translating 'cold broth' — for liquid you actually drink, use 마시다, and read 시원하다 as 'soothing'.
국물.explanation: 국물 (gungmul) = "broth; soup liquid". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 국물을 마셔요 ("I drink the broth") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 국물, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about ordering food, explaining food restrictions, and asking what to eat together and swap just one element to make it yours.
국물.shortExplanation: 국물 means "broth; soup liquid" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating 시원한 국물 as 'cold broth'. For hot soup it means refreshing/soothing as it goes down.
Saying 국물을 먹어요. Broth is a liquid you 마시다 (drink): 국물을 마셔요.
Conjugating 뜨겁다 as 뜨겁어요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 뜨거워요.

포장해 주세요.nuance: 포장해 주세요 is the all-purpose 'to go' or 'pack it up' request — for a café drink ordered fresh, a bakery item, or restaurant leftovers. 포장 (包裝) literally means 'wrapping/packaging.' Plain polite -요 for all staff; the even shorter clipped form 포장이요 works as a quick answer to a binary dine-in question; 반말 포장해 줘 is friends-only. The near alternative is 가져갈게요 ('I'll take it away') — the dividing line is who does the action: 포장해 주세요 asks staff to actively pack the item, while 가져갈게요 simply announces you're taking it; in practice both achieve takeout but 포장해 주세요 is more specific. Another alternative is 싸 주세요 ('wrap it up') — homey and natural for restaurant leftovers but slightly informal for a fresh café order. The English-speaker mistake is defaulting to 테이크아웃 해 주세요 — understood at chains but 포장 is the fully native word, and 테이크아웃 컵 refers specifically to the cup type, not the whole transaction.
포장해 주세요.explanation: 포장해 주세요 (pojanghae juseyo) means "To go, please / Pack it up". Say it as one set phrase — for example 포장해 주세요. ("Please pack it to go."). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
포장해 주세요.shortExplanation: 포장해 주세요 is a practical expression meaning "To go, please / Pack it up".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Defaulting to 테이크아웃 해 주세요 — understood but the natural, fully Korean word is 포장: 포장해 주세요.
Confusing 포장해 주세요 with dine-in — 포장해 주세요 is the takeout request; to eat in say 먹고 갈게요 or 여기서 먹을게요.
Using 포장 when you mean gift wrapping — in a café 포장 means 'pack to go'; for gift wrap specify 선물 포장해 주세요 so staff know the difference.

드라마.nuance: 드라마 usually means a scripted series, not a one-off movie. 영화 is movie; 예능 is variety show.
드라마.explanation: 드라마 (deurama) means "TV drama; series". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 이 드라마 본 적 있어요? ("Have you watched this drama before?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 드라마 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
드라마.shortExplanation: 드라마 means "TV drama; series" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 영화 for every streamed show. A series is usually 드라마.
Forgetting 보다: 드라마를 봐요, not 드라마를 들어요.
Using 본 적 있어요 for something you watched yesterday with a time. Use 봤어요 for a dated event.

댓글.explanation: "comment" is 댓글 (daetgeul). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 댓글을 달다 ("to leave a comment"). Watch the particle attached to 댓글 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.

자막.nuance: 자막 can mean subtitles for translation or captions on video. In streaming apps, 자막 설정 is subtitle settings.
자막.explanation: 자막 (jamak) means "subtitles; captions". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 자막이 좋아요. ("The subtitles are good."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 자막 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
자막.shortExplanation: 자막 means "subtitles; captions" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Saying 자막을 봐요 when you mean the subtitles show on screen. Use 자막이 나와요.
Forgetting that 자막 takes 이/가 when it appears: 자막이 안 나와요.

영상.nuance: 영상 is Sino-Korean: 映 (영, 'reflect/project') + 像 (상, 'image'), literally a 'projected image', and it means a video clip — the kind you watch online, on your phone, or record yourself. Draw the line carefully against 영화 (映畫, 'projected picture'), a full cinema movie: a YouTube clip is an 영상, never an 영화. It also contrasts with the casual loanword 비디오, which now sounds dated (it evoked old videotapes) and with 동영상 (動映像, 'moving image'), a near-identical, slightly more technical synonym you'll see on menus and settings. The verb pairing is the pitfall: you watch a video with 보다 + object (영상을 보다), and crucially you 'shoot/take' one with 찍다 — 영상을 찍다 — not 만들다 unless you mean editing/producing it. English 'make a video' tempts learners into 영상을 만들다, but for simply recording, 찍다 is the natural choice.
영상.explanation: 영상 (yeongsang) means "video". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 영상을 봐요 ("I watch a video"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 영상 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
영상.shortExplanation: 영상 means "video" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling an online clip an 영화. 영화 is a cinema film; a short clip is an 영상. 'Watch a YouTube video' = 유튜브 영상을 보다.
Saying 영상이 봐요 for 'I watch a video'. 보다 is transitive: 영상을 봐요.
Using 영상을 만들다 for simply recording on your phone. To capture footage use 찍다 (영상을 찍다); reserve 만들다 for producing/editing a finished video.

공유하다.nuance: 공유하다 is broader than sending. 보내다 is to send; 공유하다 emphasizes making content available or passing it along.
공유하다.explanation: 공유하다 (gongyuhada) = "to share". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 영상을 공유했어요. ("I shared the video.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 공유하다, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
공유하다.shortExplanation: 공유하다 means "to share" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 나누다 for social media sharing. Use 공유하다 for links, videos, and files.
Forgetting the object: 영상을 공유했어요, 링크를 공유했어요.
Mixing 공유하다 with 저장하다. Sharing is not saving.

와이파이.nuance: 와이파이 is the loanword for local wireless internet (the spoken form follows the English 'Wi-Fi'), and the key distinction English speakers must hold is 와이파이 vs 데이터: 와이파이 is the free signal you join from a router, while 데이터 is your paid mobile-data allowance — running out of one doesn't affect the other. It also differs from 인터넷, the network as a whole; 와이파이 is just one way to reach it. The pitfall is the connection particle: you connect 와이파이에 (to the wifi, a destination) with 연결하다, not 와이파이로, because here the wifi is where you're attaching, not a tool you act through. And like other tech that simply stops responding, a dead signal is 와이파이가 안 돼요 (it won't function), not 와이파이가 없어요, which claims there's no network at all.
와이파이.explanation: 와이파이 (waipai) = "wifi". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 와이파이가 있어요 ("there is wifi") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 와이파이, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
와이파이.shortExplanation: 와이파이 means "wifi" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 와이파이로 연결해요 to mean 'connect to the wifi'. 연결하다 takes the destination 에: 와이파이에 연결해요. (You'd use 으로 only for the means, e.g. 와이파이로 영상을 봐요 'watch videos over wifi'.)
Mixing up 와이파이 and 데이터. If the router signal is gone you can still use 데이터; say 와이파이가 안 돼요, not 데이터가 안 돼요.
Saying 와이파이가 없어요 for a temporary outage. That means 'there's no wifi here at all'; for it failing momentarily say 와이파이가 안 돼요.

연결하다.nuance: 연결하다 is active: you connect something. 연결되다 means something is connected.
연결하다.explanation: 연결하다 (yeongyeolhada) means "to connect". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 와이파이를 다시 연결해 보세요. ("Try reconnecting the Wi-Fi."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 연결하다 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
연결하다.shortExplanation: 연결하다 means "to connect" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 연결하다 when the subject is the Wi-Fi itself. 와이파이가 연결됐어요 is natural for 'the Wi-Fi is connected.'
Confusing 연결하다 with 공유하다. 연결하다 connects; 공유하다 shares content.
Forgetting 을/를 for what you connect: 와이파이를 연결해요.

누르다.nuance: 누르다 is the go-to verb for pressing or pushing down — elevator buttons, doorbells, app icons, keypad keys, the 'like' button — and modern Korean life is so full of buttons that nailing it instantly sounds fluent. It is a textbook 르-irregular verb: before a vowel ending, the 르 transforms and an extra ㄹ appears, so the stem becomes 눌ㄹ-, giving 눌러요 and past 눌렀어요, while consonant endings stay regular (누릅니다, 누르고, 누르지 마세요). The meaning contrast to lock in is with 밀다 and 당기다: 누르다 is pressing DOWN on a surface or button, 밀다 is pushing a door/object away from you (문을 밀다 'push the door'), and 당기다 is pulling it toward you (문을 당기다) — so a door says 미세요/당기세요, never 누르세요, but a doorbell beside it says 누르세요. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: writing the un-irregular '누르어요' instead of 눌러요, and over-extending 'press/push' to doors, where Korean insists on 밀다 rather than 누르다.
누르다.explanation: 누르다 (nureuda) = "to press, to push (a button)". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 눌러요 plus one useful sentence like 몇 층 누르세요? ("Which floor should I press?"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 누르고 싶어요 for what you want, 누를 수 있어요 for what you can, 누를 수 없어요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about basic everyday communication.
누르다.shortExplanation: 누르다 means "to press, to push (a button)" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 누르다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 눌러요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
It's a 르-irregular: the polite form is 눌러요 (never '누르어요') and the past is 눌렀어요.
For pushing a door or object away (not pressing a button), use 밀다 — a door reads 미세요/당기세요, not '누르세요'.
Mark the button with 을/를: 버튼을 누르다, and for a long press add 길게 (길게 누르다).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 누르다 becomes 누를 수 있어요 ("can") and 누를 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

conjugationTips.title: Irregular stem
conjugationTips.body: 누르다 has an irregular stem (르). Memorize its polite form 눌러요 as the anchor and build the other forms from there.

ㅋㅋ.nuance: ㅋㅋ is the texted shape of the snicker 크크/큭큭 (ㅋ is the consonant for the 'k' giggle), and among Korean 20-30s it is the default 'I'm-relaxed-and-friendly' marker — even more than a real laugh, it signals you're at ease, so chats feel cold without it. Length is meaning: ㅋㅋ is a polite chuckle, ㅋㅋㅋㅋㅋ is genuine laughter, and you stretch the string to match how funny something is (it helps that ㅋ sits under one key, so spamming it is effortless). Its near-rival ㅎㅎ is the softer cousin (a smile, not a laugh), so swapping them shifts tone — ㅋㅋ is funny, ㅎㅎ is gentle/warm. The sharp English-speaker pitfall is the lone ㅋ: in English a solo 'lol' is harmless, but a single ㅋ (or ㅋ.. / ㅋ?) can read as cold, sarcastic, even passive-aggressive — the texting equivalent of a flat 'ha,' so never go below ㅋㅋ. And keep all of it out of messages to a boss, professor, or stranger, where laughter letters look unserious; there you write plain-polite sentences with no ㅋ at all.
ㅋㅋ.explanation: ㅋㅋ (kk (keukeu)) means "haha / lol — laughter sound, from 크크 / 큭큭 (the giggle/snicker sound). The most-used reaction in Korean chats. (casual slang — fine with friends, never in formal work messages)". Say it as one set phrase — for example ㅋㅋ ("haha"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
ㅋㅋ.shortExplanation: ㅋㅋ is a practical expression meaning "haha / lol — laughter sound, from 크크 / 큭큭 (the giggle/snicker sound). The most-used reaction in Korean chats. (casual slang — fine with friends, never in formal work messages)".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Sending a single ㅋ to someone sensitive — unlike a solo English 'lol' it can read as cold, bored, or sarcastic; always use at least ㅋㅋ to sound warm
Using ㅋㅋ in a formal/work message to soften it the way you might in English — to a senior it just looks unprofessional; drop the laughter entirely and keep the message plain-polite
Treating ㅋ and ㅎ as interchangeable — ㅋㅋ means something is funny, ㅎㅎ means you're smiling/being gentle; using ㅋㅋ where ㅎㅎ fits can make a kind moment sound like you're laughing AT them

usagePhrases.note: the safe default; two ㅋ already reads as warm, not curt — never drop to a single ㅋ, which lands like a flat 'ha'

대박.nuance: 대박 literally means 'a big hit / jackpot' (대 大 'big' + 박 = jackpot), and as a reaction it explodes out for anything extreme — amazingly good, but also shocking or unbelievably bad. It is youth slang and firmly casual: 대박 alone is banmal among friends; for even a little politeness say 대박이에요, though that still reads as informal in flavor. The variant ladder is 대박 → 대박이다 → 대박이에요 → 완전 대박 (intensified). The dividing line against 헐 is emotional direction: 헐 leans toward shock/dismay ('oh no, whoa'), while 대박 leans toward 'wow, that's enormous' — though both can appear together as 헐 대박. Because it's casual slang, the English-speaker pitfall is using it in formal or hierarchical settings — to a boss or elder, 대박 sounds flippant and disrespectful; use 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요 instead. A second pitfall is assuming it's always positive: Koreans say 대박 at a car crash too, meaning 'unbelievable/shocking.'
대박.explanation: 대박 (daebak) = "Awesome! / wow / no way — a big reaction to something amazing, shocking, or extreme.". Treat it as a ready-made line rather than separate words: 대박 ("awesome / wow"). Learn the situation it belongs to, and notice the reply it tends to invite.
대박.shortExplanation: 대박 is a practical expression meaning "Awesome! / wow / no way — a big reaction to something amazing, shocking, or extreme.".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 대박 with a boss, professor, or elder — it's casual slang and sounds disrespectful in formal settings; use 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요.
Assuming 대박 is only for good news — it reacts to anything extreme, including shocking bad events; tone and context decide the meaning.
Adding -요 as 대박요 — that's not natural; the polite form is 대박이에요, since 대박 is a noun that needs the 이에요 copula.

헐.nuance: 헐 is a pure interjection of shock — the involuntary sound that comes out when something startling, dismaying, or unbelievable hits you. It's hugely common in texting and casual conversation among friends and younger people. Because it's a raw exclamation there is no polite form: there is no 헐요 or 헐이에요; it lives entirely in banmal territory. The dividing line against 대박 is emotional direction: 헐 carries surprise often tinged with 'oh no' or dismay, while 대박 leans toward 'wow, that's enormous' — that's why 헐 어떡해 (shock + worry) is a natural pair but 대박 어떡해 is odd. Also don't confuse 헐 with 헉: 헐 is drawn-out disbelief ('whoa, no way'), while 헉 is a sharp one-syllable gasp of fright or physical surprise. The English-speaker pitfall is using 헐 in a professional or respectful setting — to an elder or boss it sounds childish and rude; in those moments use 어머 for neutral surprise or a full 정말요? 그런 일이. A second pitfall is trying to write 헐요 to be polite — simply switch words.
헐.explanation: 헐 (heol) means "Whoa / OMG / no way — a gut reaction of shock, disbelief, or mild dismay.". Say it as one set phrase — for example 헐 ("whoa / OMG"). What matters is the situation and how polite it sounds, so copy it whole from the examples instead of translating word by word.
헐.shortExplanation: 헐 is a practical expression meaning "Whoa / OMG / no way — a gut reaction of shock, disbelief, or mild dismay.".
commonMistakes: Do not add another polite ending to a phrase that is already complete.
Use the whole expression in the situation shown by the examples.
Using 헐 with a boss, elder, or in a formal email — it's casual youth slang and sounds immature/rude; use 어머 or 정말요? instead.
Trying to make a polite version like 헐요 — it doesn't exist; 헐 is a raw interjection that stays casual, so switch words for politeness.
Mixing up 헐 and 헉 — 헐 is disbelief/dismay ('whoa, no way'), while 헉 is a startled gasp of fright; they aren't interchangeable.

과제.explanation: 과제 (gwaje) = "assignment; homework". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 과제가 있어요. ("There is an assignment.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 과제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
과제.shortExplanation: 과제 means "assignment; homework" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.

Using 숙제 for every university assignment. 과제 is often more natural.
Forgetting the object marker when needed: 과제를 끝내요.
Confusing 과제 with 문제. 문제 is a question/problem; 과제 is an assigned task.

중간고사.nuance: 중간 means middle; 고사 is exam. In daily student talk, 시험 is more general, while 중간고사 is specifically the midterm.
중간고사.explanation: 중간고사 (junggangosa) means "midterm exam". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 중간고사 전에 ("before the midterm"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 중간고사 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
중간고사.shortExplanation: 중간고사 means "midterm exam" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 중간고사 for every test. Use 시험 for general exams.
Confusing 중간고사 with 기말고사. Midterm comes in the middle; final comes at the end.
Forgetting the timing phrase: 중간고사 전에, 중간고사 동안, 중간고사 끝나고.

기말고사.nuance: 기말 means the end of the term. 기말고사 is final exam; 중간고사 is midterm exam.
기말고사.explanation: "final exam" is 기말고사 (gimalgosa). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 기말고사 준비 ("final exam preparation"). Watch the particle attached to 기말고사 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
기말고사.shortExplanation: 기말고사 means "final exam" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 기말고사 before the middle of the semester. That is 중간고사.
Saying 시험을 치다/보다 both work for taking an exam; 시험을 만들다 does not mean take an exam.
Using 에 with 기말고사 when the sentence is about results. Say 기말고사에서 좋은 성적을 받다.

usagePhrases.note: Noun phrase.
보다 is used for taking exams.

examples.ko: 기말고사에서 좋은 성적을 받기 위해 매일 공부해야 해요.
