학기.nuance: 학기 is an academic term; 방학 is vacation/break between terms.
학기.explanation: 학기 (hakgi) = "semester; school term". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 이번 학기 ("this semester") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 학기, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
학기.shortExplanation: 학기 means "semester; school term" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 학기 for a single class period. A class period is 수업 or 시간.
Confusing 학기 with 학년. 학기 is semester; 학년 is grade/year.
Adding 에 before 동안: say 한 학기 동안, not 한 학기에 동안.

usagePhrases.note: Common school time phrase.
학기 works naturally with 동안.

examples.ko: 이번 학기 동안 매일 한국어를 공부하기로 했어요.

ex.en: I decided to ask the professor.

교수님.nuance: Use 선생님 for school teachers or language teachers, and 교수님 for university professors.
교수님.explanation: "professor" is 교수님 (gyosunim). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 교수님께 물어봐요. ("I ask the professor."). Watch the particle attached to 교수님 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
교수님.shortExplanation: 교수님 means "professor" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a university professor 선생님 is understandable, but 교수님 is more natural.
Using 교수 without 님 when addressing or referring respectfully.
Using 한테 in formal writing to a professor; 께 is more respectful.

usagePhrases.note: 께 is respectful 'to'.
Honorific verb ending for the professor.

examples.en: I decided to ask the professor before the midterm.

수업.nuance: 수업 is Sino-Korean 授業 — 授 'give/confer' + 業 'work/study', literally 'conferring instruction', i.e. the lesson or class session itself (the activity and time period). The set verb is 수업을 듣다 'listen to a class' = attend/take it; from the teacher's side it is 수업을 하다 'give/teach a class'. Three near-neighbors confuse learners: 수업 (the lesson event) vs 교실(教室, the room it happens in) vs 과목(科目, the subject like 'math' or 'history') vs 강의(講義, a university lecture). So 'I have three classes today' = 수업 세 개, but 'I take three subjects' = 과목 세 개. The English-speaker pitfall is using 하다 to mean 'take a class' (수업을 하다 actually means 'to teach', which is what a professor does) — as a student you 듣다 a class. Also, 'go to class' is 수업에 가다 (event as destination with 에).
수업.explanation: 수업 (sueop) means "class / lesson". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 수업을 듣다 ("take / attend a class"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 수업 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.
수업.shortExplanation: 수업 means "class / lesson" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
A student saying 수업을 하다 to mean 'I take a class' — 수업을 하다 means to TEACH a class. Students say 수업을 듣다.
Confusing 수업 (lesson) with 교실 (room): you 'attend a 수업', but you 'sit in a 교실'.
Using 과목 and 수업 interchangeably. 과목 is the subject (math); 수업 is the actual class session. 'Math class' = 수학 수업, but 'How many subjects?' = 과목이 몇 개?

usagePhrases.note: 듣다 'listen' is the set verb for attending a class
Scheduling; the class is the subject, so 이
늦다 takes 에 for the event you're late to
Subject-noun modifier; cf. 수학 수업 'math class'

examples.en: Do you have class today?
examples.note: Casual schedule check; 있어요 for a class existing on the timetable

examples.en: I usually attend class diligently.
examples.note: 수업을 듣다 = attend; 열심히 = 'diligently', a habitual collocation

examples.en: I'm sorry for being late to class.
examples.note: 늦다 + 에 marks the event; -아서 gives the reason

ex.en: I have to present tomorrow.

발표하다.nuance: 발표하다 is Sino-Korean 發表 — 發 'issue/emit' + 表 'express/show outwardly' — so 'issue something into the open'. It has two senses: (1) give a presentation/talk in front of an audience (수업에서 발표하다), and (2) officially announce/release information (정부가 결과를 발표하다 — the government announced the results). Contrast it with 설명하다 (說明, 'explain'): 설명하다 is clarifying so someone understands a point, while 발표하다 is the public act of presenting or announcing as a whole. Also distinguish 발표하다 from 말하다 'to say' — 발표하다 implies prepared, formal, to-an-audience delivery. A particle nuance: in the 'present' sense the location uses 에서 (수업에서), but the content shown is an object (자료를 발표하다). As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (발표해요, 발표했어요, formal 발표합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (발표 안 해요, 발표 못 해요).
발표하다.explanation: 발표하다 (balpyohada) = "to present". Don't try to memorize all fifteen forms at once; anchor on 발표해요 plus one useful sentence like 결과를 발표하다 ("to announce the results"). After that the endings carry the meaning — 발표하고 싶어요 for what you want, 발표할 수 있어요 for what you can, 발표 못 해요 for what you can't. Keep the stem, change the ending, and one verb gives you a dozen sentences about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations.
발표하다.shortExplanation: 발표하다 means "to present" and is practiced through polite conversation forms.
commonMistakes: Do not use the dictionary form 발표하다 as a complete polite sentence.
Use 발표해요 as the default until you know the relationship is casual.
Using 설명하다 when you mean giving a presentation — 설명하다 = explain a point for understanding; the public/prepared delivery is 발표하다.
Marking the venue with 에 instead of 에서 in the 'present' sense — an action you perform IN a place uses 에서: 수업에서 발표해요.
Forming the negative as 안 발표해요 — split it: 발표 안 해요 (impossible = 발표 못 해요).

conjugationTips.title: ㄹ / 을 — can & will
conjugationTips.body: To say "can" or the future, attach ㄹ/을 to the stem: a vowel-final stem takes ㄹ and a consonant-final stem takes 을. 발표하다 becomes 발표할 수 있어요 ("can") and 발표할 거예요 ("will"). That is why 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (not 가을), while 먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요. The same ㄹ/을 choice drives 거예요 and the noun-describing form.

usagePhrases.note: Safe polite present form.
Short everyday negative.
Useful for choices and plans.
Ability or possibility.
Requirement or obligation.
결과 = results; what you make public takes 을/를

examples.en: I'm presenting in class tomorrow.
examples.note: Doing a presentation IN a place = 에서: 수업에서 발표해요

examples.en: Shall we present this material together?
examples.note: ~ㄹ까요? proposes; 자료 = the material shown

examples.en: I'm so nervous I can't present.
examples.note: 긴장하다 = be nervous; impossible split: 발표 못 해요

ex.ko: 장학금을 받기 위해 좋은 성적이 필요해요.
ex.en: Good grades are necessary in order to get a scholarship.

성적.nuance: 성적 means academic grades, marks, or results, written 成績 (成 'to accomplish, achieve' + 績 'achievement, merit'), literally 'accomplished achievements' — the outcome of your effort. Distinguish it from 점수, a single numeric 'score' on one test (시험 점수 90점), and from 시험, the 'exam' itself: you take a 시험, get a 점수 on it, and your overall 성적 reflects the term. Note the directional verbs that pair with it: 성적이 나오다 (results 'come out'/are released), 성적을 받다 (you 'receive' them), 성적이 오르다/떨어지다 (they rise/fall). The English-speaker pitfall is using 시험 where you mean the resulting grade ('my exam was good' → say 성적이 좋아요), and choosing the wrong particle: with descriptive 좋다 or motion 나오다/오르다 it's 이/가, only with 받다 is it 을/를.
성적.explanation: 성적 (seongjeok) means "grades". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 성적이 좋아요 ("grades are good"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 성적 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.
성적.shortExplanation: 성적 means "grades" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 시험이 좋아요 to mean 'my grades are good'; 시험 is the exam, the result is 성적, so say 성적이 좋아요.
Saying 성적을 좋아요 by treating grades as an object; 좋다 is descriptive, so use 성적이 좋아요.
Using 점수 for the whole term's standing; 점수 is one test's score, the cumulative record is 성적.

usagePhrases.note: 좋다 is descriptive, so 성적 takes 이
나오다 (come out) takes the subject marker 이
받다 (receive) takes the object marker 을
오르다 (rise) takes the subject marker 이

examples.en: My grades are good.
examples.note: simple descriptive: 좋다 takes the subject marker 이

examples.en: The grades come out next week.
examples.note: 성적이 나오다 = results are released/posted

examples.ko: 이번에 성적이 많이 올라서 부모님이 정말 기뻐하셨어요.
examples.romanization: ibeone seongjeogi mani ollaseo bumonimi jeongmal gippeohasyeosseoyo.
examples.en: My grades went up a lot this time so my parents were really pleased.
examples.note: real life: 올라서 gives the reason; 기뻐하시다 (honorific) for parents

ex.ko: 장학금을 받기 위해 좋은 성적이 필요해요.
ex.en: Good grades are necessary in order to get a scholarship.

장학금.nuance: 장학금 is the award money granted to a student to support their studies — for merit (성적 장학금), need, or special talent — money you do not repay, unlike a loan. The hanja 奬學金 is 奬 (encourage/reward) + 學 (study/learning) + 金 (money/gold), literally 'study-encouraging money', so the very word frames it as funds that reward and enable learning. Distinguish it sharply from 학자금 (學資金, 'study-capital'), which is the broader pool of money for education and often appears in 학자금 대출 (a student loan you must repay): a 장학금 is given to you, whereas 학자금 대출 is borrowed. Also unlike a plain 돈 (money) or 용돈 (allowance), 장학금 specifically denotes an academic award. The natural verbs are 장학금을 받다 (formally receive) and the colloquial 장학금을 타다 (win/get one), plus 장학금을 신청하다 (apply) and 장학금이 나오다 (it comes through). The English-speaker pitfall is calling it just 돈 — saying 학교에서 돈을 받았어요 to mean a scholarship loses the meaning; the award is 장학금, and confusing it with the repayable 학자금 대출 reverses who gives money to whom.
장학금.explanation: "scholarship" is 장학금 (janghakgeum). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 장학금을 받아요 ("receive a scholarship"). Watch the particle attached to 장학금 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help first, then vary one word.
장학금.shortExplanation: 장학금 means "scholarship" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a scholarship plain 돈. 돈 is money in general; an academic award is specifically 장학금. Say 장학금을 받았어요, not 돈을 받았어요, when a school funds your study.
Confusing 장학금 with 학자금 (대출). A 장학금 is granted and not repaid; 학자금 대출 is a student loan you must pay back. They are opposite directions of obligation.
Using 사다 or 벌다 for getting a scholarship. You neither buy nor earn-by-working a scholarship; you 받다 (receive) or 타다 (win) it: 장학금을 받아요.

usagePhrases.note: 받다 (receive) takes 를; a scholarship is awarded to you
신청하다 (to apply/request) is the verb for putting in an application
나오다 describes the award money being granted/disbursed
타다 colloquially means to be awarded a prize or scholarship

examples.en: I got a scholarship.
examples.note: The proud one-liner: 받다 plus past -았어요, 를 marking the award.

examples.ko: 성적이 좋아서 이번 학기에 장학금을 신청했어요.
examples.romanization: seongjeogi joaseo ibeon hakgie janghakgeumeul sincheonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: My grades were good, so I applied for a scholarship this term.
examples.note: -아서 gives the reason (good grades); 신청하다 is the act of applying.

examples.ko: 전액 장학금을 타서 등록금 걱정이 없어졌어요.
examples.romanization: jeonaek janghakgeumeul taseo deungnokgeum geokjeongi eopseojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: I won a full scholarship, so my tuition worries are gone.
examples.note: 전액 (full amount) modifies it; 타다 (win) plus the relief of 걱정이 없어지다.

ex.en: I asked the professor a question in order to change my major.

전공.nuance: 전공 is your academic major — the single specialized field you concentrate on at university — written 專攻 (專 'exclusive, sole' + 攻 'to attack, devote effort to'), literally 'to devote oneself exclusively', i.e. to specialize. It can also act as a verb with 하다: 한국어를 전공하다 ('to major in Korean'). The key contrast is 전공 vs 과목: a 과목 is any one of the many courses on your timetable, whereas 전공 is the one field you commit to — you take many 과목 but have one 전공. It also differs from 학과, the 'academic department' that houses the major. The English-speaker pitfall is calling a major 과목 (제 과목은..., wrong) and forgetting that with the verb form the field takes 을/를: not 한국어 전공해요 but 한국어를 전공해요; as a plain noun, though, 전공이 뭐예요 uses 이/가.
전공.explanation: 전공 (jeongong) = "major". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 전공이 뭐예요 ("what is your major") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 전공, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help and swap just one element to make it yours.
전공.shortExplanation: 전공 means "major" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 제 과목은 한국어예요 for 'my major is Korean'; a university major is 전공, so use 제 전공은 한국어예요.
Saying 한국어 전공해요 without a particle; the verb form needs 를: 한국어를 전공해요.
Confusing 전공 with 학과; 전공 is the field you study, 학과 is the department, e.g. 한국어학과.

usagePhrases.note: 전공 + 뭐 (what) asks the field of study
정하다 (decide) takes the object marker 을
바꾸다 (change) takes the object marker 을
전공 modifies 수업 to mean a course in one's major

examples.en: My major is Korean.
examples.note: 전공 + 은 marks the topic; 이에요/예요 states it

examples.en: What's your major?
examples.note: the everyday question to a university student

examples.en: I changed my major from economics to psychology.
examples.note: real life: 에서...으로 = 'from...to', 바꾸다 = change

ex.en: I go to an academy in order to get good at Korean.

학원.nuance: 학원 is a private after-school academy (cram school) where students pay for extra lessons — English, math, piano, taekwondo — written 學院 (學 'study' + 院 'institution, hall'). The 院 'institution' element links it to 병원 (病院 hospital), 대학원 (大學院 graduate school), and 미용원/미장원, so the family is learnable. Sharply distinguish 학원 (a supplementary private institute) from 학교 (學校, the regular public/formal school) and from 대학원 (graduate school) — a child attends 학교 by day and 학원 in the evening. The verb of choice is 다니다, which implies habitual commuting/membership, with the 에 particle: 학원에 다니다 ('attend an academy regularly'), not the one-off 가다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 학교 for any place of learning, or marking the destination with 를 (학원를 다녀요, wrong) instead of 에.
학원.explanation: 학원 (hagwon) means "private academy". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 학원에 다녀요 ("attend an academy"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 학원 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about classroom communication, study plans, and asking for repetition or help, then change a single part.
학원.shortExplanation: 학원 means "private academy" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling a cram school 학교; the formal school is 학교, the private institute is 학원.
Saying 학원을 다녀요; the verb 다니다 takes the 에 particle for the place: 학원에 다녀요.
Using 가다 for habitual attendance; for ongoing enrollment Koreans say 다니다, e.g. 학원에 다녀요.

usagePhrases.note: 다니다 (commute/attend) takes the destination marker 에
끝나다 (end) takes the subject marker 이
subject name 영어 modifies 학원 bare
끝나다 + 고 = 'after it ends', then do the next thing

examples.en: I go to an English academy.
examples.note: 학원에 다니다 = attend regularly; 에 marks where you go

examples.en: The academy lets out at nine.
examples.note: 끝나다 takes 이/가; 에 marks the clock time

examples.ko: 학교 끝나고 바로 학원에 가야 해서 너무 피곤해요.
examples.romanization: hakgyo kkeunnago baro hagwone gaya haeseo neomu pigonhaeyo.
examples.en: I have to go straight to the academy after school so I'm exhausted.
examples.note: real life: a very Korean routine; 가야 해서 gives the reason

ex.en: Which line do I transfer to if I want to get to Seoul Station?

호선.nuance: 호선 is for subway line labels, not for bus routes. Say 2호선 for Line 2, but 버스 노선 for a bus route.
호선.explanation: 호선 (hoseon) means "subway line number". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 몇 호선이에요? ("Which line is it?"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 호선 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.
호선.shortExplanation: 호선 means "subway line number" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 2노선 for Line 2. Subway lines use 호선: 2호선.
Using 호선 for bus routes. Use 노선 for buses.
Forgetting 으로/로 with transfers: 1호선으로 갈아타세요.

usagePhrases.note: Natural question when checking a route.
으로 marks the line you change to.

examples.en: Which line do I transfer to if I want to get to Seoul Station?
examples.note: Route question plus transfer.

ex.en: Please go to platform 3.

승강장.nuance: 승강장 乘降場 stacks 乘 (board/get on) + 降 (alight/get off) + 場 (place/field) = 'the place where you board and get off', i.e. the platform along the tracks. It is the formal term on signage and in announcements; the everyday spoken equivalent is 플랫폼 (the English loanword), and 타는 곳 ('boarding place') is the plain-Korean label posted in many stations — all three point to the same spot. The crucial contrast is with 정류장 停留場 (a bus/tram STOP at the roadside) and 역 (the whole STATION building): the 승강장 is the specific edge where you stand beside the train, inside the 역. As a 場 place-noun it takes 에서 for waiting (승강장에서 기다려요) and 으로 for moving toward it (승강장으로 가요). The English-speaker pitfall is treating the platform as something you wait 'for': you wait for the TRAIN on the platform, so it's 승강장에서 기차를 기다려요, never 승강장을 기다려요.
승강장.explanation: 승강장 (seunggangjang) = "platform". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 승강장에서 기다리다 ("wait on the platform") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 승강장, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
승강장.shortExplanation: 승강장 means "platform" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 승강장을 기다려요 — you don't wait for the platform; you wait for the train there: 승강장'에서' 기차'를' 기다려요.
Mixing up 승강장 with 정류장 — 승강장 is the train/subway platform inside a station, while 정류장 is a roadside bus stop.
Confusing 승강장 with 역 — 역 is the entire station; the 승강장 is only the boarding strip beside the tracks.

usagePhrases.note: 에서 + 기다리다; the place where the waiting happens
number + 번 (counter) + 승강장; matches station signage
direction 으로 + 가다; head toward the platform
안전선 安全線 = safety line; '승강장 안전선 안쪽으로' is the classic announcement

examples.en: I'm waiting for the train on the platform.
examples.note: simple; 에서 marks the location of waiting

examples.en: Please go to platform 3.
examples.note: everyday direction; 으로 (toward) + 가세요 (polite go)

examples.en: Please step back behind the platform safety line.
examples.note: real announcement you'll actually hear; 안쪽으로 (toward the inside) + 물러나다 (step back)

ex.en: This route has a long service interval.

노선.nuance: 노선(路線) is Sino-Korean 路 'road' + 線 'line' — literally a 'road-line' — meaning a transit route/line for both buses and subways; the famous 노선도(路線圖) 'route map' (圖 = diagram) is the colored subway map newcomers squint at. The key usage split: for a specific subway line Koreans say the number + 호선 (2호선 'Line 2'), while 노선 is the general word for a route's path, used heavily for buses (버스 노선). Pitfalls: don't conflate 노선 'the route itself' with 노선도 'the map of routes' — one is the line, the other the diagram. And don't say 2노선 for Line 2; the counter is 호선. Apps like 카카오맵/네이버지도 list every 노선 and timetable.
노선.explanation: 노선 (noseon) means "route, (transit) line". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 노선도를 봐요. ("I look at the route map."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 노선 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.
노선.shortExplanation: 노선 means "route, (transit) line" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 2노선 for 'Line 2'.
Subway lines use the counter 호선: 2호선, 9호선. 노선 is the generic 'route' word, mainly for buses. → 2호선.
Confusing 노선 with 노선도.
노선 = the route/line itself. 노선도 = the printed/onscreen map of routes (圖 diagram). Asking for a 노선 when you want the map gets you the wrong thing.
Using 길 for a bus route.
길 = a street/road or a way to walk. A scheduled transit route is 노선 (버스 노선), not 길.

usagePhrases.en: I look at the route map.
usagePhrases.note: 노선도 = route map (圖 'diagram'), the colored subway map
which streets/stops the bus follows
다니다 = run/operate regularly; 이제 = 'now/anymore'
바뀌다 = (intransitive) get changed; route revisions happen

examples.ko: 이 버스 노선이 우리 집 앞을 지나가요.
examples.romanization: i beoseu noseoni uri jip apeul jinagayo.
examples.en: This bus route passes in front of my house.
examples.note: 지나가다 = pass by; a convenient route

examples.ko: 처음 왔을 때 지하철 노선도가 너무 복잡해 보였어요.
examples.romanization: cheoeum wasseul ttae jihacheol noseondoga neomu bokjapae boyeosseoyo.
examples.en: When I first arrived, the subway route map looked so complicated.
examples.note: 아 보이다 = 'looks/seems'; the newcomer feeling

examples.ko: 앱에서 노선이랑 막차 시간까지 다 확인할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: aebeseo noseonirang makcha sigankkaji da hwaginhal su isseoyo.
examples.en: In the app you can check everything, even the route and the last-train time.
examples.note: 이랑 = casual 'and'; 까지 = 'even/up to'

ex.en: I am trying to top up my transit card.

교통카드.nuance: 교통카드(交通+card) literally welds the Sino-Korean 교통 'traffic/transport' onto the English 'card', and names the rechargeable tap-to-ride card (T머니, 캐시비, or a 후불 credit card) for buses, the subway, and even some taxis. The make-or-break verb is 찍다 'to tap/stamp', never 누르다 'to press a button' — you lay the card flat on the reader, you don't push anything. A prepaid card you 충전 'top up' at convenience stores; the gate beeps your 잔액 'remaining balance'. Don't confuse it with a plain 카드, which to a Korean means a credit/debit card for shopping; the tap-to-ride one is always the full 교통카드. English 'swipe' also misleads — there is no magnetic swipe, only a contactless 찍다.
교통카드.explanation: 교통카드 (gyotongkadeu) means "transit card (T-money etc.)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 교통카드를 찍어요. ("I tap the transit card."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 교통카드 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.
교통카드.shortExplanation: 교통카드 means "transit card (T-money etc.)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 교통카드를 눌러요 for tapping in.
누르다 means to press a button; you tap a card flat on the reader, which is 찍다. → 교통카드를 찍어요.
Using bare 카드 to mean the transit card.
To a Korean 카드 alone = a credit/debit card for buying things. The tap-to-ride card must be the full 교통카드 to be unambiguous.
Saying 교통카드를 채워요 for topping up.
채우다 = fill a physical container; money value on a card is 충전하다. → 교통카드를 충전해요.

usagePhrases.note: the verb is 찍다 (to tap/stamp on the reader), never 누르다

usagePhrases.en: I top up the transit card.
usagePhrases.note: 충전(充電) literally 'charge electricity' — reused for adding cash value

usagePhrases.en: The transit card balance is low.
usagePhrases.note: 잔액 = remaining balance; the exact phrase the gate flashes

usagePhrases.en: Can I use a transit card?
usagePhrases.note: 돼요? = 'does it work?', the polite way to ask a cabbie or shop

examples.en: Do you have a transit card?
examples.note: simplest form — just 있다 + the noun

examples.en: I topped up my transit card at the convenience store.
examples.note: 에서 marks where the action happens; CU/GS25 all do it

examples.ko: 요즘은 지갑 없이 휴대폰으로 교통카드를 찍어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun jigap eopsi hyudaeponeuro gyotongkadeureul jjigeoyo.
examples.en: These days I tap the transit card with my phone instead of a wallet.

ex.en: Please top up my transit card with 10,000 won.
ex.note: Transit-card top-up phrase; the card takes 에 when money is added.

충전.nuance: For transit cards, 충전 is a top-up. For phones, it is battery charging. The object matters: 교통카드를 충전하다 versus 휴대폰을 충전하다.
충전.explanation: "top-up; charge" is 충전 (chungjeon). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 교통카드를 충전하다 ("to top up a transit card"). Watch the particle attached to 충전 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.
충전.shortExplanation: 충전 means "top-up; charge" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 사다 for adding money to a transit card. Buy the card with 사다, but add value with 충전하다.
Saying 돈을 교통카드에서 충전해요. Use 교통카드에 충전해요 because the money is added onto the card.
Confusing 충전 with 잔액. 충전 is the action; 잔액 is the remaining balance.

usagePhrases.en: to top up a transit card
usagePhrases.note: The card is the object being topped up.

usagePhrases.en: Please top it up with 10,000 won.
usagePhrases.note: Natural request at a station or convenience store.
충전 often comes with checking the remaining balance.

examples.en: Please top up my transit card with 10,000 won.
examples.note: 에 marks where the money is added.

examples.en: I topped up my transit card before taking the subway.
examples.note: A practical pre-ride action.

examples.en: If the balance is low, top it up here.
examples.note: Connects the balance problem to the action.

ex.en: I go from Seoul to Busan by KTX.

KTX.nuance: KTX (Korea Train eXpress, spoken letter-by-letter as 케이티엑스) is the fast premium train Koreans set against three cheaper options: the 고속버스, the slower 무궁화호, and the mid-tier ITX-새마을. The boundary worth fixing is KTX vs SRT — both are bullet trains, but KTX is run by 코레일 (Korail) and SRT is a separate operator from 수서역, so the booking app differs. Note it behaves grammatically more like a proper noun than 버스: 'by KTX' is naturally KTX로/으로, where buses prefer 타고. It collocates with 타다, 예매하다, 표, and the seat tiers 특실/일반실/자유석/입석. The signature English-speaker pitfall is reading the letters in English; a Korean always says 케이티엑스, sounding each letter Korean-style. A second trap is booking on the wrong app — for KTX you need 코레일톡, not the SRT app.
KTX.explanation: KTX (KTX) = "KTX (high-speed train)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: KTX 타다 ("to take the KTX") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside KTX, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
KTX.shortExplanation: KTX means "KTX (high-speed train)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Reading KTX as English letters — Koreans say 케이티엑스, so pronounce each letter in Korean.
Booking on the wrong app — KTX is Korail, so use 코레일톡, not the SRT app (SRT is a separate high-speed operator from 수서역).
Saying KTX를 타고 가요 is fine, but defaulting to KTX버스 — KTX is a train (기차), never a bus.

usagePhrases.note: read aloud as '케이티엑스'; Korea's flagship high-speed rail
done on the 코레일톡 (Korail Talk) app or at the station 매표소
특실(特室) 'special room' = first class, roomier; 일반실(一般室) = standard
자유석(自由席) = no assigned seat, cheaper; sit anywhere in the 자유석 cars, unlike 입석 (standing)

examples.en: I go from Seoul to Busan by KTX.
examples.note: with a named train/vehicle, 으로/로 'by means of' is natural here, unlike with 버스+타고

examples.ko: KTX 표가 비싸지만 빠르니까 자주 타요.

표.nuance: 표 is the general ticket word. 입장권 is more specifically an admission ticket for entering a venue, so KTX 표 should not be replaced with 입장권.
표.explanation: 표 (pyo) = "ticket". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: KTX 표 ("KTX ticket") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 표, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
표.shortExplanation: 표 means "ticket" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 입장권 for KTX tickets. For trains, 표 is the natural general word.
Confusing 표 with 매표소. 표 is the ticket; 매표소 is the place that sells tickets.
Forgetting the counter 장 when buying: 표 한 장 주세요.

usagePhrases.note: The ticket object in train travel.
예매하다 is the advance booking action.
매진 describes ticket or seat availability.

examples.ko: 부산 가는 KTX 표를 예매하려고 해요.
examples.romanization: busan ganeun KTX pyoreul yemaeharyeogo haeyo.
examples.en: I am trying to book a KTX ticket to Busan.
examples.note: The chapter's core ticket-counter sentence.

examples.en: Are there tickets to Busan?
examples.note: Natural availability question.

examples.en: If the tickets are sold out, check the next train.
examples.note: Ticket availability plus fallback.

ex.en: I am going to the ticket counter to book a KTX ticket.

매표소.nuance: 매표소 is the selling place for tickets. 표 is the ticket itself, and 예매하다 is the booking action.
매표소.explanation: "ticket counter / ticket office" is 매표소 (maepyoso). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 매표소에 가다 ("to go to the ticket counter"). Watch the particle attached to 매표소 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.
매표소.shortExplanation: 매표소 means "ticket counter / ticket office" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 매표소 with 표. 매표소 is the place; 표 is the ticket.
Using 에서 when only naming the destination. Say 매표소에 가요, but 매표소에서 예매해요.
Calling every service desk 매표소. It is specifically for ticket sales.

예매하다.en: to book a ticket in advance

예매하다.nuance: 예매하다 is ticket-centered and usually means the seat or ticket is secured before departure or showtime. 예약하다 is broader and can mean reserving a restaurant, hotel, appointment, or service.
예매하다.explanation: "to book or buy a ticket in advance" is 예매하다 (yemaehada). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like KTX 표를 예매하다 ("to book a KTX ticket"). Watch the particle attached to 예매하다 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.
예매하다.shortExplanation: 예매하다 means "to book or buy a ticket in advance" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 예약하다 for every ticket situation. It may be understood, but KTX/movie/concert tickets naturally use 예매하다.
Forgetting the object: 표를 예매하다, not just KTX를 예매하다 when you mean the ticket.
Confusing 예매하다 with 사다. 사다 is buy in general; 예매하다 adds advance booking.

usagePhrases.note: 표 is the object; 예매하다 is the booking action.

usagePhrases.en: I booked it in the app.
usagePhrases.note: 에서 marks where the booking action happened.

examples.romanization: busan ganeun KTX pyoreul yemaeharyeogo haeyo.
examples.en: I am trying to book a KTX ticket to Busan.
examples.note: Natural ticket-counter or app sentence.

편도.nuance: 편도 is the opposite of 왕복. It answers the ticket type question, not the destination question.
편도.explanation: 편도 (pyeondo) = "one-way ticket". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 편도 한 장 ("one one-way ticket") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 편도, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
편도.shortExplanation: 편도 means "one-way ticket" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 한쪽 for a one-way ticket. Use 편도.
Confusing 편도 with 편의점. They only sound partly similar.
Forgetting the counter when buying: 편도 한 장 주세요.

usagePhrases.note: Tickets are counted with 장.
Short counter answer.

examples.en: I will book the ticket to Busan one-way.
examples.note: 으로/로 marks ticket type here.

ex.en: If you have decided the return time too, book it round-trip.

왕복.nuance: 왕복 is the ticket-plan pair of 편도. The question 편도예요, 왕복이에요? is a normal ticket-counter question.
왕복.explanation: 왕복 (wangbok) means "round trip". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 왕복 표 ("round-trip ticket"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 왕복 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.
왕복.shortExplanation: 왕복 means "round trip" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 돌아오는 표 when the counter simply asks ticket type. 왕복 is the compact ticket word.
Confusing 왕복 with 반복. 반복 means repetition.
Buying 왕복 when your return time is not fixed can be inconvenient; 편도 may be safer.

usagePhrases.note: The return is included.
으로 marks the ticket type.

examples.en: I booked a round trip from Seoul to Busan.
examples.note: Useful when both directions are fixed.

ex.ko: KTX 표가 매진이면 다음 기차로 예매하세요.
ex.en: If the KTX tickets are sold out, book the next train.

매진.nuance: 매진 is for tickets and seats. 품절 is for products on a shelf or in an online store.
매진.explanation: "sold out for tickets or seats" is 매진 (maejin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 표가 매진이에요. ("The tickets are sold out."). Watch the particle attached to 매진 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off first, then vary one word.
매진.shortExplanation: 매진 means "sold out for tickets or seats" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 품절 for train tickets. Say 매진.
Saying 매진하다 for the customer's action. The ticket is 매진되다 or 매진이에요.
Forgetting that 매진 often needs a fallback sentence: 매진이면 다음 기차로 가요.

usagePhrases.note: Ticket availability sentence.
되다 makes the sold-out state.

examples.ko: KTX 표가 매진이면 다음 기차로 예매하세요.
examples.romanization: KTX pyoga maejinimyeon daeum gicharo yemaehaseyo.
examples.en: If the KTX tickets are sold out, book the next train.
examples.note: 매진 plus V면 creates the fallback plan.

ex.en: I was late to the appointment because of a bus delay.

지연.nuance: 지연 sounds more official than 늦다. Use 늦다 for a person being late and 지연 for a service, schedule, or system delay.
지연.explanation: 지연 (jiyeon) = "delay". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 버스 지연 ("bus delay") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 지연, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
지연.shortExplanation: 지연 means "delay" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 사람이 지연됐어요 for a person. Say 사람이 늦었어요.
Using 늦다 when the service delay is the topic. For announcements, 지연되다 is more natural.
Adding a particle before 때문에: say 버스 지연 때문에, not 버스 지연이 때문에.

usagePhrases.note: Noun compound for the cause.
지연되다 in past tense.

examples.en: I was late to the appointment because of a bus delay.
examples.note: N 때문에 names the cause.

ex.ko: 이 노선은 배차 간격이 길어서 택시로 갈게요.
ex.en: This route has a long service interval, so I will go by taxi.

배차 간격.nuance: 배차 간격 is not the travel time. It is the gap between one bus or train and the next one.
배차 간격.explanation: 배차 간격 (baecha gangyeok) means "interval between buses or trains". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 배차 간격이 길어요. ("The interval between buses or trains is long."). In Korean the particle or ending next to 배차 간격 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off, then change a single part.
배차 간격.shortExplanation: 배차 간격 means "interval between buses or trains" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 배차 간격 with 소요 시간. 소요 시간 is how long the trip takes.
Using it for one delayed vehicle. 지연 is delay; 배차 간격 is the normal interval.
Forgetting 이/가 with the measured interval: 배차 간격이 길어요.

usagePhrases.en: The interval between buses or trains is long.
usagePhrases.note: Long interval means more waiting.
Useful with transit apps.

examples.ko: 이 노선은 배차 간격이 길어서 택시로 갈게요.
examples.romanization: i noseoneun baecha gangyeogi gireoseo taeksiro galgeyo.
examples.en: This route has a long service interval, so I will go by taxi.
examples.note: Connects route information to a transport choice.

ex.en: If you miss the last train, you have to take the first train.

막차.nuance: 막차 fuses the native prefix 막- 'last/final' with 차(車) 'vehicle', literally 'the last vehicle', and it dominates Korean nightlife because the subway stops near midnight and missing it means a pricey taxi. Its exact opposite is 첫차 'first vehicle'. Two collocations are everywhere: 막차 끊기다 'the last service is cut off (gone)' and 막차 놓치다 'miss the last one'. The key pitfall is the English verb 'miss' — Korean uses 놓치다 'let slip', NEVER 잃어버리다 'lose (an object)', so 막차를 잃어버렸어요 sounds like you misplaced a train. Also note 막차 시간 is the DEPARTURE time, so a learner who reads it as an arrival time will stroll up just as the doors close.
막차.explanation: 막차 (makcha) = "last train / last bus". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 막차를 놓쳤어요. ("I missed the last train.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 막차, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about using buses, subways, taxis, and asking where to get on or off and swap just one element to make it yours.
막차.shortExplanation: 막차 means "last train / last bus" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Saying 막차를 잃어버렸어요 for missing the last train.
잃어버리다 = lose a physical object. Failing to catch a train is 놓치다. → 막차를 놓쳤어요.
Treating 막차 시간 as the arrival time.
It is the departure time of the final train. Arrive a few minutes early or you literally watch it leave.
Saying 막 차 with a space or as 마지막 차 in casual speech.
The fixed word is one token, 막차. 마지막 차 is grammatical but stilted; locals just say 막차.

usagePhrases.note: 놓치다 = to miss (let slip) a vehicle you meant to catch
means its DEPARTURE time, not arrival — leave early

usagePhrases.en: I have to catch the last train.
usagePhrases.note: 아야 하다 = obligation 'must'

usagePhrases.en: The last train is gone (service has ended).
usagePhrases.note: 끊기다 = service is cut off for the night

examples.en: What time is the last train?
examples.note: bare schedule question, the survival phrase

examples.en: Let's hurry before the last train is gone.
examples.note: 기 전에 = 'before ~'; classic end-of-night line

examples.ko: 막차 놓쳐서 결국 택시 타고 왔어요.
examples.romanization: makcha notchyeoseo gyeolguk taeksi tago wasseoyo.
examples.en: I missed the last train, so in the end I came by taxi.
examples.note: 아서 = cause→result; 결국 'in the end' adds the resignation

ex.en: I am going to a senior coworker's housewarming this weekend.

집들이.nuance: 집들이 is a pure native-Korean word (no hanja): 집 'house' + 들이 (from 들이다, 'to bring/take in'), so it literally evokes 'bringing people into the house' — the housewarming party thrown after an 이사 (移徙, moving). Don't confuse the event with the move itself: you do 이사 first (the act of relocating), THEN 집들이 (the celebration). Also distinguish it from 집들이 선물 vs a generic 선물 — the classic gifts are pointed: 휴지 (toilet paper), because it 'unrolls smoothly' (everything in the new home going smoothly), and 세제 (laundry detergent), whose bubbles symbolize prosperity 'bubbling up.' These are warm, traditional choices, not cheap ones — an English speaker may misread practical household items as an awkward gift. It's a relaxed gathering where the host usually cooks or orders in for friends.
집들이.explanation: 집들이 (jipdeuri) means "housewarming party". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 집들이를 하다 ("have a housewarming"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 집들이 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
집들이.shortExplanation: 집들이 means "housewarming party" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't read 휴지 or 세제 as a cheap or odd gift — they're traditional, well-wishing choices (smooth unrolling / bubbling prosperity), and bringing them is the thoughtful, expected move.
Don't confuse 집들이 (the party) with 이사 (the act of moving): the sequence is 이사 first, then 집들이. Saying 집들이 when you mean the move itself is wrong.
Don't take the particle 을 for attendance — you 집들이에 가다 (go TO it); 집들이를 하다 is only for the host throwing it.

usagePhrases.note: Said of the host throwing the party
Particle 에 for the event; you attend as a guest
Classic choices: 휴지 (toilet paper) and 세제 (detergent)
The host inviting friends over to the new place

examples.en: There's a housewarming this weekend.
examples.note: Basic 있다 sentence; 집들이 takes the subject marker 가

examples.ko: 집들이에 갈 때 보통 휴지나 세제를 사 가요.
examples.romanization: jipdeurie gal ttae botong hyujina sejereul sa gayo.
examples.en: When going to a housewarming, people usually buy toilet paper or detergent to bring.
examples.note: 사 가다 = 'buy and bring'; these gifts carry traditional good-luck meaning

examples.ko: 이사하고 친구들 불러서 집들이를 했는데 분위기가 정말 좋았어요.
examples.romanization: isahago chingudeul bulleoseo jipdeurireul haenneunde bunwigiga jeongmal joasseoyo.
examples.en: After moving I invited friends over for a housewarming, and the mood was really nice.
examples.note: Real situation; -는데 links the setup to the warm, casual atmosphere of the event

ex.en: People often bring toilet paper as a housewarming gift, you know.

휴지.nuance: 휴지 is the hanja word 休紙 — literally '休 rest/discard + 紙 paper,' i.e. 'paper to be used up and tossed' — and in real life it covers BOTH rolled toilet paper and the flat table tissue you wipe your mouth with; context tells you which. The contrast to learn is 휴지 vs 티슈 vs 화장지: 티슈 is the soft pop-up/pocket pack you carry, 화장지 is the more formal/printed label for toilet roll, and 휴지 is the broad everyday word. Note 휴지통 ('휴지 + bin') means the wastebasket, so don't picture only paper. The pitfall is the particle and the verb: you wipe WITH it, so 휴지로 닦다 (means 로, vowel-final), never 휴지를 닦다 (which would mean wiping the paper itself). Also 휴지 is uncountable-feeling but a torn square is 한 칸 and a roll is 한 통/한 롤.
휴지.explanation: 휴지 (hyuji) = "toilet paper". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 휴지로 닦다 ("to wipe with tissue/toilet paper") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 휴지, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.
휴지.shortExplanation: 휴지 means "toilet paper" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Don't say 휴지를 닦아요 to mean 'wipe with tissue'; the tool takes 로 — 휴지로 닦아요.
Don't equate 휴지 only with toilet paper; it also means table tissue. The pocket pack you carry is 티슈.
Don't write 휴지으로; 휴지 ends in a vowel, so it's 휴지로.

usagePhrases.note: 휴지 ends in a vowel → 로; 닦다 = to wipe clean
칸 = a partition/square; the perforated section you tear off

usagePhrases.en: to completely run out of toilet paper
usagePhrases.note: 떨어지다 = run out; the panic phrase in a stall
휴지 + 통(bin); the small trash can, often beside the toilet

examples.en: Please pass me some tissue.
examples.note: simple: 좀 softens the request; 주세요 = please give

examples.en: There's no toilet paper in the restroom.
examples.note: everyday: existence with 없다, subject 가; the stall-emergency line

examples.en: I wiped my mouth with a tissue and threw it in the trash.
examples.note: real-situation: shows 휴지 as table tissue + 휴지통 (bin) in one breath

ex.en: I bought detergent as the housewarming gift, you see.

세제.nuance: 세제 is practical rather than fancy. In 집들이 culture, practical household gifts can feel considerate because they help the new home run smoothly.
세제.explanation: 세제 (seje) = "detergent". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 세제를 사다 ("to buy detergent") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 세제, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about daily routines at home, sleep, doors, windows, and simple requests and swap just one element to make it yours.
세제.shortExplanation: 세제 means "detergent" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Confusing 세제 with 세금. 세제 is detergent; 세금 is tax.
Using it for soap in general. Soap is 비누; detergent is 세제.
Forgetting that gift role uses 로: 선물로 세제를 가져가요.

usagePhrases.note: Object marker 를.

usagePhrases.en: to bring detergent as a housewarming gift
usagePhrases.note: 선물로 marks the gift role.

examples.en: It is okay to bring detergent as a housewarming gift.
examples.note: Practical gift sentence.

ex.en: We are the same age, but at first I use polite speech.

동갑.nuance: 동갑 is useful because Korean relationships often adjust around age. Still, being 동갑 does not mean you immediately use 반말; closeness and setting matter too.
동갑.explanation: 동갑 (donggap) = "same age". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 우리 동갑이에요. ("We are the same age.") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 동갑, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about basic everyday communication and swap just one element to make it yours.
동갑.shortExplanation: 동갑 means "same age" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Assuming 동갑 means you can use 반말 immediately. Ask or wait for the other person to suggest it.
Using 친구 only because someone is the same age. 친구 implies relationship, not just age.
Forgetting final consonant pronunciation: 동갑 sounds like dong-gap, with the final ㅂ pronounced clearly before a vowel.

usagePhrases.note: Common age-discovery sentence.

usagePhrases.en: If we are the same age, can we speak casually?
usagePhrases.note: Age does not automatically remove politeness; you still check.

examples.en: If we are about the same age, can I say we are the same age?
examples.note: Socially careful age question.

ex.en: At first, I tend to call them seonbaenim.

선배.nuance: 선배 (先輩, 'earlier-generation/fellow') means someone senior to you who entered the same school, university, company, or field BEFORE you — a relationship that structures enormous amounts of Korean social life. The sharp contrast: a 선배 is defined by entering EARLIER, while a 상사 is defined by RANK — your 선배 may or may not be your boss, and your boss may not be your 선배 if they transferred in. Also distinguish 선배 from 어른 (an elder/adult by age generally). Unlike 상사, you CAN and do address a 선배 directly, adding 님 for politeness: 선배님. A 선배 traditionally looks after their 후배 (junior), often picking up the meal tab. Register: warm but respectful, deeply tied to hierarchy. The English-speaker pitfall: English has no real equivalent and learners default to 'senior' = 'boss' — but 선배 is about timing, not authority; treating every 선배 as a 상사 (or vice versa) misreads the relationship. Mark whom you learn from with 한테/에게.
선배.explanation: 선배 (seonbae) = "senior (colleague or schoolmate)". Treat it as a building block that needs a frame: 회사 선배 ("a senior at work") shows how it actually behaves. The grammar lives in the particle or ending beside 선배, so notice that piece as you read, not just the dictionary meaning. Begin from a complete sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations and swap just one element to make it yours.
선배.shortExplanation: 선배 means "senior (colleague or schoolmate)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Equating 선배 with 'boss.' A 선배 joined before you but may hold no authority; a boss with power is a 상사.
Confusing 선배 (joined before you) with 후배 (joined after you). They are mirror opposites — get the direction right.
Dropping 님 when speaking TO a senior. To their face it's 선배님; bare 선배 in direct address can sound too casual.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 (company) + 선배 — someone who joined before you, not necessarily your boss.
Add 님 to address a 선배 respectfully to their face.
한테 marks the source you learn FROM; 배우다 = learn.
대학 (university) + 선배 — an older schoolmate from the same university.

examples.en: A senior at work helped me a lot.
examples.note: 선배가 + 도와주다 (help, with benefit); past 도와줬어요.

examples.en: Senior, please show me this.
examples.note: Direct address 선배님 + 알려 주세요 (kindly tell/show me).

examples.en: I really respect that senior.
examples.note: 선배를 + 존경하다 (respect); 를 marks the object of respect.

ex.en: Even with a junior, it is good to use polite speech at first.

후배.nuance: 후배 (後輩, 'later-generation/fellow') is the mirror image of 선배: someone who entered the same school, company, or field AFTER you, regardless of their age in some cases (entry timing usually outweighs age). The contrast to keep straight is purely directional — 선배 = earlier, 후배 = later — and neither word is about workplace RANK (that's 상사 vs 부하). Within Korea's senior-junior culture, the 선배 is expected to look after the 후배: guiding them at work, answering questions, and famously treating them to meals or coffee (후배한테 밥 사 주다). Register: friendly and caring, but still hierarchy-aware. The key English-speaker pitfall is honorifics: you do NOT attach 님 to 후배 — 님 elevates seniors, so '후배님' is unnatural; you address a junior by name or with 씨. Many learners over-apply 님 to everyone out of caution, which actually misfires here. Also, don't assume a 후배 is younger or lower-ranked — they're simply LATER to the group.
후배.explanation: 후배 (hubae) means "junior (colleague or schoolmate)". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 회사 후배 ("a junior at work"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 후배 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about talking about work, schedules, tasks, and obligations, then change a single part.
후배.shortExplanation: 후배 means "junior (colleague or schoolmate)" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Adding 님 to 후배 ('후배님'). 님 honors seniors; a junior is addressed by name or with ~씨, not 님.
Mixing up 후배 (joined after you) and 선배 (joined before you). They are exact opposites — direction matters.
Assuming 후배 means 'younger.' It marks LATER entry to the group, not necessarily a younger age.

usagePhrases.note: 회사 + 후배 — someone who joined the company after you.
가르치다 = teach; seniors often guide their 후배.

usagePhrases.en: to treat a junior (buy for them)
usagePhrases.note: 한테 marks the receiver; 사 주다 = buy (for someone's benefit).
대학 + 후배 — a younger schoolmate from the same university.

examples.en: I have one junior.
examples.note: 후배가 + 한 명 (one person) + 있다; 명 is the counter for people.

examples.en: I bought my junior a coffee.
examples.note: 후배한테 + 사 주다, past 사 줬어요; the 줬 shows you did it FOR them.

examples.en: That junior is really good at their work.
examples.note: 후배는 + 일을 잘하다 (be good at work).

ex.en: What title should I use?

호칭.nuance: 호칭 is not just a word choice; it signals age, role, closeness, and respect. When unsure, asking 어떤 호칭을 쓰면 될까요? is safer than guessing too casually.
호칭.explanation: 호칭 (hoching) means "form of address / title". Learn it inside a frame, not as a bare word: a useful first chunk is 호칭을 정하다 ("to decide on a title/form of address"). In Korean the particle or ending next to 호칭 signals its job — topic, subject, object, place, time, method, or description — so read the examples for the small piece beside it. Start with one real sentence about basic everyday communication, then change a single part.
호칭.shortExplanation: 호칭 means "form of address / title" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Calling an older coworker by first name without checking. Use a title or ask first.
Using 씨 with everyone. It can be neutral, distant, or awkward depending on workplace hierarchy.
Forgetting 님 in respectful titles such as 선배님, 사장님, 교수님.

usagePhrases.en: to decide on a title/form of address
usagePhrases.note: Common after age or role is known.
Safe learner question.

examples.ko: 처음엔 선배님 같은 호칭을 쓰는 편이에요.
examples.romanization: cheoeumen seonbaenim gateun hochingeul sseuneun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: At first, people tend to use a title like seonbaenim.
examples.note: Polite title choice.

ex.en: If elders are there too, be careful with your tone.

어르신.nuance: 어르신 is respectful and warm. 어른 simply means adult or grown-up; 어르신 adds social respect for age.
어르신.explanation: "elder; older person respectfully" is 어르신 (eoreusin). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 어르신이 계세요. ("An elder is there."). Watch the particle attached to 어르신 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
어르신.shortExplanation: 어르신 means "elder; older person respectfully" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Using 어른 when you need respectful tone. 어르신 is safer for elders.
Pairing 어르신 with 있다 in polite speech. Use 계시다: 어르신이 계세요.
Using 반말 around elders just because the setting is casual.

usagePhrases.note: 계시다 is the honorific form of 있다.
께 and 여쭤보다 both add respect.

examples.en: If elders are there too, I will ask, 'May I help?'
examples.note: Respectful presence plus polite help offer.

ex.ko: 눈치 있게 챙기면 분위기가 덜 어색해요.
ex.en: If you take care of things tactfully, the mood is less awkward.

눈치.nuance: 눈치 is a native-Korean word (눈 'eye' + 치) and one of the most essential Korean social concepts: the radar for sensing what others feel and what's appropriate without being told. The distinctions learners trip on are between its set phrases: 눈치가 빠르다 ('quick eye') is high praise, 눈치가 없다 is a real social criticism, 눈치를 보다 means cautiously reading someone's mood (often a boss's, with a slightly self-conscious feel), and 눈치(를) 채다 means to catch on / notice something. So 보다 and 채다 are not interchangeable — one is ongoing wariness, the other is a moment of realization. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 눈치 to 'eyes' or vision because of 눈; it has nothing to do with eyesight and everything to do with social perceptiveness. Living in Korea you'll use and need this word daily.
눈치.explanation: "social awareness, ability to read the room" is 눈치 (nunchi). The word itself is easy; what matters is the company it keeps, like 눈치가 빠르다 ("to be quick to read situations"). Watch the particle attached to 눈치 in each example — that little marker, not the word, tells you whether it is the topic, the subject, the object, or a place. Copy one full sentence about basic everyday communication first, then vary one word.
눈치.shortExplanation: 눈치 means "social awareness, ability to read the room" and is learned through practical beginner sentence frames.
commonMistakes: Do not memorize this only as an English translation; memorize one Korean sentence frame.
Translating it as 'eyes' or eyesight because of 눈 — 눈치 is the social skill of reading people, not vision
Confusing 눈치를 보다 (cautiously read someone's mood) with 눈치를 채다 (notice/catch on to something)
Saying 눈치가 좋다 for 'quick-witted' — the set phrase is 눈치가 빠르다; 좋다 sounds off here

usagePhrases.en: to be quick to read situations
usagePhrases.note: 빠르다 (fast) is the highest compliment — your social radar is sharp
없다 (lacking) = can't read the room at all; a genuine criticism

usagePhrases.en: to read someone's mood / walk on eggshells
usagePhrases.note: 보다 (watch) = checking how others feel, often a superior, before acting
채다 = to catch (on); 눈치챘어 = I noticed / I figured it out

examples.en: He's really quick to pick up on things.
examples.note: 눈치 빠르다 drops 가 in casual speech; the go-to banmal compliment for social sharpness

examples.ko: 저는 눈치가 없어서 분위기를 잘 못 읽어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun nunchiga eopseoseo bunwigireul jal mot ilgeoyo.
examples.en: I'm a bit clueless, so I don't read the mood well.
examples.note: 분위기를 읽다 = read the atmosphere; a humble self-description in polite speech

examples.ko: 사장님 눈치 보느라 일찍 못 가요.
examples.romanization: sajangnim nunchi boneura iljjing mot gayo.
examples.en: I can't leave early because I'm watching the boss's mood.
examples.note: -느라 = on account of (doing); 눈치 보다 toward a superior is classic office reality
